questions.f: A managed package namespace prefix can be up to 40 alphanumeric characters, must start with a letter and can't contain two consecutive underscores.
questions.x: Namespace prefixes are globally unique and capped at 15 alphanumeric characters with the letter and underscore rules. 40 characters is far above the allowed length.

questions.t: A 1GP packaging org can own only one managed package, so global Apex is the only way to share code across a partner's 1GP packages.
questions.f: A 1GP packaging org can own several managed packages, so they can share one namespace and call each other's public Apex.
questions.x: In 1GP each packaging org owns one package and each namespace maps to one package, so cross-package code sharing has to go through global Apex. Sharing a namespace across packages is a 2GP capability.

questions.t: A 1GP patch version can't add or delete components; that kind of change needs a new major or minor version.
questions.f: A 1GP patch version can add new components but can't delete them; only deletions need a new major or minor version.
questions.x: Patches are deliberately narrow: they can't add or delete components, add global modifiers, new web services or new dependencies. Adding a component therefore requires a major or minor release, not a patch.

questions.t: A package dependency version such as 1.3.0.LATEST fixes the major, minor and patch numbers and picks up only the newest build.
questions.f: A package dependency version such as 1.3.0.LATEST fixes only the major number and picks up the newest minor, patch and build.
questions.x: LATEST applies only to the build segment, so moving to a new base release means editing the specifier. It does not float the minor or patch numbers.

questions.t: The sf package version displaydependencies command outputs a package version's dependency graph as GraphViz DOT code.
questions.f: The sf package version displaydependencies command outputs a package version's dependency graph as a Mermaid diagram.
questions.x: With calculateTransitiveDependencies enabled, displaydependencies emits GraphViz DOT, optionally ordered root-last and labelled with 04t IDs. It does not produce Mermaid syntax.

questions.t: Salesforce's dependency support matrix lets an unlocked package depend on managed 1GP, managed 2GP and other unlocked packages.
questions.f: Salesforce's dependency support matrix lets an unlocked package depend only on other unlocked packages, not on managed ones.
questions.x: The matrix allows unlocked packages to depend on first-generation managed, second-generation managed and unlocked packages. Restricting them to unlocked-only is wrong; it is managed 2GP depending on unlocked that is marked not recommended.

questions.t: A default transaction security policy requires step-up authentication for UI report exports of more than 10,000 records.
questions.f: A default transaction security policy requires step-up authentication for UI report exports of more than 1,000 records.
questions.x: Salesforce's default guardrail against post-takeover exfiltration kicks in above 10,000 exported records. A 1,000-record threshold understates it by a factor of ten.

questions.t: When Salesforce knows an account is compromised, the user must pass an identity challenge and reset the password before getting back in.
questions.f: When Salesforce knows an account is compromised, the user must wait for an administrator to unfreeze the account before getting back in.
questions.x: Salesforce's remediation is self-service: an identity challenge followed by a password reset. It does not depend on an admin manually unfreezing the account.

questions.t: Where phishing-resistant MFA isn't feasible yet, CISA recommends number matching to counter MFA push-bombing.
questions.f: Where phishing-resistant MFA isn't feasible yet, CISA recommends SMS one-time codes to counter MFA push-bombing.
questions.x: CISA's interim fix for push-bombing is number matching, which makes the user confirm a code shown at login. FIDO/WebAuthn remains the phishing-resistant goal; SMS codes are not the recommended answer.

questions.t: The Step-Up Authentication Period setting makes users re-verify after a set number of minutes, up to a maximum of two hours.
questions.f: The Step-Up Authentication Period setting makes users re-verify after a set number of minutes, up to a maximum of 24 hours.
questions.x: Step-up policies can force periodic re-verification, but the period tops out at two hours. A 24-hour ceiling overstates the limit.

questions.t: Session security level policies can require High Assurance for Manage Users, but they cannot block access to it.
questions.f: Session security level policies can block access to Manage Users, but they cannot require High Assurance for it.
questions.x: Manage Users and Manage Permission Sets and Profiles accept a step-up requirement but have no Block option, unlike other protected setup areas. The false version reverses which option exists.

questions.t: A connected app that requires a High Assurance session blocks JWT bearer flow logins, because only OAuth flows with a user approval step can meet it.
questions.f: A connected app that requires a High Assurance session blocks web server flow logins, because only OAuth flows without a user approval step can meet it.
questions.x: Raising a session to High Assurance needs an interactive approval step, which the web server, user-agent and refresh token flows have. Server-to-server flows such as JWT bearer lack it and are blocked.

questions.t: Users on the Salesforce Integration user license are API-only, and that API-only setting cannot be turned off.
questions.f: Users on the Salesforce Integration user license are API-only by default, but an admin can turn that setting off to allow UI access.
questions.x: The license provisions the Minimum Access - API Only Integrations profile, and its API-only restriction is fixed. Object and field access is then granted with permission sets.

questions.t: API Access Control, which blocks API access except through admin-approved connected apps, is turned on by request to Salesforce Customer Support.
questions.f: API Access Control, which blocks API access except through admin-approved connected apps, is turned on by an admin from Setup.
questions.x: API Access Control is not self-service; an org has to ask Customer Support to enable it. Because it can cut off unlisted integrations, clients should be inventoried first.

questions.t: Salesforce Well-Architected calls for a separate API-only user per integration, and lists one shared integration user for several systems as an anti-pattern.
questions.f: Salesforce Well-Architected calls for one shared API-only user across integrations, and lists a separate integration user per system as an anti-pattern.
questions.x: A dedicated user per integration keeps each one's permissions narrow and its activity traceable. A single shared API user, especially with Modify All Data, is the named anti-pattern.

questions.t: App Deployment is the lightest section of the Platform App Builder exam outline, at 10% of the exam.
questions.f: User Interface is the lightest section of the Platform App Builder exam outline, at 10% of the exam.
questions.x: The published outline weights App Deployment at 10%, the smallest share. User Interface carries 17%, so it is not the lightest section.

questions.t: A training provider's summary lists the Platform App Builder exam as 60 scored questions with a 63% passing score.
questions.f: A training provider's summary lists the Platform App Builder exam as 60 scored questions with a 75% passing score.
questions.x: Global Knowledge summarises the exam as 60 scored multiple-choice questions with a 63% pass mark, to be confirmed against the official exam guide. 75% is not the stated threshold.

questions.t: Trailhead's prep module expects Platform App Builder candidates to have about six months of experience building on the Salesforce Platform.
questions.f: Trailhead's prep module expects Platform App Builder candidates to have about two years of experience building on the Salesforce Platform.
questions.x: The official prep module sets roughly six months of experience with platform capabilities, licensing, app design and deployment options. Two years overstates the expected background.

questions.t: In NIST CSF 2.0, cybersecurity supply chain risk management sits under the Govern Function as GV.SC.
questions.f: In NIST CSF 2.0, cybersecurity supply chain risk management sits under the Identify Function as ID.SC.
questions.x: CSF 2.0 places supply chain risk management in Govern, as GV.SC with ten Subcategories. It is not filed under Identify.

questions.t: A CSF Target Profile holds the outcomes an organization has selected and prioritized, while a Current Profile records outcomes it already achieves.
questions.f: A CSF Current Profile holds the outcomes an organization has selected and prioritized, while a Target Profile records outcomes it already achieves.
questions.x: The Current Profile describes what is being achieved today and how well; the Target Profile describes the prioritized outcomes the organization is aiming for. The false statement swaps them.

questions.t: NIST says organizations should move to a higher CSF Tier only when risk, mandates or cost-benefit justify it, not treat Tiers as maturity levels to chase.
questions.f: NIST says organizations should move to the Adaptive CSF Tier in every case, treating Tiers as maturity levels to chase.
questions.x: The Tiers (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive) describe rigor, and NIST advises progressing only when justified. Reaching Adaptive is not a universal goal.

questions.t: A SOC 2 Type 2 report tests whether controls operated effectively over a period, while a Type 1 assesses their design as of a single date.
questions.f: A SOC 2 Type 1 report tests whether controls operated effectively over a period, while a Type 2 assesses their design as of a single date.
questions.x: Type 1 is a point-in-time look at control design; Type 2 covers a period, often six to twelve months, and adds operating-effectiveness testing. The false statement swaps the types.

questions.t: A SOC 3 report is a general-use summary without detailed control tests and can be shared freely, unlike a SOC 2 report.
questions.f: A SOC 2 report is a general-use summary without detailed control tests and can be shared freely, unlike a SOC 3 report.
questions.x: SOC 2 reports are meant for knowledgeable readers and include control descriptions, tests and results. SOC 3 leaves those out so it can be distributed freely.

questions.t: Salesforce describes its SOC 2 reports as covering security, availability and confidentiality, without naming processing integrity or privacy.
questions.f: Salesforce describes its SOC 2 reports as covering security, availability and privacy, without naming processing integrity or confidentiality.
questions.x: Salesforce's compliance site lists security, availability and confidentiality for its SOC 2 reports. Privacy and processing integrity are the two trust services categories it does not name.

questions.t: A Salesforce Health Check score reflects org security settings, so it would not reveal an over-scoped integration token.
questions.f: A Salesforce Health Check score includes connected app token scopes, so it would reveal an over-scoped integration token.
questions.x: Health Check measures configuration settings against a baseline, not people or third-party apps. An integration token with excessive scope sits outside what it scores.

questions.t: The August 2025 Salesloft Drift data theft used stolen OAuth tokens from that integration, not a flaw in core Salesforce.
questions.f: The August 2025 Salesloft Drift data theft exploited a flaw in the core Salesforce API, not stolen tokens from that integration.
questions.x: Google's threat intelligence team found the attacker queried orgs with stolen Drift OAuth tokens and said core Salesforce was not at fault. Blaming a platform flaw gets the attack vector wrong.

questions.t: Salesforce calls MFA, permission sets and login IP restrictions customer 'configurables', and paid add-ons such as Shield 'enhanceables'.
questions.f: Salesforce calls Shield and Security Center customer 'configurables', and MFA, permission sets and login IP restrictions paid 'enhanceables'.
questions.x: In Salesforce's shared responsibility framing, configurables are the built-in settings customers must set up, while enhanceables are paid products layered on top. The false version swaps the two groups.

questions.t: Without Shield, Enterprise, Unlimited and Performance Editions get seven Event Monitoring log types free, each kept for one day.
questions.f: Without Shield, Enterprise, Unlimited and Performance Editions get seven Event Monitoring log types free, each kept for 30 days.
questions.x: The free tier covers seven log types, such as Login and Logout, with only one-day retention. Longer retention and the other log types need Shield or the Event Monitoring add-on.

questions.t: Only daily event log files integrate with the Event Monitoring Analytics app; hourly files must be imported into visualization tools by hand.
questions.f: Only hourly event log files integrate with the Event Monitoring Analytics app; daily files must be imported into visualization tools by hand.
questions.x: The Event Monitoring Analytics app consumes the daily files, which are also the complete record for a date. Hourly files can be incomplete and need manual import.

questions.t: Event log objects can be queried with SOQL roughly 25 to 45 minutes after an event, and they keep the data for 30 days.
questions.f: Event log objects can be queried with SOQL roughly 25 to 45 minutes after an event, and they keep the data for one year.
questions.x: The event log object channel holds its data for 30 days and requires the View Event Log Object Data permission. The one-year default is for paid event log files, not these objects.

questions.t: Declaring an Apex class with sharing enforces record sharing for its queries, but it does not enforce field-level security.
questions.f: Declaring an Apex class with sharing enforces field-level security for its queries, but it does not enforce record sharing.
questions.x: The with sharing keyword controls which records the code can see; field access still needs user mode, stripInaccessible or describe checks. The false statement swaps the two layers.

questions.t: If a permission set grants View All Fields on an object, the FieldPermissions object reports PermissionsRead as true for every field on it.
questions.f: If a permission set grants View All Fields on an object, the FieldPermissions object reports PermissionsEdit as true for every field on it.
questions.x: View All Fields overrides per-field settings for reading, so PermissionsRead shows true across the object. It is a read grant and does not make every field editable.

questions.t: Field-level security on formula and auto-number fields can grant only Read access, since those fields can't be edited.
questions.f: Field-level security on formula and auto-number fields can grant only Edit access, since those fields can't be hidden.
questions.x: Formula and auto-number fields accept only the Read field permission, because their values aren't entered by users. The false statement invents an Edit-only rule that the platform doesn't have.

questions.t: A permission set with Session Activation Required grants its permissions only while a session is activated for it, and they lapse at logout or timeout.
questions.f: A permission set with Session Activation Required grants its permissions from the user's next login, and they last until the assignment is removed.
questions.x: Session-based permission sets tie access to an activated session, so the permissions end when the session ends through logout, timeout or an admin. The false statement describes an ordinary standing assignment.

questions.t: Leave a permission set's LicenseId empty when the set will be assigned to users on different license types.
questions.f: Set a permission set's LicenseId to one user license when the set will be assigned to users on different license types.
questions.x: A permission set tied to a license is meant for users on that license, so a set shared across license types should leave LicenseId blank. Setting a specific license fits only sets used by one license type or drawing on a permission set license.

questions.t: A permission set assignment with an expiration date ends at 11:59 PM on that date in the time zone chosen for it.
questions.f: A permission set assignment with an expiration date ends at 12:00 AM at the start of that date in the time zone chosen for it.
questions.x: With assignment expiration enabled, access runs through the whole end date and expires at 11:59 PM in the selected time zone. It does not end at the very start of that day.

questions.t: In Salesforce's permission-set-led model, the Minimum Access - Salesforce profile is the baseline, with access added through permission sets.
questions.f: In Salesforce's permission-set-led model, the Standard User profile is the baseline, with access added through permission sets.
questions.x: Trailhead recommends Minimum Access - Salesforce, or a clone, because it grants very few permissions. Standard profiles can grant more than users need and their object permissions can't be edited.

questions.t: A permission granted by both a user's profile and a permission set stays in effect until it is removed from both.
questions.f: A permission granted by both a user's profile and a permission set is revoked once it is removed from the profile.
questions.x: Access is the union of every source, so taking a permission off the profile leaves the permission set's grant in place. It has to be removed in both places.

questions.t: Trailhead's least-privilege guidance for agents and integrations says to start read-only and add write access only after testing and approval.
questions.f: Trailhead's least-privilege guidance for agents and integrations says to start with edit access and remove what goes unused after testing.
questions.x: The guidance favours starting read-only, returning only required data, and adding write access once the read-only design is tested and approved. Starting broad and trimming later is the opposite approach.

questions.t: Contact Manager and Group Editions can only assign standard profiles, while Professional Edition and above can create custom profiles.
questions.f: Professional Edition can only assign standard profiles, while Contact Manager and Group Editions and above can create custom profiles.
questions.x: Custom profiles are available in Professional, Enterprise, Unlimited, Performance and Developer Editions. Contact Manager and Group Editions are the ones limited to the standard profiles, so the false statement reverses the editions.

questions.t: The permissions on a standard profile can't be edited, though admins can still change its session settings and password policies.
questions.f: The session settings and password policies on a standard profile can't be edited, though admins can still change its permissions.
questions.x: Standard profiles lock their permissions, but a few settings such as custom app and tab settings, session settings and password policies stay editable. The false statement swaps which part is locked.

questions.t: Moving a user to a profile on a different license type frees a seat in the old license pool and uses one in the new pool.
questions.f: Moving a user to a profile on a different license type keeps the seat in the old license pool and adds one in the new pool.
questions.x: A profile is bound to a user license, so switching to a profile on another license type moves the user's seat from one pool to the other. The old seat is released rather than held alongside the new one.

questions.t: In Lightning Experience, the MFA action on a List View or Report Event transaction security policy isn't supported and is upgraded to Block.
questions.f: In Lightning Experience, the MFA action on a List View or Report Event transaction security policy isn't supported and is downgraded to Notify.
questions.x: Salesforce replaces the unsupported MFA action with the stricter Block action for these events in Lightning. It does not fall back to a notification, which would stop nothing.

questions.t: In a transaction security Apex condition, evaluate() returning true fires the policy's action, while returning false lets the user proceed.
questions.f: In a transaction security Apex condition, evaluate() returning false fires the policy's action, while returning true lets the user proceed.
questions.x: A class implementing TxnSecurity.EventCondition signals a match by returning true, which triggers the block, MFA or notification. The false version inverts the return values.

questions.t: New transaction security policies are created disabled and are switched on with the Status toggle on the Actions tab.
questions.f: New transaction security policies are created enabled and are switched off with the Status toggle on the Actions tab.
questions.x: A freshly created policy starts inactive, so it does nothing until an author with Modify Transaction Security Policies turns it on. It is not live on save.

questions.t: Once an architecture decision record is accepted it is not edited; a changed decision gets a new ADR that supersedes and links to the old one.
questions.f: Once an architecture decision record is accepted it is edited in place when the decision changes, and its status is updated to show the revision.
questions.x: ADRs form an append-only log: accepted records stay as written and a new record supersedes them, so the log shows how long each decision governed the work. Editing in place would erase that history.

questions.t: Michael Nygard's 2011 ADR template has five parts: a title, the context, the decision, a status and the consequences.
questions.f: Michael Nygard's 2011 ADR template has five parts: a title, the context, the options considered, the decision and the consequences.
questions.x: Nygard's original template lists title, context, decision, status and consequences. Recording the serious alternatives with their pros and cons was added by later guidance, not part of his five sections.

questions.t: Salesforce Architects' sample ADR on single-org versus multi-org scores the options against the Well-Architected pillars Trusted, Easy and Adaptable.
questions.f: Salesforce Architects' sample ADR on single-org versus multi-org scores the options against a generic list of cost, time and risk.
questions.x: The Salesforce blog example deliberately grounds its evaluation in the Well-Architected pillars rather than generic pros and cons, weighing factors like sharing, limits, licensing and deployment pipelines under each.

questions.t: In Salesforce Diagrams, the Marketing, Strategy & Sales style explains why a team is doing something, while Documentation & Implementation explains how.
questions.f: In Salesforce Diagrams, the Documentation & Implementation style explains why a team is doing something, while Marketing, Strategy & Sales explains how.
questions.x: Marketing, Strategy & Sales diagrams show capabilities and products that deliver business value, the why. Documentation & Implementation diagrams give an implementation-ready view of the solution, the how.

questions.t: In the Documentation & Implementation style, Level 2 diagrams show integration points and data-flow direction, but time-based sequencing is kept for Level 3.
questions.f: In the Documentation & Implementation style, Level 2 diagrams show integration points and data-flow direction, and time-based sequencing is kept for Level 4.
questions.x: Level 3 is the process or interaction view that adds sequenced steps and data flows. Level 4 is the narrower double-click into one part of a process for fine-grained technical detail.

questions.t: The Reference Architecture Gallery has examples of every Salesforce Diagrams type except data models, which sit in a separate Data Model Gallery on developer.salesforce.com.
questions.f: The Reference Architecture Gallery has examples of every Salesforce Diagrams type except roadmaps, which sit in a separate Roadmap Gallery on developer.salesforce.com.
questions.x: Data models are the one diagram type kept out of the Reference Architecture Gallery; they live in the Data Model Gallery on developer.salesforce.com. Roadmaps are included in the main gallery.

questions.t: When an orchestration work item is assigned to a queue, the first member to finish its screen flow completes it and it disappears for the others.
questions.f: When an orchestration work item is assigned to a queue, every member must finish its screen flow before it is marked complete.
questions.x: Group and queue work items are first-come, first-served: one completion closes the item and a simultaneous second submission errors. No requirement exists for all members to complete it.

questions.t: Orchestration work items assigned to a public group are owned by the automated process user rather than by any group member.
questions.f: Orchestration work items assigned to a public group are owned by the group member who was added to the group first.
questions.x: Only items assigned directly to a user are owned by that user; group items, and queue items whose queue isn't tied to the work item object, belong to the automated process user.

questions.t: Configuration changes to the Experience Builder Orchestration Work Guide component show only on the live site, not in the Builder preview.
questions.f: Configuration changes to the Experience Builder Orchestration Work Guide component show only in the Builder preview, not on the live site.
questions.x: Salesforce notes that this component's settings don't render in Experience Builder's preview, so admins must check the live site. The false version inverts where the changes appear.

questions.t: A flow that contains a Wait element can't be referenced by a Subflow element in another flow.
questions.f: A flow that contains a Loop element can't be referenced by a Subflow element in another flow.
questions.x: Salesforce Help excludes flows with a Wait element from being called as subflows. Loop elements carry no such restriction.

questions.t: Subflow input and output variables with API names longer than 40 characters cause a save error in the calling flow.
questions.f: Subflow input and output variables with API names longer than 80 characters cause a save error in the calling flow.
questions.x: The cutoff that breaks saving the parent flow is 40 characters for the child's input and output variable API names, so names between 41 and 80 characters would already fail.

questions.t: If a referenced subflow has no active version, the call succeeds only for flow admins and fails at runtime for other users.
questions.f: If a referenced subflow has no active version, the call succeeds for all users by running its latest saved version.
questions.x: Falling back to an inactive latest version only works when a flow admin runs the parent. For ordinary users the subflow call fails at runtime, so the child must be activated.

questions.t: A Lightning web component appears in Experience Builder's drag-and-drop Components panel when its js-meta.xml declares the lightningCommunity__Page target.
questions.f: A Lightning web component appears in Experience Builder's drag-and-drop Components panel when its js-meta.xml declares the lightningCommunity__Theme_Layout target.
questions.x: The lightningCommunity__Page target puts an exposed component in the Components panel. Theme_Layout instead makes it a theme layout for LWR sites, not a draggable component.

questions.t: Once a Lightning web component is placed on an Experience Cloud site, you can't add a new required property to it.
questions.f: Once a Lightning web component is placed on an Experience Cloud site, you can add new required properties but can't add optional ones.
questions.x: After a component is in use on a site or in a managed package, adding a required property, removing one or tightening min and max is blocked. The false version flips which change is restricted.

questions.t: New Experience Cloud sites default to strict Content Security Policy, so components calling third-party hosts need those hosts allowlisted.
questions.f: New Experience Cloud sites default to relaxed Content Security Policy, so components can call any third-party host without allowlisting.
questions.x: Strict CSP is the default for new sites. To reach outside hosts, admins adjust the security level and add the hosts to the allowlist; nothing is open by default.

questions.t: A single SOAP API convertLead() call accepts at most 100 LeadConvert objects.
questions.f: A single SOAP API convertLead() call accepts at most 200 LeadConvert objects.
questions.x: The SOAP API caps each convertLead() call at 100 LeadConvert objects, so larger volumes must be split into more calls. 200 is double the documented limit.

questions.t: During lead conversion, standard lead fields map to account, contact and opportunity fields automatically, but custom lead fields need an admin-defined mapping.
questions.f: During lead conversion, both standard and custom lead fields map to account, contact and opportunity fields automatically, with no admin mapping needed.
questions.x: Only standard fields carry over by default. Without a mapping set up by an administrator, custom lead field values stay behind on the converted lead.

questions.t: When a lead is converted into an existing contact, only the contact's empty fields are filled from the lead; existing values are kept.
questions.f: When a lead is converted into an existing contact, all of the contact's fields are overwritten with the lead's values.
questions.x: Merging into existing records fills blanks and preserves current values, IDs included. The only overwrite offered is the option to replace the contact's Lead Source.

questions.t: Under the Customer Data Platform license, one Data 360 unified profile can merge up to 50,000 source profiles.
questions.f: Under the Customer Data Platform license, one Data 360 unified profile can merge up to 5,000 source profiles.
questions.x: The identity resolution limits table caps a single unified profile at 50,000 merged source profiles. The 5,000 figure is ten times too low; 5,000 is the ceiling for data streams, not merged profiles.

questions.t: In streaming mode, the Data 360 Ingestion API accepts request bodies of up to 200 KB.
questions.f: In streaming mode, the Data 360 Ingestion API accepts request bodies of up to 2 MB.
questions.x: Streaming ingestion is meant for small, frequent payloads, so each request body is limited to 200 KB. Larger loads belong in bulk mode, which takes CSV files of up to 150 MB.

questions.t: Rows returned by a Data 360 Query API query can be re-read for 24 hours without incurring further consumption charges.
questions.f: Rows returned by a Data 360 Query API query can be re-read for 1 hour without incurring further consumption charges.
questions.x: The Query API guide keeps results available for 24 hours, so paging through stored rows is cheaper than running the query again. One hour understates that window.

questions.t: In a Data 360 segment, criteria in one container must match on the same related record, while separate containers are evaluated independently.
questions.f: In a Data 360 segment, criteria in one container are evaluated independently, while criteria in separate containers must match on the same related record.
questions.x: A single container ties its criteria to one related record, so 'scarf AND yellow' there finds yellow-scarf buyers. Splitting them across containers lets each criterion match a different purchase; the false statement reverses this.

questions.t: A Data 360 waterfall segment places each person in the first of its ordered segments that they match, making the buckets mutually exclusive.
questions.f: A Data 360 waterfall segment places each person in the last of its ordered segments that they match, making the buckets mutually exclusive.
questions.x: Waterfalls evaluate their segments in order and stop at the first match, which is how each customer gets only the best offer they qualify for. It is the first match that wins, not the last.

questions.t: Data 360 rapid publish segments refresh every 1 or 4 hours and look only at the past 7 days of engagement data.
questions.f: Data 360 rapid publish segments refresh every 12 or 24 hours and look only at the past 7 days of engagement data.
questions.x: Rapid publish trades a short 7-day lookback for frequent refreshes every 1 or 4 hours. Schedules such as every 12 or 24 hours belong to standard segments.

questions.t: A Data 360 data lake object in the Engagement category requires an event time field recording when the engagement happened, which must not change.
questions.f: A Data 360 data lake object in the Profile category requires an event time field recording when the engagement happened, which must not change.
questions.x: The event time field is mandatory for Engagement data, which is time-stamped behaviour such as web visits. Profile DLOs hold demographic and contact data keyed by a unique ID and use a record modified field instead.

questions.t: On Profile and Other data lake objects, the record modified field tells Data 360 which version of a record is newest when data arrives out of order.
questions.f: On Profile and Other data lake objects, the primary key field tells Data 360 which version of a record is newest when data arrives out of order.
questions.x: The record modified field carries the timestamp used to keep the latest version when records arrive out of sequence. The primary key only identifies which record it is, not which version is newer.

questions.t: A Data 360 data lake object API name can be up to 40 characters long and can't contain two consecutive underscores.
questions.f: A Data 360 data lake object API name can be up to 80 characters long and can't contain two consecutive underscores.
questions.x: DLO API names are limited to 40 characters of letters, digits and underscores, must start with a letter and can't use double underscores. The 80-character figure doubles the real limit.

questions.t: A deleted custom field and its data are kept for up to 15 days, counting against the object's field allocation until hard-deleted.
questions.f: A deleted custom field and its data are kept for up to 30 days, counting against the object's field allocation until hard-deleted.
questions.x: Deleted fields linger for up to 15 days so they can be restored, and they still consume allocation in the meantime. Thirty days is the wrong retention window; Erase or Purge starts the hard delete sooner.

questions.t: A custom address field uses nine custom fields from an object's allocation, while a geolocation field uses three.
questions.f: A custom address field uses three custom fields from an object's allocation, while a geolocation field uses nine.
questions.x: Compound fields count more than once against the per-object limit: geolocation counts as three and a custom address as nine. The false statement swaps the two figures.

questions.t: All long and rich text area fields on one object share a combined budget of 1,638,400 characters.
questions.f: All long and rich text area fields on one object share a combined budget of 131,072 characters.
questions.x: There's no count limit on long and rich text fields, but together they can't exceed 1,638,400 characters per object. 131,072 is the maximum length of a single such field, not the shared budget.

questions.t: In Salesforce Duplicate Management, an object can have up to 5 active matching rules.
questions.f: In Salesforce Duplicate Management, an object can have up to 3 active matching rules.
questions.x: Each object allows five active matching rules. Three is the number of matching rules a single duplicate rule can reference, which is a different limit.

questions.t: A duplicate rule set to BypassSharingRules still catches duplicates the saving user can't see.
questions.f: A duplicate rule set to EnforceSharingRules still catches duplicates the saving user can't see.
questions.x: BypassSharingRules ignores sharing when matching, so hidden duplicates are still detected. EnforceSharingRules respects sharing, so a duplicate invisible to the user won't block or flag their save.

questions.t: Datacloud.FindDuplicates.findDuplicates() accepts at most 50 unsaved records per call, all of the same object type.
questions.f: Datacloud.FindDuplicates.findDuplicates() accepts at most 200 unsaved records per call, all of the same object type.
questions.x: The Apex method checks records against active duplicate rules in batches of up to 50 records of one object. 200 overstates the batch size.

questions.t: In Apex Enterprise Patterns, triggers are not listed as service layer callers because trigger logic belongs in the Domain layer.
questions.f: In Apex Enterprise Patterns, triggers are not listed as service layer callers because trigger logic belongs in the Selector layer.
questions.x: Object-specific behaviour such as validation and defaulting on insert or update lives in Domain classes, which is where trigger logic goes. Selectors only centralise SOQL queries.

questions.t: In Apex Enterprise Patterns, a service runs with sharing by default and elevates access only inside a private without sharing inner class.
questions.f: In Apex Enterprise Patterns, a service runs without sharing by default and enforces access only inside a private with sharing inner class.
questions.x: Service classes default to enforcing sharing and confine any elevated access to a private without sharing inner class. The false statement inverts that default.

questions.t: When one service calls another in Apex Enterprise Patterns, the outer Unit of Work is passed in rather than the inner service creating its own.
questions.f: When one service calls another in Apex Enterprise Patterns, the inner service creates and commits its own Unit of Work rather than receiving the outer one.
questions.x: commitWork should run once per scope, so a nested service reuses the caller's Unit of Work. A second Unit of Work would split the DML into separate commits.

questions.t: For hierarchy custom settings, getInstance merges fields across the hierarchy, while getValues returns only what is stored at that exact level.
questions.f: For hierarchy custom settings, getValues merges fields across the hierarchy, while getInstance returns only what is stored at that exact level.
questions.x: getInstance takes each field from the lowest level where it is defined, giving the effective values. getValues leaves fields not defined at that level null; the false statement swaps the methods.

questions.t: In a hierarchy custom setting, user-level values override profile-level values, which override the organization default.
questions.f: In a hierarchy custom setting, profile-level values override user-level values, which override the organization default.
questions.x: The most specific defined value wins: user beats profile, and profile beats the org default. Ranking profile above user reverses the hierarchy.

questions.t: Reading a custom setting with its Apex methods uses the application cache, while querying it with SOQL bypasses the cache.
questions.f: Querying a custom setting with SOQL uses the application cache, while reading it with its Apex methods bypasses the cache.
questions.x: The caching benefit comes from the custom settings methods such as getInstance. A SOQL query on a setting skips the cache and counts like any other query.

questions.t: Trailhead lists a security review fee of $999 per paid solution, charged on the first submission and again on each resubmission after a failure.
questions.f: Trailhead lists a security review fee of $999 per paid solution, charged only once on the first submission, with resubmissions free.
questions.x: Paid solutions pay $999 for the initial review and pay it again every time they resubmit after failing. Free solutions don't pay; resubmissions of paid ones are not free.

questions.t: A package submitted for AgentExchange security review must be Managed-Released, so beta and unmanaged packages are rejected.
questions.f: A package submitted for AgentExchange security review must be at least Managed-Beta, so only unmanaged packages are rejected.
questions.x: Only Managed-Released packages are accepted for review. Beta versions are turned away just like unmanaged packages.

questions.t: Solutions that passed the AgentExchange security review are typically re-reviewed about once a year.
questions.f: Solutions that passed the AgentExchange security review are typically re-reviewed about once every three years.
questions.x: Approval isn't permanent: Salesforce re-reviews listed solutions roughly annually and can ask for a review at any time. Three years overstates the interval.

questions.t: A namespace for 2GP packaging is created in a separate Developer Edition org and then linked to the Dev Hub through the Namespace Registries app.
questions.f: A namespace for 2GP packaging is created directly in the Dev Hub org and then registered there through the Namespace Registries app.
questions.x: Namespaces aren't created in the Dev Hub: you register one in its own Developer Edition org, then use Link Namespace in the Dev Hub's Namespace Registries app to connect it.

questions.t: Packages in one namespace expose public Apex to each other with the @namespaceAccessible annotation, while global Apex is visible across namespaces.
questions.f: Packages in one namespace expose public Apex to each other with the @TestVisible annotation, while global Apex is visible across namespaces.
questions.x: @namespaceAccessible makes public Apex usable by sibling packages sharing a namespace. @TestVisible is about exposing members to test classes, not to other packages.

questions.t: Salesforce prefers namespaced scratch orgs for package development, using the --no-namespace flag mainly to test an installed package.
questions.f: Salesforce prefers scratch orgs created with --no-namespace for package development, using namespaced ones mainly to test an installed package.
questions.x: Scratch orgs inherit the project namespace so new metadata gets the package prefix, which is the preferred development setup. The --no-namespace flag is for testing an installed package; the false statement swaps the roles.

questions.t: Standard SAML just-in-time provisioning requires the Email, LastName, ProfileId and Username attributes to create a user.
questions.f: Standard SAML just-in-time provisioning requires the Email, FirstName, ProfileId and Username attributes to create a user.
questions.x: The required User attributes for standard JIT are Email, LastName, ProfileId and Username. FirstName is optional, like Role or Department.

questions.t: For external users, SAML just-in-time provisioning matches accounts on Account.AccountNumber and contacts on Contact.Email.
questions.f: For external users, SAML just-in-time provisioning matches accounts on Account.Name and contacts on Contact.Email.
questions.x: Account lookup uses the account number and contact lookup uses email, with multiple matches treated as an error. Account name isn't the matching key.

questions.t: Custom SAML just-in-time provisioning uses an Apex class that implements the Auth.SamlJitHandler interface.
questions.f: Custom SAML just-in-time provisioning uses an Apex class that implements the Auth.RegistrationHandler interface.
questions.x: The generated SAML JIT handler implements Auth.SamlJitHandler with createUser and updateUser methods. A registration handler is the OpenID Connect counterpart used by authentication providers.

questions.t: A login from outside an org's trusted IP ranges can succeed after an identity challenge, but a login outside a profile's login IP ranges is denied.
questions.f: A login from outside a profile's login IP ranges can succeed after an identity challenge, but a login outside an org's trusted IP ranges is denied.
questions.x: Trusted IP ranges only skip the verification challenge, while profile login IP ranges are a hard allowlist with no fallback. The false statement swaps the two controls.

questions.t: SAML bearer assertion and JWT bearer flows always enforce profile IP restrictions, whatever a connected app's IP relaxation policy says.
questions.f: SAML bearer assertion and JWT bearer flows always skip profile IP restrictions, whatever a connected app's IP relaxation policy says.
questions.x: These server-to-server flows ignore IP relaxation and always apply the profile's ranges, which matters when an integration's egress IPs change.

questions.t: Since Winter '26, a single trusted IP range can cover at most 16,777,216 IPv4 addresses.
questions.f: Since Winter '26, a single trusted IP range can cover at most 65,536 IPv4 addresses.
questions.x: The range size cap is 16,777,216 IPv4 addresses, and the same cap applies to profile ranges. 65,536 is far smaller than the real limit.

questions.t: Each subquery in a Salesforce GraphQL API query counts as a separate request against API rate limits.
questions.f: A Salesforce GraphQL API query counts as a single request against API rate limits, however many subqueries it contains.
questions.x: The GraphQL limits count every subquery as one request, so one call with several subqueries consumes several API calls. Treating the whole query as one call undercounts usage.

questions.t: A Salesforce GraphQL API subquery returns 10 records by default, so pagination is needed to read more.
questions.f: A Salesforce GraphQL API subquery returns 200 records by default, so pagination is needed to read more.
questions.x: Without a page size, only 10 records come back per subquery; the ceiling is 2,000. A 200-record default is wrong.

questions.t: Mutations in the Salesforce GraphQL API are generally available from API version 66.0.
questions.f: Mutations in the Salesforce GraphQL API are generally available from API version 59.0.
questions.x: GraphQL mutations were beta from v59.0 through v65.0 and became GA in v66.0. v59.0 is where the beta began, not GA.

questions.t: Salesforce counts most records as about 2 KB of data storage, but each person account as 4 KB.
questions.f: Salesforce counts most records as about 2 KB of data storage, but each person account as 8 KB.
questions.x: A person account is an Account plus a Contact, so it is counted at 4 KB. 8 KB is the figure for a campaign record.

questions.t: Performance and Unlimited Editions add 120 MB of data storage per user license, while Enterprise Edition adds 20 MB.
questions.f: Enterprise Edition adds 120 MB of data storage per user license, while Performance and Unlimited Editions add 20 MB.
questions.x: On top of the 10 GB minimum, Performance and Unlimited get 120 MB per license and Enterprise gets 20 MB. The false statement swaps the editions.

questions.t: A Developer sandbox gets 200 MB of data storage, which can be upgraded to 400 MB.
questions.f: A Developer sandbox gets 1 GB of data storage, which can be upgraded to 2 GB.
questions.x: Developer sandboxes start at 200 MB of data storage (upgradable to 400 MB). The 1 GB / 2 GB figures belong to Developer Pro sandboxes.

questions.t: A single region on a Lightning page can hold up to 100 components.
questions.f: A single region on a Lightning page can hold up to 25 components.
questions.x: The FlexiPage limit is 100 components per region. 25 is far below the real cap.

questions.t: In Dynamic Interactions, only Lightning web components can fire source events, while Aura or LWC components can be targets.
questions.f: In Dynamic Interactions, Aura or LWC components can fire source events, while only Lightning web components can be targets.
questions.x: Sources must be Lightning web components; targets may be either LWC or Aura. The false statement reverses which side allows Aura.

questions.t: If a property's type differs between a Lightning web component's JavaScript and its js-meta.xml, the configuration file's type wins in Lightning App Builder.
questions.f: If a property's type differs between a Lightning web component's JavaScript and its js-meta.xml, the JavaScript type wins in Lightning App Builder.
questions.x: The builder uses the type declared in the component's configuration file when the two disagree, not the type implied by the JavaScript.

questions.t: Platform Cache includes 10 MB of capacity in Enterprise Edition and 30 MB in Unlimited and Performance Editions.
questions.f: Platform Cache includes 30 MB of capacity in Enterprise Edition and 10 MB in Unlimited and Performance Editions.
questions.x: Enterprise orgs get 10 MB and Unlimited and Performance get 30 MB, with other editions at 0 MB unless more is bought. The false statement swaps the editions.

questions.t: A single item stored in Platform Cache can be at most 100 KB, for both org and session cache.
questions.f: A single item stored in Platform Cache can be at most 1 MB, for both org and session cache.
questions.x: Items over 100 KB throw Cache.ItemSizeLimitExceededException. 1 MB is the minimum partition size, not the item limit.

questions.t: The maximum time-to-live for a Platform Cache org cache entry is 172,800 seconds, or 48 hours.
questions.f: The maximum time-to-live for a Platform Cache org cache entry is 86,400 seconds, or 24 hours.
questions.x: Org cache entries can live up to 48 hours. 24 hours is the org cache default TTL, not its maximum.

questions.t: FIPS 200 states its minimum security requirements as 17 security-related areas, such as access control and incident response.
questions.f: FIPS 200 states its minimum security requirements as 20 security-related areas, such as access control and incident response.
questions.x: FIPS 200 lists 17 areas spanning management, operational and technical concerns. They map to SP 800-53 control families, but the standard itself names 17, not 20.

questions.t: Under FIPS 200, a system gets the low impact level only when its confidentiality, integrity and availability ratings are all low.
questions.f: Under FIPS 200, a system gets the low impact level when at least two of its confidentiality, integrity and availability ratings are low.
questions.x: FIPS 200 uses the high-water mark: the overall level is the highest of the three FIPS 199 ratings, so low applies only if all three are low. A majority of low ratings isn't enough.

questions.t: FIPS 200 took effect when approved in March 2006, and federal agencies were expected to comply within one year.
questions.f: FIPS 200 took effect when approved in March 2006, and federal agencies were expected to comply within three years.
questions.x: The standard was effective on approval on 9 March 2006 with a one-year compliance window. Three years overstates the deadline.

questions.t: HHS treats a cloud provider that stores ePHI for a customer as a business associate even if it holds only encrypted data and no decryption key.
questions.f: HHS treats a cloud provider that stores ePHI for a customer as a mere conduit if it holds only encrypted data and no decryption key.
questions.x: Lacking the key doesn't change the provider's status: maintaining ePHI makes it a business associate. The conduit exception covers only transmission services with transient storage.

questions.t: Under Salesforce's HIPAA BAA, the customer rather than Salesforce must encrypt PHI it transmits through covered services.
questions.f: Under Salesforce's HIPAA BAA, Salesforce rather than the customer must encrypt PHI the customer transmits through covered services.
questions.x: The BAA places encryption of transmitted PHI, and stored PHI where the customer controls it, on the customer. That duty is why Shield Platform Encryption features in HIPAA designs.

questions.t: Salesforce's BAA restrictions bar adding patients to Slack, whether as users or as guests.
questions.f: Salesforce's BAA restrictions allow adding patients to Slack as guests, but not as full users.
questions.x: Slack's HIPAA conditions forbid patients as either users or guests, and keep PHI out of profiles, statuses and workspace names. Guest access is not an exception.

questions.t: A Classic Encryption Text (Encrypted) custom field can hold at most 175 characters.
questions.f: A Classic Encryption Text (Encrypted) custom field can hold at most 255 characters.
questions.x: The encrypted text type caps values at 175 characters, which is why Classic Encryption suits short values like ID numbers. 255 is the limit for a plain Text field.

questions.t: Classic Encryption protects Text (Encrypted) fields with AES using 128-bit master keys.
questions.f: Classic Encryption protects Text (Encrypted) fields with AES using 256-bit master keys.
questions.x: Classic Encryption uses 128-bit AES. The 256-bit AES options belong to Shield Platform Encryption.

questions.t: Seeing the unmasked value of a Classic Encryption field requires the View Encrypted Data permission.
questions.f: Seeing the unmasked value of a Classic Encryption field requires the Manage Encryption Keys permission.
questions.x: Users without View Encrypted Data see a masked value. Manage Encryption Keys is a Platform Encryption permission and has no role in Classic Encryption.

questions.t: A Centralized Salesforce Center of Excellence model suits single-org environments, while a Federated model suits multi-org or multi-region estates.
questions.f: A Federated Salesforce Center of Excellence model suits single-org environments, while a Centralized model suits multi-org or multi-region estates.
questions.x: A Centralized CoE controls all Salesforce work, which fits one org. In a Federated model business units keep control and the CoE advises, which fits multi-org estates; the false statement swaps them.

questions.t: In a Salesforce Center of Excellence, the Design Authority is usually the first subteam formed and reviews designs for security, compliance and architectural fit.
questions.f: In a Salesforce Center of Excellence, Demand Intake is usually the first subteam formed and reviews designs for security, compliance and architectural fit.
questions.x: The Design Authority comes first and is the most complex subteam, reviewing designs. Demand Intake handles incoming requests rather than design review.

questions.t: Trailhead suggests a Salesforce Center of Excellence hold weekly operational meetings and monthly strategy and roadmap meetings.
questions.f: Trailhead suggests a Salesforce Center of Excellence hold monthly operational meetings and quarterly strategy and roadmap meetings.
questions.x: The suggested rhythm is weekly for operations and monthly for strategy and roadmap. Monthly and quarterly is slower than Trailhead's guidance.

questions.t: Scale Test needs a Full Copy sandbox hosted on Hyperforce, although the production org itself doesn't have to be on Hyperforce.
questions.f: Scale Test needs the production org to be hosted on Hyperforce, although the Full Copy sandbox itself doesn't have to be on Hyperforce.
questions.x: Load tests run in the Full Copy sandbox, so that sandbox must be on Hyperforce; production can stay where it is. The false statement puts the requirement on the wrong org.

questions.t: Scale Test slots must be booked at least two weeks in advance, and cancellations need at least one week's notice.
questions.f: Scale Test slots must be booked at least one week in advance, and cancellations need at least two weeks' notice.
questions.x: Booking needs two weeks' notice and cancelling needs one. The false statement swaps the two lead times.

questions.t: Of the two Scale Test permission sets, only ScaleTestingServiceAdvancedUserPS includes the Test Scheduler.
questions.f: Of the two Scale Test permission sets, only ScaleTestingServiceStandardUserPS includes the Test Scheduler.
questions.x: Access comes through a standard or an advanced permission set, and only the advanced one grants the scheduler used to book test windows.

questions.t: A Business Rules Engine decision matrix returns one row even if several match, while a decision table can return multiple matching outcomes.
questions.f: A Business Rules Engine decision table returns one row even if several match, while a decision matrix can return multiple matching outcomes.
questions.x: Matrices are simple lookups that return a single matching row. Decision tables support comparison operators and can return several outcome sets; the false statement swaps them.

questions.t: A Branch element in a Business Rules Engine expression set supports up to six prioritized paths, including the default path.
questions.f: A Branch element in a Business Rules Engine expression set supports up to ten prioritized paths, including the default path.
questions.x: Branch elements are capped at six paths counting the default. Ten overstates the limit.

questions.t: Business Rules Engine decision tables read their rows from Salesforce records, while decision matrices hold rows typed in or imported from CSV.
questions.f: Business Rules Engine decision matrices read their rows from Salesforce records, while decision tables hold rows typed in or imported from CSV.
questions.x: Because decision tables are sourced from records, they refresh when the data changes. Decision matrices are populated by hand or by CSV import.

questions.t: A Salesforce flow can have up to 50 versions in every edition, and inactive old versions count toward that cap.
questions.f: A Salesforce flow can have up to 100 versions in every edition, and inactive old versions count toward that cap.
questions.x: The cap is 50 versions per flow, and unused versions still count, so they should be deleted before the limit is hit. 100 doubles the real figure.

questions.t: Flow interviews already running when a new version is activated finish on the version they started with.
questions.f: Flow interviews already running when a new version is activated switch to the new version at their next element.
questions.x: Activation affects only new interviews; in-flight ones are not migrated and complete on their original version.

questions.t: A flow version's API version for running the flow doesn't move forward with new releases; it changes only when a Manage Flow user edits it.
questions.f: A flow version's API version for running the flow moves forward automatically with each new release, unless a Manage Flow user pins it.
questions.x: Each version keeps the runtime API version it was saved with until someone with Manage Flow changes it, ideally after reading the release notes in between. It is not upgraded automatically.

questions.t: When flows are deployed as active, flows with screens are exempt from the flow test coverage requirement, while autolaunched flows are not.
questions.f: When flows are deployed as active, autolaunched flows are exempt from the flow test coverage requirement, while flows with screens are not.
questions.x: The Apex coverage requirement applies to active processes and autolaunched flows; screen flows are excluded. The false statement reverses the exemption.

questions.t: The Automated Process User Email Address used as the sender for scheduled flow emails must be an organization-wide email address.
questions.f: The Automated Process User Email Address used as the sender for scheduled flow emails must be the Default Workflow User's own email address.
questions.x: Process Automation Settings requires an organization-wide email address as the sender for scheduled flow email. The Default Workflow User sets the running user, not the sender address.

questions.t: Process Automation Settings can send flow error emails to the Apex Exception Email recipients instead of the last person who modified the flow.
questions.f: Process Automation Settings can send flow error emails to the Default Workflow User instead of the last person who modified the flow.
questions.x: The error-email option reroutes unhandled flow fault emails to the Apex Exception Email recipients. The Default Workflow User is the running user for time-based automation, not an error recipient.

questions.t: In a Context Service definition, context tags are short aliases that consuming applications use to query nodes and attributes directly.
questions.f: In a Context Service definition, context mappings are short aliases that consuming applications use to query nodes and attributes directly.
questions.x: Tags are the aliases applications query by. Mappings do a different job: they link nodes to objects or DMOs and attributes to fields.

questions.t: Extending a standard context definition keeps its inherited parts read-only and picks up Industry Cloud updates, while cloning gives a fully editable copy.
questions.f: Cloning a standard context definition keeps its inherited parts read-only and picks up Industry Cloud updates, while extending gives a fully editable copy.
questions.x: An extension inherits standard nodes, attributes and mappings as read-only and receives automatic updates. A clone is independent and fully editable; the false statement swaps the two options.

questions.t: Transposable child nodes, which store data as key-value pairs, are available only in custom context definitions or on custom nodes.
questions.f: Transposable child nodes, which store data as key-value pairs, are available only in standard context definitions shipped by industry clouds.
questions.x: Key-value transposable nodes, such as Color = Blue, can be used only in custom definitions or on custom nodes. Standard definitions can't be modified, so they aren't where you add them.

questions.t: In Product Configurator configuration rules, only an Error message blocks submission; Information and Warning messages don't.
questions.f: In Product Configurator configuration rules, both Warning and Error messages block submission; only Information messages don't.
questions.x: Rule messages come in three severities, and only Error stops the rep from submitting. Warnings are advisory.

questions.t: An admin can assign a Product Configurator flow to a product classification so that many products share the same configuration UI.
questions.f: An admin can assign a Product Configurator flow to a price book so that many products share the same configuration UI.
questions.x: Configurator flows are assigned to a product or to a product classification. Price books play no part in choosing the configuration UI.

questions.t: In Product Configurator, the Instant Pricing toggle controls whether each selection is priced as it is made.
questions.f: In Product Configurator, the Product Validation toggle controls whether each selection is priced as it is made.
questions.x: There are two toggles: Product Validation checks each selection, and Instant Pricing prices it immediately. Pricing is controlled by Instant Pricing, not Product Validation.

questions.t: In the Salesforce CPQ price waterfall, Regular Price reflects automatic volume discounts and Customer Price reflects the rep's manual discounts.
questions.f: In the Salesforce CPQ price waterfall, Customer Price reflects automatic volume discounts and Regular Price reflects the rep's manual discounts.
questions.x: The waterfall applies volume discounts to reach Regular Price, then the rep's manual discounts to reach Customer Price. The false statement swaps the two fields.

questions.t: Salesforce CPQ filter rules narrow which products can go into a bundle, while selection rules add, remove or hide bundle options.
questions.f: Salesforce CPQ selection rules narrow which products can go into a bundle, while filter rules add, remove or hide bundle options.
questions.x: Filter rules restrict the products available to a bundle; selection rules act on options by adding, removing, hiding, enabling or disabling them. The false statement reverses the two.

questions.t: The Salesforce CPQ JavaScript Quote Calculator Plugin must run in both the browser and Node, so browser globals such as window may not exist.
questions.f: The Salesforce CPQ JavaScript Quote Calculator Plugin runs only in the browser, so browser globals such as window are always available.
questions.x: The QCP is an ES6 module that has to work in both environments, so it can't rely on browser-only globals. Assuming window is always present breaks server-side calculation.

questions.t: Salesforce closed its acquisition of Vlocity on June 1, 2020, and renamed the business Salesforce Industries.
questions.f: Salesforce closed its acquisition of Vlocity on June 1, 2019, and renamed the business Salesforce Industries.
questions.x: The Vlocity deal closed in June 2020, after which the business became Salesforce Industries. 2019 is a year too early.

questions.t: The Omnistudio standard runtime works only with the standard data model, while the managed package runtime supports package objects and standard objects.
questions.f: The Omnistudio managed package runtime works only with the standard data model, while the standard runtime supports package objects and standard objects.
questions.x: The legacy managed package runtime handles both the packages' custom objects and the standard data model. The standard runtime is limited to the standard data model.

questions.t: Salesforce Architects suggest Flow for employee-facing processes and OmniScript as the default for external users and industry-specific processes.
questions.f: Salesforce Architects suggest OmniScript for employee-facing processes and Flow as the default for external users and industry-specific processes.
questions.x: The Industries guidance points internal processes to Flow and external or industry-specific journeys to OmniScript. The false statement swaps the two tools.

questions.t: In a Salesforce Pricing procedure, a Stop Pricing element ends processing early, while a List Group runs its elements only when a condition holds.
questions.f: In a Salesforce Pricing procedure, a List Group ends processing early, while a Stop Pricing element runs its elements only when a condition holds.
questions.x: List Group wraps conditional elements and Stop Pricing halts the procedure; contract pricing combines them so contracted lines skip standard discounts. The false statement swaps their roles.

questions.t: Salesforce Pricing elements read and write values through context tags rather than reading records directly.
questions.f: Salesforce Pricing elements read and write values by querying records directly rather than through context tags.
questions.x: Each element's input and output variables map to context tags from the procedure's context definition, which carry values between steps and back to the transaction.

questions.t: The Salesforce Pricing List Price element finds the price book entry using the product, price book and product selling model.
questions.f: The Salesforce Pricing List Price element finds the price book entry using the product, price book and account.
questions.x: List Price looks up the entry by product, price book and product selling model, then returns list price and subtotal. The account is not part of that lookup.

questions.t: In a Data 360 data stream, Incremental refresh blanks out fields that didn't change, while Partial writes only the changed fields and keeps the rest.
questions.f: In a Data 360 data stream, Partial refresh blanks out fields that didn't change, while Incremental writes only the changed fields and keeps the rest.
questions.x: Incremental mode writes new values and blanks unchanged fields, so a delta-only source can lose data. Partial is the mode that preserves untouched fields; the false statement swaps them.

questions.t: Data 360 web and mobile data streams ingest engagement data every 15 minutes and profile data every hour.
questions.f: Data 360 web and mobile data streams ingest profile data every 15 minutes and engagement data every hour.
questions.x: Engagement events arrive on the faster 15-minute cycle and profile data hourly. The false statement reverses the two schedules.

questions.t: For a website or mobile app source, all Data 360 Engagement events share one data stream, while each Profile or Other event gets its own.
questions.f: For a website or mobile app source, all Data 360 Profile events share one data stream, while each Engagement or Other event gets its own.
questions.x: After the app's event schema is uploaded, Engagement events are combined into a single stream and Profile or Other events get separate streams.

questions.t: Dynamic Forms became generally available across LWC-enabled standard objects and on mobile in Winter '24.
questions.f: Dynamic Forms became generally available across LWC-enabled standard objects and on mobile in Winter '23.
questions.x: Winter '23 added standard-object support only for account, contact and opportunity. Broad GA on LWC-enabled standard objects and mobile came in Winter '24.

questions.t: A two-column Dynamic Forms Field Section counts as three components on the page, because each column counts as a component.
questions.f: A two-column Dynamic Forms Field Section counts as one component on the page, because columns don't count as components.
questions.x: The section itself plus each of its columns counts toward component limits, so two columns make three. Treating the section as a single component undercounts it.

questions.t: Dynamic Forms field visibility rules re-evaluate while the user edits, but section visibility rules apply only after the record is saved.
questions.f: Dynamic Forms section visibility rules re-evaluate while the user edits, but field visibility rules apply only after the record is saved.
questions.x: Field-level rules respond during editing, whereas section rules are evaluated after save. The false statement swaps which rule type is live.

questions.t: In Apex, Formula.recalculateFormulas() refreshes every formula on a list of in-memory SObjects without saving the records.
questions.f: In Apex, Formula.recalculateFormulas() refreshes every formula on a list of SObjects and then saves the records to the database.
questions.x: The method recalculates formula values on records held in memory and performs no DML; it only uses SOQL when fields the formulas need are missing.

questions.t: A single Apex continuation can run at most 3 callouts in parallel, and up to 3 callouts can be chained one after another.
questions.f: A single Apex continuation can run at most 10 callouts in parallel, and up to 10 callouts can be chained one after another.
questions.x: Continuations are capped at three parallel requests and three chained requests. Ten is far above the documented continuation limit.

questions.t: An Apex continuation can wait at most 120 seconds, and timeouts set on its individual HttpRequest objects are ignored.
questions.f: An Apex continuation can wait at most 60 seconds, and timeouts set on its individual HttpRequest objects are ignored.
questions.x: The continuation's own timeout governs and tops out at 120 seconds; per-request timeouts don't apply. Sixty seconds understates the ceiling.

questions.t: A Lightning web component imports a continuation-enabled Apex method from the @salesforce/apexContinuation module rather than @salesforce/apex.
questions.f: A Lightning web component imports a continuation-enabled Apex method from the @salesforce/apex module rather than @salesforce/apexContinuation.
questions.x: Continuation methods have their own import module, @salesforce/apexContinuation; the regular @salesforce/apex module is for ordinary Apex calls. The false version swaps the two.

questions.t: A destructiveChangesPost.xml manifest deletes components after the deployment's additions and updates are applied, but before Apex tests run.
questions.f: A destructiveChangesPost.xml manifest deletes components after the deployment's additions and updates are applied, and only after Apex tests run.
questions.x: Post-destructive deletions happen once additions and updates are in, yet ahead of the test run. That ordering is why tests can catch references left behind; the false version puts the deletes after testing.

questions.t: In package.xml, custom fields are listed under the CustomField type, named in Object.Field__c form.
questions.f: In package.xml, custom fields are listed under the CustomObject type, named in Object.Field__c form.
questions.x: Fields have their own metadata type, CustomField, using the object-qualified full name. CustomObject is the type for standard and custom objects themselves.

questions.t: When sf project generate manifest builds from an org, it leaves out managed and unlocked package metadata unless --include-packages is set.
questions.f: When sf project generate manifest builds from an org, it includes managed and unlocked package metadata unless --excluded-metadata is set.
questions.x: Package-owned components are excluded by default and are added only with --include-packages. The --excluded-metadata flag drops whole metadata types; it doesn't control package metadata.

questions.t: For a Partial Copy sandbox, the copy engine takes a random sample of up to 10,000 records for each object selected in the template.
questions.f: For a Partial Copy sandbox, the copy engine takes a random sample of up to 1,000 records for each object selected in the template.
questions.x: Partial Copy sampling allows as many as 10,000 rows per selected object, inside the 5 GB storage cap. One thousand is a tenth of the real figure.

questions.t: A sandbox template copies big object definitions but never their records, even when the big object is selected.
questions.f: A sandbox template copies big object definitions, and copies their records too whenever the big object is selected.
questions.x: Big object records are never carried into a sandbox, whatever the template contains; only the definition comes across. Selecting the object doesn't change that.

questions.t: Partial Copy sampling keeps children with their parents only on master-detail and required lookups; an object linked by an ordinary lookup is sampled on its own.
questions.f: Partial Copy sampling keeps children with their parents on every lookup and master-detail relationship, so no copied row points at a missing parent.
questions.x: Only master-detail and required lookup links are enforced during sampling. Objects joined by plain lookups are sampled as top-level objects, so their rows can reference parents that weren't copied.

questions.t: Identity Connect syncs one way from Active Directory, so an edit made in Salesforce to a mapped field is overwritten on the next sync.
questions.f: Identity Connect syncs both ways with Active Directory, so an edit made in Salesforce to a mapped field is written back to AD on the next sync.
questions.x: AD is the source of truth and Identity Connect only needs read access to it; it never writes to AD. Salesforce-side edits to mapped fields are simply replaced unless the field is left out of the mapping.

questions.t: In Identity Connect, Scheduled Updates compare every user and group to correct drift, while Live Updates react to AD changes without a full comparison.
questions.f: In Identity Connect, Live Updates compare every user and group to correct drift, while Scheduled Updates react to AD changes without a full comparison.
questions.x: Live Updates push changes as they happen but can miss changes made during an outage; Scheduled Updates do the full comparison that catches them. The false version swaps the two modes.

questions.t: A Developer Edition org includes 10 Identity Connect permission set licenses, while Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited Editions pay extra for it.
questions.f: A Developer Edition org includes 100 Identity Connect permission set licenses, while Enterprise, Performance and Unlimited Editions pay extra for it.
questions.x: Identity Connect is a paid add-on in the main editions, and Developer Edition ships with ten of its permission set licenses. One hundred overstates that allowance.

questions.t: Salesforce password policies can lock users out after 3, 5 or 10 invalid login attempts, for a lockout period of 15, 30 or 60 minutes.
questions.f: Salesforce password policies can lock users out after 3, 5 or 10 invalid login attempts, for a lockout period of 1, 12 or 24 hours.
questions.x: The lockout settings offer 3, 5 or 10 attempts and a lockout of 15, 30 or 60 minutes (or 0). Lockout periods measured in many hours aren't among the options.

questions.t: Once a profile has its own password policy, later changes to the org-wide password policy no longer reach that profile's users.
questions.f: Once a profile has its own password policy, later changes to the org-wide password policy still override it for that profile's users.
questions.x: A profile-level policy replaces the org-wide one for that profile, so org-wide edits stop applying there. This drift is why admins should check which profiles carry their own settings.

questions.t: Shortening the password expiration period takes effect immediately, but lengthening it applies only from each user's next password change.
questions.f: Lengthening the password expiration period takes effect immediately, but shortening it applies only from each user's next password change.
questions.x: A shorter expiration, or switching to never expires, applies at once; a longer one waits until the user next changes the password. The false version reverses which direction is immediate.

questions.t: For Request and Reply, Salesforce's integration guidance rates External Services as a best fit and the Flow HTTP Callout action as good.
questions.f: For Request and Reply, Salesforce's integration guidance rates the Flow HTTP Callout action as a best fit and External Services as good.
questions.x: External Services, built from an OpenAPI definition and callable from Flow, gets the top rating; the lighter HTTP Callout action is rated one step lower. The false version swaps them.

questions.t: Each Apex callout's timeout can be set up to 120 seconds, and the total time of all callouts in one transaction is also capped at 120 seconds.
questions.f: Each Apex callout's timeout can be set up to 120 seconds, and the total time of all callouts in one transaction is capped at 600 seconds.
questions.x: The 120-second ceiling applies both per callout and to the sum across the transaction. There's no larger 600-second budget for the whole transaction.

questions.t: Callouts started from Apex triggers must run asynchronously, so Salesforce's guidance treats them as Fire and Forget rather than Request and Reply.
questions.f: Callouts started from Apex triggers can run synchronously, so Salesforce's guidance treats them as Request and Reply rather than Fire and Forget.
questions.x: A trigger can't wait on a synchronous callout, so trigger-based calls have to be asynchronous and belong to Fire and Forget. That's why the guidance rates triggers as suboptimal for Request and Reply.

questions.t: In a single composite API request, no more than 5 of the subrequests can be query or sObject Collections operations.
questions.f: In a single composite API request, no more than 15 of the subrequests can be query or sObject Collections operations.
questions.x: Composite allows up to 25 subrequests, but only five of them may be queries or sObject Collections calls. Fifteen overstates that sub-limit.

questions.t: A user can hold up to 10 open query cursors at once; opening another releases the oldest one.
questions.f: A user can hold up to 50 open query cursors at once; opening another releases the oldest one.
