questions.x: The cursor cap per user is ten, and exceeding it frees the oldest cursor. That's why a shared integration user should run queries serially or be split per application.

questions.t: Salesforce API query results come back in batches of 500 rows by default, and the batch size can be raised to at most 2,000.
questions.f: Salesforce API query results come back in batches of 2,000 rows by default, and the batch size can be raised to at most 10,000.
questions.x: The default query batch is 500 rows with a ceiling of 2,000. The false version shifts both numbers up, using the real maximum as the default.

questions.t: An Apex callout whose endpoint is defined by a named credential needs no separate entry in Remote Site Settings.
questions.f: An Apex callout whose endpoint is defined by a named credential also needs a matching entry in Remote Site Settings.
questions.x: A named credential carries its own URL and authentication, so the platform doesn't require a remote site entry for it. Remote site entries are needed for endpoints Apex calls directly.

questions.t: Turning on disableProtocolSecurity for a remote site lets code pass data between HTTP and HTTPS sessions, whatever protocol the user is on.
questions.f: Turning on disableProtocolSecurity for a remote site lets code skip TLS certificate checks on HTTPS callouts to that host.
questions.x: The flag allows mixing HTTP and HTTPS in either direction regardless of the user's connection, and Salesforce warns to use it only with care. It isn't a switch for certificate validation.

questions.t: In RemoteSiteSetting metadata, url, isActive and disableProtocolSecurity are required fields, while description is optional.
questions.f: In RemoteSiteSetting metadata, url and description are required fields, while isActive and disableProtocolSecurity are optional.
questions.x: The metadata type requires the URL, the active flag and the protocol-security flag; the description can be left out. The false version swaps which fields are required.

questions.t: Marking a field as an External ID indexes it automatically, but only Auto Number, Email, Number and Text fields can be External IDs.
questions.f: Marking a field as an External ID indexes it automatically, but only Text, Picklist, Date and Currency fields can be External IDs.
questions.x: External ID is the self-service route to an index, and it is limited to Auto Number, Email, Number and Text fields. Picklist, Date and Currency fields can't be flagged this way.

questions.t: Custom indexes can't be built on long text area, rich text area or encrypted text fields, or on non-deterministic formula fields.
questions.f: Custom indexes can be built on long text area and rich text area fields, but not on any formula field.
questions.x: Long and rich text areas, encrypted text and non-deterministic formulas are the excluded field types. Deterministic formulas can be indexed, so ruling out every formula is wrong too.

questions.t: By default a Salesforce index leaves out rows where the field is empty, so a filter like Field__c = null forces a full scan.
questions.f: By default a Salesforce index keeps rows where the field is empty, so a filter like Field__c = null can be served from the index.
questions.x: Empty values are omitted from indexes unless Support enables null rows on a custom index, so null filters scan the table. The false version describes the opt-in behaviour as the default.

questions.t: Under NIST SP 800-63B-4, an AAL3 session must end within 12 hours and after no more than 15 minutes of inactivity.
questions.f: Under NIST SP 800-63B-4, an AAL3 session must end within 24 hours and after no more than 1 hour of inactivity.
questions.x: AAL3 tightens reauthentication to 12 hours overall and 15 minutes idle. The 24-hour and one-hour figures are the looser AAL2 bounds.

questions.t: NIST SP 800-63-4 accepts syncable passkeys at AAL2 with user verification, but not at AAL3, which forbids exportable private keys.
questions.f: NIST SP 800-63-4 accepts syncable passkeys at both AAL2 and AAL3, as long as user verification is performed.
questions.x: Synced passkeys can leave the device, so they cap out at AAL2. AAL3 needs a cryptographic authenticator whose private key can't be exported, which user verification alone doesn't provide.

questions.t: Under NIST SP 800-63C-4, proof that the subscriber holds an authenticator, via a holder-of-key assertion or bound authenticator, is first required at FAL3.
questions.f: Under NIST SP 800-63C-4, proof that the subscriber holds an authenticator, via a holder-of-key assertion or bound authenticator, is first required at FAL2.
questions.x: FAL2 adds injection protection, a single audience and a trust agreement, but holder-of-key proof is the extra step that defines FAL3.

questions.t: NIST's 5.2.0 release of SP 800-53B in August 2025 left the control baselines unchanged and only bumped the version number to match SP 800-53.
questions.f: NIST's 5.2.0 release of SP 800-53B in August 2025 added new controls to the moderate and high baselines to match SP 800-53.
questions.x: Release 5.2.0 changed no baselines; the version was raised only for consistency with SP 800-53 and 800-53A. Baselines built on the 2020 text remain valid.

questions.t: The SP 800-53B privacy baseline applies regardless of a system's impact level, instead of coming in low, moderate and high versions.
questions.f: The SP 800-53B privacy baseline comes in low, moderate and high versions, chosen by the system's FIPS 199 impact level.
questions.x: Only the security baselines are split by impact level. The single privacy baseline is driven by the processing of personal information and tailored from a privacy risk assessment.

questions.t: Some SP 800-53 controls are assigned to no SP 800-53B baseline at all and enter a system only through tailoring.
questions.f: Every SP 800-53 control is assigned to at least the high baseline in SP 800-53B, so tailoring can only remove controls.
questions.x: The allocation tables leave some controls out of every baseline; organizations add them by supplementing during tailoring. Tailoring can add as well as remove or specialize controls.

questions.t: TOGAF stratification sorts top-level capabilities into strategic, core and supporting tiers, with the core tier being customer-facing.
questions.f: TOGAF stratification sorts top-level capabilities into strategic, core and supporting tiers, with the supporting tier being customer-facing.
questions.x: Strategic capabilities set direction, core ones face the customer, and supporting ones work behind the scenes. The false version gives the customer-facing role to the wrong tier.

questions.t: In TOGAF's maturity heat-map example, purple marks a capability that is wanted but doesn't exist yet, and red one that is two or more levels short.
questions.f: In TOGAF's maturity heat-map example, red marks a capability that is wanted but doesn't exist yet, and purple one that is two or more levels short.
questions.x: The example uses green for at target, yellow for one level short, red for two or more short and purple for a missing capability. The false version swaps red and purple.

questions.t: TOGAF suggests starting a capability map with a top-down pass of about 20 to 30 high-level capabilities, then adding bottom-up detail.
questions.f: TOGAF suggests starting a capability map with a top-down pass of about 100 to 150 high-level capabilities, then adding bottom-up detail.
questions.x: A small top-down set of roughly 20 to 30 capabilities keeps the model manageable before detail is layered in. A first pass of 100 or more is far beyond that guidance.

questions.t: The product quality model in ISO/IEC 25010:2023 has nine characteristics, each split into subcharacteristics.
questions.f: The product quality model in ISO/IEC 25010:2023 has six characteristics, each split into subcharacteristics.
questions.x: The 2023 edition, which replaced the withdrawn 2011 version, defines nine product quality characteristics. Six understates the model.

questions.t: The Well-Architected Reliability pillar's example pairs a 99.9% platform SLA with a 99.5% solution SLO, leaving an error budget.
questions.f: The Well-Architected Reliability pillar's example pairs a 99.5% platform SLA with a 99.9% solution SLO, leaving an error budget.
questions.x: A solution's objective should sit below the platform's guarantee so there's room for its own failures. The false version sets the solution target above the platform SLA, which leaves no budget.

questions.t: In the SEI Quality Attribute Workshop, stakeholders vote on brainstormed scenarios and only the top ones are refined into the full six-part form.
questions.f: In the SEI Quality Attribute Workshop, every brainstormed scenario is refined into the full six-part form before stakeholders vote on them.
questions.x: The workshop merges and prioritizes scenarios first, then refines just the highest-priority ones with source, artifact and response measure. Refining everything before voting reverses the process.

questions.t: An Apex class can contain only one @InvocableMethod, and that method takes at most one parameter, typically a list.
questions.f: An Apex class can contain several @InvocableMethod methods, and each one takes at most one parameter, typically a list.
questions.x: Salesforce limits the annotation to a single static, public or global method per outer class. The parameter rule is the same in both versions; the count of methods is what's wrong.

questions.t: When an autolaunched flow is run through the Invocable Actions API, a flow admin always runs the latest version, while other flow users run the active one.
questions.f: When an autolaunched flow is run through the Invocable Actions API, a flow admin always runs the active version, while other flow users run the latest one.
questions.x: Ordinary flow users get the active version (or the latest if none is active), but a flow admin always gets the newest version. The false version swaps the two callers.

questions.t: Email sent through the emailAlert invocable action counts against the org's daily workflow email limit.
questions.f: Email sent through the emailAlert invocable action counts against the org's daily single email limit for Apex.
questions.x: The emailAlert action reuses workflow email alerts, so it draws on the daily workflow email allocation. It isn't charged to the Apex single email limit.

questions.t: The no-code model builder in Data 360 AI Models offers regression and binary classification only; other problem types need an external model.
questions.f: The no-code model builder in Data 360 AI Models offers binary and multiclass classification only; regression needs an external model.
questions.x: Models built from scratch can predict a number (regression) or one of two outcomes (binary classification). Multiclass isn't offered, and regression is supported natively.

questions.t: Bring-your-own-LLM calls in AI Models consume 30% fewer Einstein Requests than calls to other models.
questions.f: Bring-your-own-LLM calls in AI Models consume 50% fewer Einstein Requests than calls to other models.
questions.x: BYOLLM inference runs at the customer's provider, and Salesforce discounts it by 30% in Einstein Requests. Fifty percent overstates the saving.

questions.t: A BYOM model hosted on Amazon SageMaker, Google Vertex AI or Databricks stays on that platform and is called from Data 360 through an API.
questions.f: A BYOM model hosted on Amazon SageMaker, Google Vertex AI or Databricks is imported into Data 360 and then runs there instead of on that platform.
questions.x: Bring-your-own-model keeps the model where it was trained; Data 360 sends predictor values to its endpoint and stores the results. Nothing is copied into Salesforce.

questions.t: A Data 360 data space's name and description can be edited later, but its prefix can't be changed after the data space is created.
questions.f: A Data 360 data space's prefix and description can be edited later, but its name can't be changed after the data space is created.
questions.x: The prefix is fixed at creation, so it needs choosing carefully; the name and description stay editable. The false version swaps the name and the prefix.

questions.t: A data space filter on a data lake object only limits what that data space can see; the stream still ingests and counts every record.
questions.f: A data space filter on a data lake object stops non-matching records from being ingested, so the stream counts only matching records.
questions.x: Filters are applied after ingestion, so the DLO and the stream's Total Records include everything brought in. Salesforce CRM records can't currently be pre-filtered before ingestion either.

questions.t: Only standard data bundles, such as the Salesforce CRM or Marketing Cloud Engagement bundles, can be deployed to a non-default data space.
questions.f: Standard data bundles, such as the Salesforce CRM or Marketing Cloud Engagement bundles, can be deployed only to the default data space.
questions.x: Standard bundles are exactly what can go into a non-default data space. The false version restricts them to the default data space instead.

questions.t: Salesforce's Data Quality module checks the age dimension by reporting on Last Modified Date to see what share of records is recent.
questions.f: Salesforce's Data Quality module checks the age dimension by reporting on Created Date to see what share of records is recent.
questions.x: Age is about how recently a record was updated, so the check uses Last Modified Date. Created Date says nothing about whether old records have been kept current.

questions.t: Trailhead notes that, on average, 120 business addresses and 75 phone numbers change every 30 minutes, so data quality needs continuous care.
questions.f: Trailhead notes that, on average, 120 business addresses and 75 phone numbers change every 24 hours, so data quality needs continuous care.
questions.x: The decay figure is per 30 minutes, which is why quality is treated as ongoing rather than a one-time cleanup. Per day understates how fast contact data goes stale.

questions.t: Trailhead describes data governance as setting quality policies and accountability, and data stewardship as monitoring and coordinating fixes against them.
questions.f: Trailhead describes data stewardship as setting quality policies and accountability, and data governance as monitoring and coordinating fixes against them.
questions.x: Governance defines the standards and who is accountable; stewardship carries them out by monitoring, investigating and fixing. The false version swaps the two roles.

questions.t: Price book entries can never be deleted; to retire one, set its IsActive field to false.
questions.f: Price book entries can be deleted once no opportunity line items use them; otherwise set IsActive to false.
questions.x: PricebookEntry records can't be deleted under any condition, so deactivation is the only way to retire them. The false version invents a deletion path.

questions.t: Once an opportunity has product line items, neither its price book nor its CurrencyIsoCode can be changed.
questions.f: Once an opportunity has product line items, its price book can still be changed, but its CurrencyIsoCode can't.
questions.x: Line items lock both the opportunity's price book and its currency, because every line item must come from an entry in that book and currency. Swapping the book is blocked too.

questions.t: Apex tests call Test.getStandardPricebookId() to get the standard price book's ID before inserting standard-price entries.
questions.f: Apex tests must set SeeAllData=true to query the standard price book's ID before inserting standard-price entries.
questions.x: Tests don't see org data by default, and Test.getStandardPricebookId() returns the standard book's ID without opening that access. SeeAllData isn't needed for it.

questions.t: A validation rule's error message is limited to 255 characters.
questions.f: A validation rule's error message is limited to 1,000 characters.
questions.x: The ValidationRule metadata caps the message at 255 characters, so long guidance has to be trimmed. One thousand overstates the limit.

questions.t: During a save, custom validation rules run after before-save Apex triggers and before duplicate rules are evaluated.
questions.f: During a save, custom validation rules run before before-save Apex triggers and after duplicate rules are evaluated.
questions.x: Validation sees the values that before-save automation set, and duplicate rules come afterwards. The false version reverses both neighbours in the order of execution.

questions.t: A new validation rule also applies to existing records, so a user editing an unrelated field on a non-compliant record is blocked.
questions.f: A new validation rule applies only to records created after it is activated, so editing an unrelated field on an older record still saves.
questions.x: Rules are checked on every save, old records included, which is why guards like ISNEW() or ISCHANGED() matter. Activation date doesn't exempt existing data.

questions.t: When a System.LimitException is thrown, neither the catch block nor any finally block runs.
questions.f: When a System.LimitException is thrown, the catch block is skipped, but any finally block still runs.
questions.x: LimitException is uncatchable and ends the transaction outright, so finally blocks don't get a chance either. That's why prevention, not handling, is the only defence.

questions.t: Apex unhandled-exception emails are deduplicated and throttled to 10 per hour per application server.
questions.f: Apex unhandled-exception emails are deduplicated and throttled to 100 per hour per application server.
questions.x: The throttle is ten emails an hour per app server, which makes email unreliable for tracking failures. Salesforce points to Event Monitoring's Apex Unexpected Exception logs instead.

questions.t: Across all namespaces in one transaction, a governor limit is capped at 11 times its per-namespace value, such as 1,100 SOQL queries.
questions.f: Across all namespaces in one transaction, a governor limit is capped at 3 times its per-namespace value, such as 300 SOQL queries.
questions.x: Certified packages get their own allocations, but the cross-namespace total stops at eleven times the single-namespace limit. Three times is far too low.

questions.t: In the Apex Limits class, the deprecated savepoint and rollback methods now return the DML statement counters.
questions.f: In the Apex Limits class, the deprecated savepoint and rollback methods now return the SOQL query counters.
questions.x: Savepoints and rollbacks are counted as DML statements, so their old methods mirror the DML values. They aren't tied to query counts.

questions.t: The Apex Limits class reports only per-transaction governors; org-wide allowances such as daily API requests come from System.OrgLimits.
questions.f: The Apex Limits class reports both per-transaction governors and org-wide allowances such as daily API requests, so OrgLimits isn't needed.
questions.x: Limits covers the running transaction, while OrgLimits.getAll() or getMap() returns org allowances that update in near real time. The two classes answer different questions.

questions.t: Limits.getChildRelationshipsDescribes() is deprecated because describe limits are no longer enforced.
questions.f: Limits.getChildRelationshipsDescribes() is deprecated because child relationship describes now count as SOQL queries.
questions.x: Describe calls stopped being governed, so the counter has nothing to report and newer API versions drop it. They weren't folded into the SOQL limit.

questions.t: No more than 100 scheduled Apex jobs can exist in an org at the same time.
questions.f: No more than 500 scheduled Apex jobs can exist in an org at the same time.
questions.x: The scheduler caps an org at 100 scheduled jobs, which is why scheduling from a bulk trigger is risky. Five hundred overstates the cap.

questions.t: Apex doesn't allow a single schedule's cron expression to fire the job more often than once an hour.
questions.f: Apex doesn't allow a single schedule's cron expression to fire the job more often than once every five minutes.
questions.x: The finest granularity for one Apex schedule is hourly; more frequent runs need several schedules or another approach. A five-minute floor isn't the documented rule.

questions.t: Refreshing a sandbox doesn't copy its source org's scheduled Apex jobs, so they have to be scheduled again in the sandbox.
questions.f: Refreshing a sandbox copies its source org's scheduled Apex jobs in a paused state, so they have to be resumed in the sandbox.
questions.x: Scheduled jobs simply don't come across in a refresh, so they must be recreated. The false version invents a paused copy that only needs resuming.

questions.t: Database.queryWithBinds, available from API version 57.0, resolves the bind variables in a dynamic SOQL string from a Map<String, Object>.
questions.f: Database.queryWithBinds, available from API version 57.0, resolves the bind variables in a dynamic SOQL string from a List<Object> matched by position.
questions.x: Binds are supplied as a map keyed by name, matched case-insensitively. There's no positional list form.

questions.t: String.escapeSingleQuotes() doesn't protect a numeric value that is concatenated into a SOQL string without quotes around it.
questions.f: String.escapeSingleQuotes() protects every value concatenated into a SOQL string, including numeric values without quotes around them.
questions.x: Escaping only helps when the input sits inside a quoted string literal. An unquoted number can still carry extra clauses, so typecasting or bind variables are needed.

questions.t: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks only the SELECT and FROM clauses, not WHERE, so it isn't a defense against SOQL injection.
questions.f: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks the SELECT, FROM and WHERE clauses, so it works as a defense against SOQL injection.
questions.x: Injected conditions live in the WHERE clause, which WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED doesn't cover. Binds, typecasting and allowlists remain the real defenses.

questions.t: A validation's job ID can be quick-deployed for 10 days, but the --use-most-recent flag finds only validations from the past 3 days.
questions.f: A validation's job ID can be quick-deployed for 30 days, but the --use-most-recent flag finds only validations from the past 10 days.
questions.x: Quick deploy eligibility lasts 10 days from the start of validation, and --use-most-recent looks back just 3 days, so older validations need --job-id. The false version inflates both windows.

questions.t: Quick deploy doesn't support source tracking; it overwrites the matching metadata in the org instead of merging.
questions.f: Quick deploy supports source tracking, merging the validated metadata with changes made in the org since validation.
questions.x: Quick deploy pushes the validated component set as-is and replaces what's in the org. It has no source tracking or merge step.

questions.t: Salesforce processes only one deployment per org at a time, so a long deployment blocks other releases to that org.
questions.f: Salesforce processes up to five deployments per org in parallel, so a long deployment doesn't block other releases to that org.
questions.x: Deployments to an org are handled one at a time, which is part of why pre-validating shortens the blocking window. Parallel deployments to one org aren't supported.

questions.t: A Dev Hub in an active partner business org allows 150 active scratch orgs and 300 scratch org creations per day.
questions.f: A Dev Hub in an active partner business org allows 100 active scratch orgs and 200 scratch org creations per day.
questions.x: Partner business orgs get 150 active and 300 daily. The 100 and 200 figures belong to Unlimited and Performance Edition Dev Hubs.

questions.t: A scratch org snapshot expires after 90 days, and its slot in the Dev Hub's snapshot quota is freed as soon as it expires or is deleted.
questions.f: A scratch org snapshot expires after 30 days, and its slot in the Dev Hub's snapshot quota is freed as soon as it expires or is deleted.
questions.x: Snapshots live for 90 days, with a quota equal to the hub's active scratch org allocation. Thirty days understates the lifetime.

questions.t: Each scratch org gets 500 MB of data storage and 50 MB of file storage, however many orgs its Dev Hub may create.
questions.f: Each scratch org gets 1 GB of data storage and 1 GB of file storage, however many orgs its Dev Hub may create.
questions.x: Scratch orgs are small: 500 MB for data and 50 MB for files, separate from the hub's org-count quotas. The false version inflates both.

questions.t: An OAuth 2.0 request becomes an OpenID Connect request only when its scope includes the value openid.
questions.f: An OAuth 2.0 request becomes an OpenID Connect request only when its scope includes the value profile.
questions.x: The openid scope is what turns a plain OAuth exchange into OIDC. The profile scope only asks for a group of profile claims.

questions.t: OpenID Connect says only the iss and sub claims together reliably identify a user, so email must not be used as a unique key.
questions.f: OpenID Connect says the iss and email claims together reliably identify a user, so email can be used as a unique key.
questions.x: Claims such as email or preferred_username can change or be reused, so the spec ties identity to issuer plus subject. Keying users on email is a known pitfall.

questions.t: An OpenID provider's discovery document is fetched from its issuer URL with /.well-known/openid-configuration appended.
questions.f: An OpenID provider's discovery document is fetched from its issuer URL with /.well-known/jwks.json appended.
questions.x: Discovery uses the openid-configuration path, and the document it returns then points to the JWKS signing-key URL. The JWKS isn't the discovery document itself.

questions.t: A DELETE request on a Salesforce SCIM /Users/<id> resource deactivates the user rather than deleting the record.
questions.f: A DELETE request on a Salesforce SCIM /Users/<id> resource permanently deletes the record, while a PATCH only deactivates the user.
questions.x: Both PATCH and DELETE set the user inactive; the record stays queryable and can be reactivated. Salesforce doesn't hard-delete users through SCIM.

questions.t: Salesforce's SCIM API supports PATCH and filtering, but not bulk operations or sorting.
questions.f: Salesforce's SCIM API supports PATCH, filtering and bulk operations through /Bulk, but not sorting.
questions.x: The service provider configuration advertises PATCH, filters and password changes, while bulk, sorting and ETags are unsupported. The RFC's /Bulk endpoint isn't available.

questions.t: Filtered and list responses from the Salesforce SCIM API return at most 200 results.
questions.f: Filtered and list responses from the Salesforce SCIM API return at most 1,000 results.
questions.x: Salesforce caps SCIM list and filter results at 200, including a query for all entitlements, so specific queries are needed for the rest.

questions.t: Inside an Apex trigger, a SOQL for loop adds no batching benefit, because triggers already receive their records in batches.
questions.f: Inside an Apex trigger, a SOQL for loop is needed to split Trigger.new into batches, because triggers receive all records at once.
questions.x: Trailhead points out that triggers are already batched by the platform, so the SOQL for loop's memory batching gains nothing there. It still helps for large result sets elsewhere.

questions.t: Flow bulkifies records automatically, but it has no native Map or Set, so a Get Records element inside a Loop is a common performance problem.
questions.f: Flow has native Map and Set structures, so a Get Records element inside a Loop is bulkified automatically and causes no performance problem.
questions.x: Flow merges redundant queries and DML across records, but without maps or sets a query placed inside a loop still runs per iteration. That pattern is a frequent cause of slow flows.

questions.t: Salesforce's automation decision guide matches 1 to 200 records to record-triggered Flow and bulk loads of 2,000 to 10,000 or more to an Apex trigger framework.
questions.f: Salesforce's automation decision guide matches 1 to 200 records to an Apex trigger framework and bulk loads of 2,000 to 10,000 or more to record-triggered Flow.
questions.x: Low-density automation suits Flow, while high-volume bulk API loads push toward a coded trigger framework. The false version swaps the two recommendations.

questions.t: Every External ID field on an object also uses up one of that object's custom index slots.
questions.f: External ID fields have their own index allocation, so they don't use up any of the object's custom index slots.
questions.x: Marking a field as an External ID indexes it, and that index counts against the same per-object custom index cap. Adding integration keys can quietly exhaust slots needed for tuning.

questions.t: A custom big object's index can't be edited or deleted once deployed, so changing it means building a new big object.
questions.f: A custom big object's index can be edited after deployment, as long as the big object doesn't yet hold any records.
questions.x: Big object indexes are permanent after deployment, whatever the data volume. The only way to change one is to define a new big object.

questions.t: Currency fields in multicurrency orgs can never receive a custom index, even through a Salesforce Support request.
questions.f: Currency fields in multicurrency orgs can receive a custom index, but only through a Salesforce Support request.
questions.x: The large data volumes guide lists multicurrency currency fields among the types that can't be indexed at all. Support can add indexes on many fields, but not these.

questions.t: Granular locking, which is on by default, lets group membership operations run at the same time when the roles or groups involved are unrelated.
questions.f: Granular locking, which must be enabled by Salesforce Support, lets group membership operations run at the same time when the roles or groups involved are unrelated.
questions.x: Granular locking is already on in orgs by default and relaxes the single global lock for unrelated changes. No Support request is needed to get it.

questions.t: Group membership locking can still occur while sharing calculations are deferred.
questions.f: Deferring sharing calculations prevents group membership locking until the calculations are resumed.
questions.x: Deferral suspends sharing rule and group membership calculation, but the locks on membership tables are still taken. It isn't a way to avoid lock errors.

questions.t: Even with granular locking, role reparenting, such as changing a partner account's owner, blocks almost every other group membership update.
questions.f: With granular locking, role reparenting, such as changing a partner account's owner, runs alongside other group membership updates without blocking them.
questions.x: Granular locking helps unrelated changes, but reparenting a role still takes a lock that blocks nearly all other group updates. Such changes are best scheduled apart from other jobs.

questions.t: Under NIST's PaaS model, the consumer controls its deployed applications but not the underlying servers, operating systems or storage.
questions.f: Under NIST's PaaS model, the consumer controls its deployed applications and the underlying operating systems, but not the servers or storage.
questions.x: NIST SP 800-145 leaves the network, servers, operating systems and storage to the provider in PaaS. Control over operating systems is what distinguishes IaaS.

questions.t: Access to a FedRAMP package granted through the Package Access Request Form lasts 60 days and can be extended in 30-day increments.
questions.f: Access to a FedRAMP package granted through the Package Access Request Form lasts 12 months and can be extended in 6-month increments.
questions.x: FedRAMP's quick guide gives agencies a 60-day window to review a package, extendable 30 days at a time. Long-lived access comes only after the signed ATO letter reaches the PMO.

questions.t: After an agency emails its signed ATO letter to the FedRAMP PMO, the PMO grants that agency's users permanent access to the package.
questions.f: After an agency emails its signed ATO letter to the FedRAMP PMO, the PMO grants that agency's users access to the package for one more year.
questions.x: Sending the signed ATO letter to the PMO converts the agency's temporary review access into permanent package access. There is no one-year renewal tied to the letter.

questions.t: In FedRAMP's agency playbook, the agency's authorizing official is the person who issues the ATO for a cloud service offering.
questions.f: In FedRAMP's agency playbook, the third-party assessment organization is the party that issues the ATO for a cloud service offering.
questions.x: The ATO is a risk-acceptance decision made by the agency's authorizing official after reviewing the package. Assessors produce evidence such as the Security Assessment Report but do not grant the ATO.

questions.t: The original FISMA was passed in December 2002 as part of the E-Government Act, Public Law 107-347.
questions.f: The original FISMA was passed in December 2014 as part of the E-Government Act, Public Law 107-347.
questions.x: FISMA dates from the 2002 E-Government Act. 2014 is the year of the Federal Information Security Modernization Act, which amended it and kept the acronym.

questions.t: The 2014 FISMA amendments codified the Department of Homeland Security's authority to administer security policy for non-national-security federal systems.
questions.f: The 2014 FISMA amendments codified the Department of Defense's authority to administer security policy for non-national-security federal systems.
questions.x: The modernization act gave DHS that role, including binding operational directives and the federal incident center. DoD is not the administrator for civilian systems under the act.

questions.t: For FISMA Inspector General evaluations, OMB treats a rating of Level 4 or higher on the five-level maturity scale as effective.
questions.f: For FISMA Inspector General evaluations, OMB treats a rating of Level 3 or higher on the five-level maturity scale as effective.
questions.x: OMB's threshold for an effective program is Level 4, Managed and Measurable, though IGs can judge differently given the agency's risk. Level 3 falls below that bar.

questions.t: FedRAMP requires the Control Implementation Summary / Customer Responsibility Matrix workbook as Appendix J to the provider's System Security Plan.
questions.f: FedRAMP requires the Control Implementation Summary / Customer Responsibility Matrix workbook as Appendix A to the provider's System Security Plan.
questions.x: The CIS/CRM workbook is Appendix J of the SSP and marks each control as provider, customer, shared or inherited. Appendix A is not where FedRAMP places it.

questions.t: Per NIST SP 800-210, in SaaS the provider covers access control at every layer except the consumer's application data.
questions.f: Per NIST SP 800-210, in SaaS the consumer controls access in the operating system, middleware, application and data layers.
questions.x: In SaaS almost the whole stack is the provider's job, leaving the consumer its application data. Consumer control from the OS up describes IaaS, not SaaS.

questions.t: Salesforce Health Check can compare an org's security settings against a custom baseline imported as an XML file.
questions.f: Salesforce Health Check can compare an org's security settings only against Salesforce's recommended baseline, with no custom import.
questions.x: Besides Salesforce's own baseline, Health Check accepts a custom baseline imported as XML, which Trailhead suggests agreeing with IT or compliance. So it is not limited to the default baseline.

questions.t: The Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam requires a passing score of 65% across its 60 scored questions.
questions.f: The Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam requires a passing score of 75% across its 60 scored questions.
questions.x: The exam guide sets the pass mark at 65% for the 60 scored multiple-choice questions. 75% is higher than the guide requires.

questions.t: In the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam outline, System Design is the most heavily weighted section at 15%.
questions.f: In the Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam outline, Deploying is the most heavily weighted section at 18%.
questions.x: No section exceeds 15%, and System Design is the one at that ceiling. Deploying is weighted at 14%, so the outline rewards breadth over any single area.

questions.t: The Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam guide says its questions are aligned to the Spring '23 release.
questions.f: The Development Lifecycle and Deployment Architect exam guide says its questions are aligned to the Winter '27 release.
questions.x: The guide pins the question bank to Spring '23, so newer DevOps tooling may not appear on the exam. It is not kept in step with the current release.

questions.t: In the MuleSoft Platform Architect exam outline, Governing web APIs is the heaviest section at 17%.
questions.f: In the MuleSoft Platform Architect exam outline, Deploying to CloudHub is the heaviest section at 17%.
questions.x: Governance of APIs, covering API Manager, policies and gateways, carries the largest weight. Deploying to CloudHub is weighted at 11%.

questions.t: The MuleSoft Platform Architect exam gives candidates 120 minutes for its 60 scored questions.
questions.f: The MuleSoft Platform Architect exam gives candidates 90 minutes for its 60 scored questions.
questions.x: The exam guide allows 120 minutes for 60 scored questions plus up to five unscored ones. A 90-minute limit is shorter than the guide states.

questions.t: The MuleSoft Platform Architect exam has no prerequisite credential, and Trailhead enforces no order among the MuleSoft certifications.
questions.f: The MuleSoft Platform Architect exam requires passing a MuleSoft Developer credential first, as Trailhead enforces a set order.
questions.x: The exam guide lists no prerequisite and Trailhead imposes no sequence among MuleSoft credentials. Candidates can sit the architect exam without first holding a developer credential.

questions.t: Trailhead's Nonprofit Cloud governance unit suggests roughly one Salesforce administrator per 50 users as a starting heuristic.
questions.f: Trailhead's Nonprofit Cloud governance unit suggests roughly one Salesforce administrator per 200 users as a starting heuristic.
questions.x: The unit's rule of thumb is about one admin for every 50 users, adjusted for other duties and request volume. One per 200 understates the staffing it suggests.

questions.t: Salesforce Architects advise that a finalized architectural guiding principle is superseded by a new principle rather than reworded.
questions.f: Salesforce Architects advise that a finalized architectural guiding principle is reworded in place with a new version number rather than superseded.
questions.x: Once a principle is Final, changing it means issuing a new principle that supersedes it, keeping the record clear. Editing the wording of the final principle is what the guidance avoids.

questions.t: Salesforce Architects' security governance steps say deviations and known vulnerabilities should be recorded in the technical debt register.
questions.f: Salesforce Architects' security governance steps say deviations and known vulnerabilities should be recorded only in Shield Event Monitoring.
questions.x: Security exceptions are tracked as technical debt so they get prioritized and paid down. Shield Event Monitoring is the audit and monitoring tool, not a register of accepted deviations.

questions.t: Flow's HTTP Callout action needs no OpenAPI specification, because Flow infers the request and response schema from sample JSON.
questions.f: Flow's HTTP Callout action needs an uploaded OpenAPI specification, because Flow cannot infer the schema from sample JSON.
questions.x: HTTP Callout builds its data structures from sample JSON or a live Connect for Schema call. Uploading an OpenAPI spec is the route for registering an external service from Setup.

questions.t: In Winter '24, Flow's HTTP Callout editor added POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE, which earlier required hand-editing the generated API spec.
questions.f: In Winter '24, Flow's HTTP Callout editor added GET, which earlier required hand-editing the generated API spec.
questions.x: GET was already generally available from Summer '23. Winter '24 brought the other four methods into the declarative editor.

questions.t: Flow's HTTP Callout action supports only APIs that respond with JSON.
questions.f: Flow's HTTP Callout action supports APIs that respond with either JSON or XML.
questions.x: The feature is JSON only, with shapes taken from the samples supplied. Integrations that need non-JSON payloads should use Apex callouts instead.

questions.t: A single flow test simulates either a record create or a record update, so a flow that reacts to both needs separate tests.
questions.f: A single flow test can simulate both a record create and a record update, so one test covers a flow that reacts to both.
questions.x: Each flow test is tied to one trigger event, Created or Updated. Covering both events therefore takes two tests.

questions.t: Running flow tests with the sf flow run test command requires the View All Data permission.
questions.f: Running flow tests with the sf flow run test command requires only the Run Flows permission.
questions.x: The CLI reference lists View All Data as required for sf flow run test. Run Flows on its own is not enough to run tests from the command line.

questions.t: The sf flow run test command runs flow tests asynchronously by default and returns a test run ID unless --synchronous is passed.
questions.f: The sf flow run test command runs flow tests synchronously by default and returns results unless --async is passed.
questions.x: The command is asynchronous by default, handing back a run ID; the --synchronous flag makes it wait. There is no --async flag because async is already the default.

questions.t: After a Wait element, resumed flow interviews of the same flow version and running user share one batch transaction and its governor limits.
questions.f: After a Wait element, each resumed flow interview runs in its own transaction with its own set of governor limits.
questions.x: Resumed interviews are grouped into a batch transaction, so their combined SOQL and DML can exceed limits. They do not each get a fresh limit budget.

questions.t: A Salesforce org processes up to 1,000 time-based flow resume events per hour, and extra events slip to the next hour.
questions.f: A Salesforce org processes up to 250 time-based flow resume events per hour, and extra events are discarded.
questions.x: The documented cap is 1,000 time-based resume events per hour; anything beyond it is deferred to the following hour rather than dropped.

questions.t: Record-triggered flows can use the action-level new-transaction setting only on asynchronous or scheduled paths.
questions.f: Record-triggered flows can use the action-level new-transaction setting only on the Run Immediately path.
questions.x: Since Winter '26 every flow type has the setting, but record-triggered flows are restricted to async or scheduled paths. The immediate path stays in the triggering save's transaction.

questions.t: The Health Cloud Platform permission set license grants Health Cloud standard objects for features built into core Salesforce, outside the managed package.
questions.f: The Health Cloud Platform permission set license grants the custom objects behind features in the Health Cloud managed package.
questions.x: Health Cloud needs two licenses: Health Cloud covers the managed-package objects, while Health Cloud Platform covers the core standard objects. The false statement describes the other license.

questions.t: The Health Cloud for Experience Cloud Site permission set license is not available to Partner Community users.
questions.f: The Health Cloud for Experience Cloud Site permission set license is available only to Partner Community users.
questions.x: The site license covers Experience Cloud site users but explicitly excludes Partner Community users. So it cannot be a partner-only license.

questions.t: Health Cloud requires Enterprise or Unlimited Edition running in Lightning Experience.
questions.f: Health Cloud is available in Professional, Enterprise and Unlimited editions, in Lightning Experience or Salesforce Classic.
questions.x: Salesforce's setup docs require Enterprise or Unlimited Edition and Lightning Experience. Professional Edition and Classic are not supported.

questions.t: The enableOmniStudioMetadata setting exposes Omnistudio components to the Metadata and Tooling APIs and can't be turned off once enabled.
questions.f: The enableOmniStudioMetadata setting exposes Omnistudio components to the Metadata and Tooling APIs and can be turned off at any time.
questions.x: This OmniStudioSettings switch is one-way: once components are exposed as metadata, the setting stays on. Plan for that before enabling it.

questions.t: In Omnistudio's standard data model, Data Mappers are stored in the OmniDataTransform object.
questions.f: In Omnistudio's standard data model, Data Mappers are stored in the OmniUiCard object.
questions.x: The standard model stores Omniscripts in OmniProcess, Data Mappers in OmniDataTransform and FlexCards in OmniUiCard. OmniUiCard holds FlexCards, not Data Mappers.

questions.t: Standard-runtime Omnistudio component names can't contain special characters such as underscores, so stripping them can create duplicate Data Mapper names.
questions.f: Standard-runtime Omnistudio component names can contain underscores, so migrated Data Mapper names never need changing.
questions.x: The standard runtime disallows special characters like underscores, and removing them during migration can collide names, which the Migration Assistant's assess mode flags.

questions.t: When Salesforce renamed Agentforce topics to subagents in April 2026, the Topic Selector was renamed the Agent Router.
questions.f: When Salesforce renamed Agentforce topics to subagents in April 2026, the Topic Selector was renamed the Atlas Planner.
questions.x: The rename was terminology only: topics became subagents, Topic Selector became Agent Router, and Connected Agent became Connected Subagent. There is no Atlas Planner rename.

questions.t: In Agentforce filters, context variables are fixed at session start, while custom variables are set from action outputs.
questions.f: In Agentforce filters, context variables are set from action outputs, while custom variables are fixed at session start.
questions.x: Context variables capture session context when the conversation starts; custom variables are populated later by actions. Filters on either decide which subagents or actions are available.

questions.t: An Agentforce subagent removed from the Agent Router's references can still be reached through a transition from another subagent.
questions.f: An Agentforce subagent removed from the Agent Router's references becomes unreachable, even through transitions from other subagents.
questions.x: Dropping a subagent from the router means it can't be classified directly, but another subagent can still transition to it. That makes it a deliberately gated step.

questions.t: Data 360 streaming insights can be built only on engagement data, not on streaming profile data.
questions.f: Data 360 streaming insights can be built only on streaming profile data, not on engagement data.
questions.x: Streaming insights aggregate real-time engagement events such as web and mobile page views. Streaming profile data is not a supported source.

questions.t: Unlike a calculated insight, a Data 360 streaming insight can't use existing insights as building blocks.
questions.f: Like a calculated insight, a Data 360 streaming insight can use existing insights as building blocks.
questions.x: The SQL for both is nearly identical, but streaming insights can't reference other insights. Any multi-step logic must live in a single query.

questions.t: Data 360 data action events are kept for four days, so consuming systems should be built to be durable.
questions.f: Data 360 data action events are kept for thirty days, so consuming systems can safely replay a month of history.
questions.x: The developer blog notes a four-day retention window for action events. A thirty-day replay window is far longer than what is kept.

questions.t: In a Data 360 enriched search index, each source chunk becomes three chunks: plain, metadata and generated question.
questions.f: In a Data 360 enriched search index, each source chunk becomes two chunks: plain and LLM-generated summary.
questions.x: Enrichment adds a metadata chunk and a generated-question chunk beside the plain one, tripling chunk count. Generating them also consumes Flex Credits.

questions.t: Data 360 has no keyword-only search index type; keyword matching exists only as one half of hybrid search.
questions.f: Data 360 offers a keyword-only search index type alongside vector and hybrid search indexes.
questions.x: The index types are vector, hybrid and enriched. Keyword scoring appears only inside hybrid search, which fuses it with vector similarity.

questions.t: Choosing Code Extension as a Data 360 search index chunking strategy requires the Data Cloud Architect permission set.
questions.f: Choosing Code Extension as a Data 360 search index chunking strategy requires only the Data Cloud User permission set.
questions.x: Custom Python chunking functions are selected per field after deployment, and that requires the Data Cloud Architect permission set. A basic user permission set is not enough.

questions.t: In Schema Builder, each object move on the canvas is saved automatically, and an Auto-Layout can't be undone.
questions.f: In Schema Builder, object moves are saved only when you click Save, and an Auto-Layout can be undone.
questions.x: Schema Builder autosaves the layout as you move objects, and Auto-Layout is final. There is no manual save or undo step for the arrangement.

questions.t: Schema Builder can't export a schema for reuse in another org; moving a data model between orgs needs metadata deployment.
questions.f: Schema Builder can export a schema as a file that is imported into another org to recreate the data model.
questions.x: Salesforce's considerations state that schemas can't be exported from Schema Builder. Objects and fields move between orgs as metadata instead.

questions.t: A custom field created in Schema Builder is visible and editable for most internal profiles by default.
questions.f: A custom field created in Schema Builder is visible only to the System Administrator profile by default.
questions.x: New fields default to visible and editable for internal profiles, except ones cloned from Partner User or Customer Portal Manager. That permissive default is why field access should be reviewed afterwards.

questions.t: A Lightning message channel's isExposed field defaults to false and, once set to true on a packaged or referenced channel, can't be set back.
questions.f: A Lightning message channel's isExposed field defaults to true and can be switched back to false at any time.
questions.x: isExposed starts as false; turning it on is irreversible once the channel is packaged or referenced. That matters because security review expects channels to stay unexposed.

questions.t: By default an LMS subscriber hears messages only from the active area; subscribing with APPLICATION_SCOPE extends it to the whole app.
questions.f: By default an LMS subscriber hears messages from anywhere in the app; subscribing with APPLICATION_SCOPE limits it to the active area.
questions.x: The default scope is the active tab, subtab or utility item. APPLICATION_SCOPE widens delivery so background console tabs also receive messages.

questions.t: In the Salesforce mobile app, Lightning Message Service is supported for Aura and LWC components but not for Visualforce pages.
questions.f: In the Salesforce mobile app, Lightning Message Service is supported for Aura, LWC and Visualforce pages alike.
questions.x: Mobile support covers Aura and Lightning web components only. Visualforce can use LMS in Lightning Experience on desktop, not in the mobile app.

questions.t: Org Check blocks its API calls once the org's daily API request usage reaches 90%, and warns between 70% and 90%.
questions.f: Org Check blocks its API calls once the org's daily API request usage reaches 70%, and warns between 50% and 70%.
questions.x: Below 70% Org Check runs normally, from 70% to 90% it runs with a warning, and at 90% or more it stops until the rolling 24-hour count drops.

questions.t: In Org Check, a higher score is worse: each anti-pattern found on an item adds one point.
questions.f: In Org Check, a higher score is better: each best practice an item follows adds one point.
questions.x: A blank or zero score is good, and every anti-pattern raises the score by one, so a 4 means four issues. It ranks cleanup work rather than rewarding compliance.

questions.t: Org Check reads only configuration metadata, not business records such as Accounts or Opportunities.
questions.f: Org Check reads configuration metadata and business records such as Accounts and Opportunities to score data quality.
questions.x: The app analyzes setup and code metadata through Tooling, Metadata and related APIs. It does not read record data and never changes metadata or data.

questions.t: A custom domain that serves only Experience Cloud sites tops out at 100 sites, because each Experience Cloud site counts as two.
questions.f: A custom domain that serves only Experience Cloud sites tops out at 200 sites, because each Experience Cloud site counts as one.
questions.x: The ceiling is 200 sites per domain, but an Experience Cloud site counts double, so the practical cap is 100. Counting each as one would overstate the limit.

questions.t: Until it is activated, a new custom domain in Salesforce is served over HTTP rather than HTTPS.
questions.f: Until it is activated, a new custom domain in Salesforce is served over HTTPS using Salesforce's default certificate.
questions.x: HTTPS starts only after activation, so go-live should be planned around that step. Salesforce's default Edge certificate covers only .my.salesforce.com hostnames, not custom domains.

questions.t: A sandbox's custom domain is added in the production org that owns the sandbox, using the Associated Org field.
questions.f: A sandbox's custom domain is added in the sandbox itself, using the Associated Org field.
questions.x: The Associated Org field can be edited only from production, so the domain is configured there and pointed at the sandbox. It is not set up inside the sandbox.

questions.t: SAML 2.0 was approved as an OASIS Standard in March 2005, merging SAML 1.x, Liberty ID-FF and Shibboleth.
questions.f: SAML 2.0 was approved as an OASIS Standard in March 2012, merging SAML 1.x, Liberty ID-FF and Shibboleth.
questions.x: OASIS members approved SAML 2.0 in March 2005, folding in Liberty's ID-FF and Internet2's Shibboleth. 2012 is several years too late.

questions.t: A transient SAML NameID is a one-time value discarded at session end, while a persistent NameID stays linked to the SP account until removed.
questions.f: A persistent SAML NameID is a one-time value discarded at session end, while a transient NameID stays linked to the SP account until removed.
questions.x: Transient identifiers give the user anonymity at the SP because they are thrown away after the session. Persistent identifiers keep a lasting link to the SP account.

questions.t: A SAML response sent through the browser on the HTTP POST binding must be digitally signed with XML Signature.
questions.f: A SAML response sent through the browser on the HTTP POST binding must be encrypted, while signing it is optional.
questions.x: Because the POST response passes through the user's browser, SAML requires an XML signature to protect its integrity. OASIS also notes encryption alone does not provide integrity.

questions.t: When Salesforce is the SAML service provider and several session indexes arrive, it keeps only the first one.
questions.f: When Salesforce is the SAML service provider and several session indexes arrive, it keeps only the most recent one.
questions.x: Salesforce as SP stores just the first session index, which can't exceed 512 characters. Later indexes in the same exchange are not kept.

questions.t: A Salesforce-initiated OpenID Connect single logout waits about 10 seconds before redirecting to the login page.
questions.f: A Salesforce-initiated OpenID Connect single logout waits about 60 seconds before redirecting to the login page.
questions.x: The short pause of roughly 10 seconds gives the relying party time to finish logging out. A full minute is far longer than Salesforce waits.

questions.t: The LogoutEventStream event fires for UI logouts, but simply closing the browser never publishes it.
questions.f: The LogoutEventStream event fires for UI logouts and is also published whenever the user closes the browser.
questions.x: Only explicit UI logouts publish the event, plus timeouts when Force logout on session timeout is on. Closing the browser leaves no logout event to act on.

questions.t: When a Connect REST API request exceeds the REST rate limit, Salesforce returns 503 Service Unavailable.
questions.f: When a Connect REST API request exceeds the REST rate limit, Salesforce returns 429 Too Many Requests.
questions.x: Connect REST API signals an exceeded limit with HTTP 503. Clients that only watch for 429 will miss it.

questions.t: In Apex, every ConnectApi write operation counts as one DML statement against governor limits.
questions.f: In Apex, ConnectApi write operations count only against API request limits, not against the DML statement limit.
questions.x: Each ConnectApi write costs a DML statement, and most ConnectApi calls also count toward the org's API allocation. They consume both budgets.

questions.t: ConnectApi methods run as the context user and don't support System.runAs, and most need @IsTest(SeeAllData=true) in tests.
questions.f: ConnectApi methods support System.runAs in tests, and most work with test-created data without SeeAllData=true.
questions.x: ConnectApi ignores runAs and usually needs org data, so tests typically set SeeAllData=true. Some methods instead need canned output registered with a setTest method.

questions.t: Salesforce product guidance points record integrations to Bulk API 2.0 once a job generally exceeds 2,000 records.
questions.f: Salesforce product guidance points record integrations to Bulk API 2.0 once a job generally exceeds 50,000 records.
questions.x: Below about 2,000 records, REST sObject and Composite resources fit better; above it, Bulk API 2.0's job model pays off. Waiting until 50,000 records sets the threshold far too high.

questions.t: The Composite Graph resource can run up to 500 subrequests, processing each graph all-or-nothing.
questions.f: The Composite Graph resource can run up to 100 subrequests, processing each graph all-or-nothing.
questions.x: Composite Graph raises the subrequest ceiling to 500, compared with 25 for plain Composite, and each graph succeeds or fails as a unit.

questions.t: SOAP API and the original Bulk API remain supported but are no longer enhanced, so new work should favour REST and Bulk API 2.0.
questions.f: SOAP API and the original Bulk API are still actively enhanced, so new work can favour them equally with REST and Bulk API 2.0.
questions.x: Salesforce keeps the older APIs running but invests in REST and Bulk API 2.0. New integrations should therefore start on the actively developed APIs.

questions.t: NIST SP 800-145 defines cloud computing through five essential characteristics, three service models and four deployment models.
questions.f: NIST SP 800-145 defines cloud computing through four essential characteristics, three service models and three deployment models.
questions.x: The NIST definition lists five characteristics, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS as service models, and private, community, public and hybrid as deployment models. The false counts drop a characteristic and a deployment model.

questions.t: NIST's cloud reference architecture, SP 500-292, names five actors: cloud consumer, provider, auditor, broker and carrier.
questions.f: NIST's cloud reference architecture, SP 500-292, names four actors: cloud consumer, provider, broker and carrier, with no auditor.
questions.x: SP 500-292 includes the cloud auditor as a fifth actor, responsible for independent assessment of cloud services. Leaving it out drops the role that links to programmes like FedRAMP.

questions.t: In NIST's deployment models, a community cloud serves a group of organizations with shared concerns such as mission or compliance.
questions.f: In NIST's deployment models, a hybrid cloud serves a group of organizations with shared concerns such as mission or compliance.
questions.x: A community cloud is the shared-concern model. A hybrid cloud binds two or more deployment models together so data and applications can move between them.

questions.t: In a FedRAMP Rev5 monthly POA&M, every unique vulnerability is tracked as its own item rather than grouped.
questions.f: In a FedRAMP Rev5 monthly POA&M, vulnerabilities are grouped into one item per affected security control.
questions.x: The legacy continuous monitoring playbook requires a separate POA&M entry for each unique vulnerability. Grouping them under a control would hide individual findings.

questions.t: Under FedRAMP's 2026 Collaborative Continuous Monitoring, the quarterly review is required for Classes C and D but optional for Class A.
questions.f: Under FedRAMP's 2026 Collaborative Continuous Monitoring, the quarterly review is required for every class, including Class A.
questions.x: The synchronous review after each Ongoing Certification Report is optional for Class A, recommended for Class B and required for Classes C and D.

questions.t: Salesforce Security Center keeps up to 6 months of trend data on metrics aggregated from child tenants.
questions.f: Salesforce Security Center keeps up to 24 months of trend data on metrics aggregated from child tenants.
questions.x: A Security Center parent tenant tracks posture metrics such as permission assignments and Health Check scores with up to 6 months of history. Two years overstates its retention.

questions.t: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 organizes the RMF into seven steps, and Prepare is the only step new in that revision.
questions.f: NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2 organizes the RMF into seven steps, and Monitor is the only step new in that revision.
questions.x: Revision 2 added Prepare at the front; Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize and Monitor carried over from Revision 1.

questions.t: The NIST RMF operates at three levels: the organization, the mission or business process, and the individual information system.
questions.f: The NIST RMF operates at two levels: the organization and the individual information system, with no process level.
questions.x: The RMF explicitly includes a middle mission or business process level between the organization and the system. Omitting it misdescribes how risk decisions connect.

questions.t: Under the NIST RMF, a common control authorization approves controls that many systems inherit.
questions.f: Under the NIST RMF, an authorization to use approves controls that many systems inherit.
questions.x: The RMF names the common control authorization as the decision for inheritable controls. An authorization to operate or to use applies to a single system.

questions.t: GroupMember rows exist only for a public group's direct members, so users who inherit membership through a role or subgroup aren't listed.
questions.f: GroupMember rows list every user a public group covers, including users who inherit membership through a role or subgroup.
questions.x: Only direct members get GroupMember rows; role, territory and nested-group members are represented by their group IDs. Querying GroupMember alone therefore misses inherited users.

questions.t: The GroupMember object supports create, delete, query and retrieve, but not update.
questions.f: The GroupMember object supports create, update, delete and query, so a membership row can be repointed to another user.
questions.x: GroupMember has no update call; to change membership you delete one row and insert another. Inserting a duplicate just returns the existing row.

questions.t: For a public group, the doesIncludeBosses field behind Grant Access Using Hierarchies is documented as defaulting to true.
questions.f: For a public group, the doesIncludeBosses field behind Grant Access Using Hierarchies is documented as defaulting to false.
questions.x: Regular groups default to sharing upward to members' managers in the role hierarchy. Admins clear the setting when a team's records shouldn't flow to their managers.

questions.t: The current B2C Solution Architect credential page lists two prerequisites: Platform App Builder and Platform Integration Architect.
questions.f: The current B2C Solution Architect credential page lists three prerequisites: Marketing Cloud Email Specialist, Platform App Builder and Platform Integration Architect.
questions.x: Marketing Cloud Email Specialist was a prerequisite at launch but no longer appears on the live credential page. Only App Builder and Integration Architect remain.

questions.t: In the B2C Solution Architect exam, Discovery and Customer Success is the largest section, at 27%.
questions.f: In the B2C Solution Architect exam, Architecture Design is the largest section, at 27%.
questions.x: Discovery and Customer Success carries 27%, more than Architecture Design at 18%. The weighting shows that business skills are tested heavily.

questions.t: Functional Capabilities and Business Value is the lightest B2C Solution Architect exam section, weighted at 7%.
questions.f: Integration is the lightest B2C Solution Architect exam section, weighted at 7%.
questions.x: Functional Capabilities and Business Value carries only 7%, whereas Integration is one of the heavier sections at 23%.

questions.t: In Trailhead's risk register method, probability and impact are each rated 1 to 3 and multiplied, and scores of 7 to 9 mean high exposure.
questions.f: In Trailhead's risk register method, probability and impact are each rated 1 to 3 and added, and scores of 5 to 6 mean high exposure.
questions.x: The score is the product of the two ratings, giving 1 to 9, with 1-3 low, 4-6 moderate and 7-9 high. Adding the ratings is not the method Trailhead uses.

questions.t: UK government delivery guidance says significant assumptions should be logged as risks, stating the impact if they prove false.
questions.f: UK government delivery guidance says significant assumptions should be kept off the risk register and tracked only in a separate assumption log.
questions.x: The Teal Book folds assumptions into the risk register, recording what happens if each proves false. Keeping them apart is not what it recommends.

questions.t: When a logged risk materializes, it moves to the issue log and is closed on the risk register.
questions.f: When a logged risk materializes, it stays open on the risk register and its mitigation plan is reused as the resolution.
questions.x: A risk that happens becomes an issue, which needs a prioritized resolution plan rather than mitigation. The risk entry is closed, though it stays visible for history.

questions.t: A Salesforce email alert can add up to 5 extra CC email addresses beyond its typed recipients.
questions.f: A Salesforce email alert can add up to 25 extra CC email addresses beyond its typed recipients.
questions.x: The WorkflowAlert ccEmails list is capped at five addresses. Larger audiences belong in typed recipients such as public groups or roles.

questions.t: The emailAlert invocable action takes a single input, SObjectRowId, and returns no outputs.
questions.f: The emailAlert invocable action takes recipient addresses and a template ID as inputs and returns the sent message ID.
questions.x: Template and recipients are fixed in the alert, so the caller only names the record. The action returns nothing.

questions.t: Email alerts are object-specific, so an alert built on Case can't be fired for an Account record.
questions.f: Email alerts are object-agnostic, so an alert built on Case can be fired for an Account record.
questions.x: Each alert is defined on one object and fills merge fields from that object's record. A different object needs its own alert.

questions.t: A scheduled path's batch size defaults to 200, which is also its maximum, and can be lowered to 1.
questions.f: A scheduled path's batch size defaults to 200 and can be raised to 2,000 for large volumes.
questions.x: Records due in the same minute are batched at up to 200; lowering the size helps the path's actions stay within governor limits. It cannot go above 200.

questions.t: A failed scheduled-path interview is retried up to 5 times, at roughly 15, 30, 60, 120 and 240 minutes.
questions.f: A failed scheduled-path interview is retried up to 3 times, at roughly 15, 30 and 60 minutes.
questions.x: Salesforce retries a failed scheduled path five times with growing intervals up to about four hours, sending an error email. Three retries understates it.

questions.t: $Record__Prior isn't supported in scheduled-path elements or in entry-condition formulas.
questions.f: $Record__Prior is supported in scheduled-path elements, though not in entry-condition formulas.
questions.x: Prior values aren't available when the path runs later. The Admins blog's workaround is a before-save flow that sets a switch field for the path to read.

questions.t: In Agentforce Nonprofit, a household is a business account that a Party Relationship Group record marks as a household.
questions.f: In Agentforce Nonprofit, a household is a dedicated Household custom object that contacts are linked to by lookup.
questions.x: The built-in model uses a business account plus a Party Relationship Group, which also holds household-level details. A separate Household custom object is not how it is modeled.

questions.t: In Agentforce Nonprofit, a reciprocal relationship such as spouse-to-spouse must be stored as two relationship records.
questions.f: In Agentforce Nonprofit, a reciprocal relationship such as spouse-to-spouse is stored as one record that reads correctly from both sides.
questions.x: Each direction of a reciprocal contact-contact link needs its own record. That matters for data loads and duplicate checks.

questions.t: In Agentforce Nonprofit fundraising, a GiftCommitment holds a pledge or recurring promise, while each completed payment is a GiftTransaction.
questions.f: In Agentforce Nonprofit fundraising, a GiftCommitment holds a pledge or recurring promise, while each completed payment is an Opportunity.
questions.x: Fundraising uses dedicated gift objects rather than repurposed Opportunities, with GiftTransaction recording each payment received.

questions.t: Trailhead states that Financial Services Cloud has been renamed Agentforce Financial Services.
questions.f: Trailhead states that Financial Services Cloud has been renamed Agentforce Banking.
questions.x: The new name follows the Agentforce Sales and Agentforce Service branding and covers banking, wealth and insurance. Agentforce Banking is not the product's name.

questions.t: Financial Services Cloud managed package components are one API version behind core Salesforce, while its standard objects share the core version.
questions.f: Financial Services Cloud standard objects are one API version behind core Salesforce, while its managed package components share the core version.
questions.x: The developer guide warns that FinServ-namespaced package components lag core by a version. Standard FSC objects ship with core and match its API version.

questions.t: In MCP for Agentforce, external and third-party MCP servers are registered in Agentforce Registry, while MuleSoft servers go through API Catalog.
questions.f: In MCP for Agentforce, MuleSoft MCP servers are registered in Agentforce Registry, while external and third-party servers go through API Catalog.
questions.x: Agentforce Registry is the home for external and third-party servers; MuleSoft and Salesforce standard or custom servers are registered through API Catalog. The false statement swaps the two registration paths.

questions.t: When an MCP server's tool descriptions change significantly, Agentforce Registry blocks the affected action and alerts the admin.
questions.f: When an MCP server's tool descriptions change significantly, Agentforce Registry silently adopts the new descriptions and keeps the action running.
questions.x: To guard against tool drift, the registry blocks an action whose server-side tool description changed significantly and notifies the admin, rather than quietly accepting the change.

questions.t: ISVs can package MCP server registration metadata in managed 2GP packages, but MCP tool actions and Gateway policies must be created by subscribers after install.
questions.f: ISVs can package MCP server registration metadata, MCP tool actions and Gateway policies together in managed 2GP packages.
questions.x: The four registration metadata types can ship in 2GP packages at API version 66.0 or later, but tool actions and Agentforce Gateway policies can't be packaged yet, so subscribers set them up after installing.

questions.t: To create a Salesforce file through the API, you insert a ContentVersion, and Salesforce creates the parent ContentDocument automatically.
questions.f: To create a Salesforce file through the API, you insert a ContentDocument first, then attach the bytes with a ContentVersion.
questions.x: ContentDocument supports query, update and delete but not create. Inserting a ContentVersion with no ContentDocumentId makes the platform generate the parent document for you.

questions.t: On a ContentDocumentLink, ShareType C grants Collaborator access, letting the user edit the file as well as view it.
questions.f: On a ContentDocumentLink, ShareType C grants Inferred access, taken from the linked record or library permission.
questions.x: ShareType values are V for Viewer, C for Collaborator (view plus edit) and I for Inferred. The false statement assigns the meaning of I to C.

questions.t: Deleting a ContentDocument cascades to its links, but those cascaded ContentDocumentLink deletions don't fire ContentDocumentLink triggers.
questions.f: Deleting a ContentDocument cascades to its links, and each cascaded ContentDocumentLink deletion fires the ContentDocumentLink delete trigger.
questions.x: When a document is deleted its versions and links go with it, but the link deletions happen without running ContentDocumentLink triggers, so trigger logic that relies on them will miss those deletes.

questions.t: Data 360's Suggest Tags feature reads object and field metadata, not field values, and every suggestion needs administrator approval.
questions.f: Data 360's Suggest Tags feature scans stored field values, and its suggestions are applied automatically without administrator approval.
questions.x: Suggest Tags works only from metadata about objects and fields and never inspects the data itself. An administrator must approve each proposed tag before it takes effect.

questions.t: In a hierarchical Data 360 tag taxonomy, a child tag inherits the governance policies attached to its parent tag.
questions.f: In a hierarchical Data 360 tag taxonomy, a parent tag inherits the governance policies attached to each of its child tags.
questions.x: Building tags as a hierarchy lets policies flow downward, so a child tag picks up its parent's policies. Inheritance does not run upward from children to parents.

questions.t: The Platform Data Architect exam gives the Data Governance section a 10% weighting.
questions.f: The Platform Data Architect exam gives the Data Governance section a 25% weighting.
questions.x: Data Governance makes up 10% of the Platform Data Architect exam, covering GDPR-compliant data models and enterprise governance programs. 25% overstates its share.

questions.t: A Visualforce standard controller enforces the user's object access and runs in user mode, while a custom controller runs in system mode.
questions.f: A Visualforce custom controller enforces the user's object access and runs in user mode, while a standard controller runs in system mode.
questions.x: Standard controllers reuse the standard page logic and respect the user's permissions. Custom controllers are Apex classes that run in system mode, so the developer must enforce access; the false statement swaps the two.

questions.t: A Visualforce page's view state, stored in an encrypted hidden form field, is capped at 170 KB.
questions.f: A Visualforce page's view state, stored in an encrypted hidden form field, is capped at 1 MB.
questions.x: Component state, field values and the controller are serialized into view state with a 170 KB ceiling, which is why developers use transient variables and narrower queries to keep it small.

questions.t: Adding lightningStylesheets to a Visualforce page gives it the Lightning look, but it isn't supported in Experience Cloud sites or PDF rendering.
questions.f: Adding lightningStylesheets to a Visualforce page gives it the Lightning look everywhere, including Experience Cloud sites and PDF rendering.
questions.x: The lightningStylesheets attribute styles pages in Lightning Experience and the mobile app only. Experience Cloud sites and renderAs PDF output don't get that styling.

questions.t: To be wired to a Lightning web component, an Apex method must be static and annotated @AuraEnabled(cacheable=true).
questions.f: To be wired to a Lightning web component, an Apex method must be an instance method annotated @AuraEnabled(cacheable=false).
questions.x: Wired Apex has to be static, public or global, and marked cacheable=true, which also means it may only read data. Non-cacheable or mutating methods must be called imperatively.

questions.t: Wired Apex data in a Lightning web component is refreshed by passing the previously emitted wire value to refreshApex().
questions.f: Wired Apex data in a Lightning web component is refreshed automatically by Lightning Data Service whenever the underlying records change.
questions.x: Lightning Data Service doesn't manage results from Apex, so stale wired Apex values must be refreshed explicitly with refreshApex(), which returns a promise.

questions.t: A wire adapter only provisions data once every dynamic parameter in its config has a value; an undefined parameter means nothing is fetched.
questions.f: A wire adapter provisions data as soon as the component connects, treating any undefined dynamic parameter in its config as null.
questions.x: The wire service waits until all reactive config values are defined before running the adapter. Passing null to wired Apex still invokes it, but undefined does not.
