questions.t: In a managed 2GP, setting ancestorVersion to HIGHEST always resolves to the highest promoted version, keeping the upgrade path linear.
questions.f: In a managed 2GP, setting ancestorVersion to HIGHEST always resolves to the newest beta build, keeping the upgrade path linear.
questions.x: Only versions promoted to managed-released can be ancestors, and HIGHEST picks the highest of those. Beta builds never qualify as ancestors.

questions.t: Building a managed 2GP version on anything other than the highest promoted version requires the --skip-ancestor-check flag.
questions.f: Building a managed 2GP version on anything other than the highest promoted version requires the --branch flag.
questions.x: Branching away from the highest promoted version, for example to abandon a flawed release, must be acknowledged with sf package version create --skip-ancestor-check.

questions.t: A managed 2GP patch version can never be the direct ancestor of a non-patch version.
questions.f: A managed 2GP patch version can be the direct ancestor of a non-patch version if both share the same major number.
questions.x: Patches may chain to other patches with matching major and minor numbers, but a non-patch version must name a non-patch ancestor, or use HIGHEST.

questions.t: The legacy Salesforce Data Mask package is installed in production, but its masking jobs run only in sandboxes.
questions.f: The legacy Salesforce Data Mask package is installed in each sandbox, and its masking jobs can run in production as well.
questions.x: Data Mask is installed in the production org so configurations carry into refreshed sandboxes, yet jobs execute only in sandboxes to prevent masking real production records by accident.

questions.t: A Salesforce Data Mask job bypasses triggers, validation rules and flows, and deletes the masked object's Field History Tracking when it finishes.
questions.f: A Salesforce Data Mask job runs triggers, validation rules and flows, and logs each masked value in the object's Field History Tracking.
questions.x: Masking skips automation, including managed-package automation, to run efficiently, and it wipes field history for the masked object so old values aren't left behind.

questions.t: Service for the legacy Salesforce Data Mask package ends on December 31, 2026, with customers directed to Data Mask & Seed.
questions.f: Service for the legacy Salesforce Data Mask package ends on December 31, 2026, with customers directed to Shield Platform Encryption.
questions.x: Salesforce labels the Data Mask package legacy and names Data Mask & Seed as its successor; Shield Platform Encryption protects production data at rest and isn't the replacement.

questions.t: A profile with the External Identity license can access up to ten custom objects, and custom objects from managed packages don't count toward that.
questions.f: A profile with the External Identity license can access up to ten custom objects, including any custom objects installed from managed packages.
questions.x: External Identity grants a short list of standard objects plus at most ten custom objects per profile. Managed-package custom objects are excluded from the count.

questions.t: For External Identity users, Salesforce recommends staying under 10 million unique logins per month to avoid extra charges or degraded functionality.
questions.f: For External Identity users, Salesforce recommends staying under 1 million unique logins per month to avoid extra charges or degraded functionality.
questions.x: The guidance is 10 million unique logins a month; beyond that customers may face added cost and reduced functionality and should talk to Salesforce first.

questions.t: Experience Cloud objects such as Cases, Orders and Tasks aren't included in the External Identity license; users need a Community license for them.
questions.f: Experience Cloud objects such as Cases, Orders and Tasks are included in the External Identity license once the default profile is cloned.
questions.x: The license is identity-focused and excludes service objects like Cases, Contracts, Orders and Tasks. Cloning the profile can't grant objects the license lacks; upgrading users to a Community license can.

questions.t: The default refresh token policy on a Salesforce connected app is that the refresh token is valid until revoked.
questions.f: The default refresh token policy on a Salesforce connected app is that the refresh token expires if not used for 90 days.
questions.x: Out of the box, a refresh token never expires on its own and works until a user or admin revokes it. Inactivity windows and fixed lifetimes are options an admin has to choose.

questions.t: With Salesforce refresh token rotation enabled, every refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, and rotation can't be turned off once on.
questions.f: With Salesforce refresh token rotation enabled, every refresh issues a new refresh token while the old one stays valid, and rotation can be turned off at any time.
questions.x: Rotation replaces the refresh token on each use so a stolen token dies at the next legitimate refresh. Salesforce makes the setting irreversible once enabled.

questions.t: A Salesforce refresh token IP allowlist can hold at most 256 IP addresses across all of its ranges.
questions.f: A Salesforce refresh token IP allowlist can hold at most 16 IP ranges, with no cap on the addresses they cover.
questions.x: The allowlist, used with the web server flow, blocks refresh requests from outside its ranges and is capped at 256 addresses in total, not a count of ranges.

questions.t: The SOAP API partner WSDL is loosely typed and works against any org, while the enterprise WSDL is strongly typed to one org's schema.
questions.f: The SOAP API enterprise WSDL is loosely typed and works against any org, while the partner WSDL is strongly typed to one org's schema.
questions.x: ISVs use the partner WSDL because it isn't tied to a specific object model. The enterprise WSDL mirrors one org's objects and fields and must be regenerated when they change; the false statement swaps them.

questions.t: The SOAP API create() and update() calls accept at most 200 records per call, and a larger request fails entirely.
questions.f: The SOAP API create() and update() calls accept at most 2,000 records per call, and a larger request fails entirely.
questions.x: Synchronous SOAP writes are capped at 200 records per call, which is why very large loads are usually sent through Bulk API 2.0 instead.

questions.t: SOAP API login() calls count toward a login rate limit of 3,600 calls per user per hour.
questions.f: SOAP API login() calls count toward a login rate limit of 3,600 calls per org per day.
questions.x: The login rate limit is applied per user and per hour, at 3,600 calls. It is separate from the org's rolling 24-hour API request allocation.

questions.t: UI API batch object-info requests accept up to 2,000 objects, while batch create, update and delete accept up to 200 records per request.
questions.f: UI API batch object-info requests accept up to 200 objects, while batch create, update and delete accept up to 2,000 records per request.
questions.x: Metadata-only batch reads of object info can cover up to 2,000 objects, but record writes in a batch are capped at 200. The false statement reverses the two numbers.

questions.t: UI API supports HTTP caching: a client sends an ETag back in If-None-Match and gets 304 Not Modified if its copy is still current.
questions.f: UI API supports HTTP caching: a client sends an ETag back in If-None-Match and gets 204 No Content if its copy is still current.
questions.x: UI API responses include ETags, and a conditional request whose ETag still matches is answered with 304 Not Modified, returning headers only.

questions.t: When sending integers of 2^31 or larger to User Interface API, clients must pass them as quoted strings.
questions.f: When sending integers of 2^31 or larger to User Interface API, clients must pass them in scientific notation.
questions.x: Large integers at or above 2^31 have to be sent as quoted strings so they aren't mangled as JSON numbers; scientific notation isn't the documented format. Dates, separately, use ISO 8601.

questions.t: Even in a Hyperforce Operating Zone, setup metadata such as object names and custom Apex code, plus search queries, is stored in the United States.
questions.f: In a Hyperforce Operating Zone, setup metadata such as object names and custom Apex code, plus search queries, never leaves the zone.
questions.x: Salesforce documents administrative data, including object names, URLs, Apex code and search queries (not results), as stored in the US, one of the zone's defined exceptions.

questions.t: Customers who joined the EU Operating Zone before December 17, 2024 have their data stored in Germany.
questions.f: Customers who joined the EU Operating Zone before December 17, 2024 have their data stored in Switzerland.
questions.x: AWS hosting for the zone is in Germany and Switzerland. Customers onboarded before the December 2024 cutoff are stored in Germany, while new customers choose a country at signup.

questions.t: Under NIST's IaaS model, the consumer controls the operating systems, storage and deployed applications, and may have limited control over host firewalls.
questions.f: Under NIST's IaaS model, the provider controls the guest operating systems and deployed applications, and the consumer controls only application settings.
questions.x: IaaS hands the consumer the most control of the three service models: guest OS, storage and applications are theirs to run. Controlling only application settings describes SaaS, not IaaS.

questions.t: In NIST SP 500-292, the IaaS provider controls the host operating system and the hypervisors that expose virtual machines.
questions.f: In NIST SP 500-292, the IaaS consumer controls the host operating system and the hypervisors that expose virtual machines.
questions.x: The provider owns the physical resources plus the host OS and hypervisor layer; the consumer is responsible for guest operating systems, middleware and applications on top.

questions.t: Salesforce Engineering describes Hyperforce as replacing rather than patching infrastructure resources, an immutable infrastructure approach.
questions.f: Salesforce Engineering describes Hyperforce as patching infrastructure resources in place, a mutable infrastructure approach.
questions.x: Hyperforce defines infrastructure as version-controlled code and swaps out resources instead of patching them in place, which is what immutable infrastructure means.

questions.t: Under NIST's SaaS definition, the consumer doesn't control servers, storage or application capabilities, except possibly limited user-specific application settings.
questions.f: Under NIST's SaaS definition, the consumer doesn't control servers or storage but does control the application's capabilities and its runtime.
questions.x: NIST leaves the SaaS consumer only limited, user-specific configuration. Controlling the application and its runtime is closer to PaaS, where consumers deploy their own apps.

questions.t: Trailhead's cloud security module uses Gmail as its example of Software as a Service.
questions.f: Trailhead's cloud security module uses Gmail as its example of Infrastructure as a Service.
questions.x: Gmail is a fully managed application that users simply consume, so Trailhead presents it as SaaS. IaaS would mean renting raw compute, storage and networks.

questions.t: Salesforce's SaaS explainer lists WebEx (1995) and NetSuite (1998) as SaaS examples that predate Salesforce's 1999 launch of web-based CRM.
questions.f: Salesforce's SaaS explainer lists WebEx (1995) and NetSuite (1998) as SaaS examples that followed Salesforce's 1993 launch of web-based CRM.
questions.x: The explainer places Salesforce's web-based CRM in 1999, after early hosted offerings like WebEx and NetSuite, in the late-1990s rise of modern SaaS.

questions.t: Under the EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework, a service's overall SEAL rating is the lowest level it reaches on any of the eight sovereignty objectives.
questions.f: Under the EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework, a service's overall SEAL rating is the average of the levels it reaches across the eight sovereignty objectives.
questions.x: The framework takes the weakest objective as the overall score, so one low rating caps the whole service. It doesn't average the objectives.

questions.t: Shield Cache-Only Keys apply to field-level encryption only, not to Database Encryption.
questions.f: Shield Cache-Only Keys apply to Database Encryption only, not to field-level encryption.
questions.x: Cache-Only Keys keep the data encryption key in a customer-run key service called through a named credential, and they are supported only for field-level encryption.

questions.t: Salesforce re-fetches Shield Cache-Only Keys after cache flushes, which happen at least every 72 hours, so the customer's key service becomes an org dependency.
questions.f: Salesforce fetches Shield Cache-Only Keys once at setup and caches them permanently, so the customer's key service isn't an org dependency.
questions.x: Cached keys are flushed at least every 72 hours and must be fetched again, so if the customer's key service is down, encrypted data can become unavailable.

questions.t: The 2021 GDPR standard contractual clauses come in four modules, covering controller and processor transfers in each combination.
questions.f: The 2021 GDPR standard contractual clauses come in two modules, covering only controller-to-controller and controller-to-processor transfers.
questions.x: The June 2021 SCCs have four modules: controller-to-controller, controller-to-processor, processor-to-processor and processor-to-controller.

questions.t: Per Salesforce's FAQ, EU exporters relying on SCCs or BCRs for US transfers must run a transfer impact assessment, while DPF-based transfers need none.
questions.f: Per Salesforce's FAQ, EU exporters relying on the DPF for US transfers must run a transfer impact assessment, while SCC- or BCR-based transfers need none.
questions.x: The DPF is an adequacy decision, so transfers to certified US recipients don't need a TIA. Transfers under SCCs or BCRs still carry the Schrems II duty to assess the destination's laws.

questions.t: GDPR Article 49 derogations, such as explicit consent, are meant for occasional transfers and not for routine, systematic data flows.
questions.f: GDPR Article 49 derogations, such as explicit consent, are the preferred basis for routine, systematic data flows such as CRM replication.
questions.x: Derogations are the last resort after adequacy and appropriate safeguards, and regulators treat them as exceptional. Systematic replication needs adequacy, SCCs or BCRs.

questions.t: In a Hyperforce Operating Zone, MySearch, Chatbot and some Einstein features aren't part of the OZ products, so license parity must be checked before buying.
questions.f: In a Hyperforce Operating Zone, MySearch, Chatbot and all Einstein features are included in the OZ products, so license parity is guaranteed.
questions.x: Salesforce vets each feature for data leaving the zone and drops ones that would. MySearch, Chatbot and some Einstein features are excluded from the OZ SKUs.

questions.t: Each Salesforce user has exactly one user license but can hold several permission set licenses on top of it.
questions.f: Each Salesforce user has exactly one permission set license but can hold several user licenses on top of it.
questions.x: The user license is the single base license; permission set licenses are optional add-ons that unlock extra features, and a user can have many.

questions.t: A permission set license on its own grants nothing visible; it unlocks permissions that a permission set or profile then has to switch on.
questions.f: A permission set license on its own grants its feature immediately, with no permission set or profile needed to switch it on.
questions.x: Licenses set the ceiling. Admins assign the PSL and then give the user a permission set or profile that actually enables the feature.

questions.t: ISV permission set license definitions work only in second-generation managed packages, and only for net-new packages.
questions.f: ISV permission set license definitions work in both first- and second-generation managed packages, including existing packages.
questions.x: PermissionSetLicenseDefinition is a 2GP-only feature limited to net-new packages and US-based paying production subscribers, so 1GP and existing packages can't use it.

questions.t: An org can have up to 200 active user access policies, and each policy can hold up to 20 actions.
questions.f: An org can have up to 20 active user access policies, and each policy can hold up to 200 actions.
questions.x: Since GA, the active-policy ceiling is 200 per org, while a single policy is capped at 20 grant or revoke actions. Twenty active policies was the old closed-beta limit.

questions.t: When a user matches several active user access policies, only the active policy with the lowest order value applies.
questions.f: When a user matches several active user access policies, all matching policies apply, in ascending order value.
questions.x: The order field, an integer from 0 to 10,000, decides precedence: only the lowest-valued matching active policy runs for that user.

questions.t: User access policies can use profiles and roles as criteria, but can't assign or revoke a profile or role as an action.
questions.f: User access policies can use profiles and roles as criteria, and can also assign a new profile or role to matching users as an action.
questions.x: Policy actions cover permission sets, groups, licenses, public groups and queues only. Profiles and roles can filter users but aren't assignable through a policy.

questions.t: Trailhead names missing CRUD and field-level security enforcement as the most common reason solutions fail the AppExchange security review.
questions.f: Trailhead names cross-site scripting as the most common reason solutions fail the AppExchange security review.
questions.x: The review tests common web threats like injection and XSS, but the top failure cause Trailhead cites is code that doesn't enforce CRUD and field-level security.

questions.t: In a 2020 survey of 157 practitioners, cost was the most frequently chosen criterion in build-vs-buy component decisions, picked by 77%.
questions.f: In a 2020 survey of 157 practitioners, component size was the most frequently chosen criterion in build-vs-buy component decisions, picked by 77%.
questions.x: Cost led the criteria at 77%, ahead of support, longevity and fit. Component size was rarely weighted, which the authors saw as underestimating integration effort.

questions.t: In a 2020 build-vs-buy survey, about 90% of practitioners considered in-house development, and none considered commercial off-the-shelf components alone.
questions.f: In a 2020 build-vs-buy survey, about 90% of practitioners considered commercial off-the-shelf components alone, and none considered in-house development.
questions.x: Most respondents weighed building in-house, often alongside open-source or COTS parts, while no one relied on COTS alone. The false statement inverts the findings.

questions.t: Each org gets 5,000 Einstein Next Best Action strategy requests a month at no charge, and every load or refresh of a page with the component counts.
questions.f: Each org gets 50,000 Einstein Next Best Action strategy requests a month at no charge, and only accepted recommendations count as requests.
questions.x: The free entitlement is 5,000 requests a month, with an add-on adding 10,000. Page loads, refreshes, field updates on the page, strategy tests and REST calls all consume requests.

questions.t: The Einstein Next Best Action component on a Lightning record page can show at most four recommendations.
questions.f: The Einstein Next Best Action component on a Lightning record page can show at most ten recommendations.
questions.x: When configuring the component the admin chooses how many recommendations to show, up to a maximum of four, plus whether to show a reject button.

questions.t: Recommendation strategy flows for Einstein Next Best Action can't call subflows, so shared logic must be duplicated or moved into invocable actions.
questions.f: Recommendation strategy flows for Einstein Next Best Action can call subflows, so shared logic can be reused across strategies.
questions.x: Subflows aren't supported in recommendation strategy flows. Reusable logic has to be copied into each strategy or packaged as an invocable action.

questions.t: B2C Commerce runs on its own platform with its own APIs, while B2B Commerce runs on the Salesforce Lightning Platform alongside CRM data.
questions.f: B2B Commerce runs on its own platform with its own APIs, while B2C Commerce runs on the Salesforce Lightning Platform alongside CRM data.
questions.x: B2C Commerce descends from the Demandware acquisition and keeps a separate platform, whereas B2B Commerce is built on the core Lightning Platform. The false statement swaps them.

questions.t: Storefront Next, the recommended option for new B2C Commerce sites, is built on React and React Router and runs on Managed Runtime.
questions.f: Storefront Next, the recommended option for new B2C Commerce sites, is built on Lightning Web Components and runs on the Lightning Web Runtime.
questions.x: Storefront Next is a React-based, server-side-rendered storefront on Managed Runtime. LWC on LWR is how B2B and D2C stores are built in Experience Builder.

questions.t: The B2C Commerce documentation positions SCAPI as the main API for customization, ahead of the older OCAPI.
questions.f: The B2C Commerce documentation positions OCAPI as the main API for customization, ahead of the newer SCAPI.
questions.x: The B2C Commerce API (SCAPI) is the primary customization API and backs the build-your-own storefront option; OCAPI is the older interface.

questions.t: The Heroku Connect demo plan caps sync at 10,000 rows across all mappings, with a 10-minute minimum polling interval.
questions.f: The Heroku Connect demo plan caps sync at 100,000 rows across all mappings, with a 1-minute minimum polling interval.
questions.x: The demo plan is deliberately small: 10,000 rows total and polling no more often than every 10 minutes. Enterprise and Shield plans set row allocations by contract.

questions.t: Heroku Eco dynos go to sleep after 30 minutes of inactivity, so the next request waits a few seconds while they wake.
questions.f: Heroku Eco dynos go to sleep after 24 hours of inactivity, so the next request waits a few seconds while they wake.
questions.x: Eco dynos sleep after half an hour without traffic, adding a short delay to the first request afterward. That makes them a poor fit for latency-sensitive production apps.

questions.t: Heroku AppLink currently runs only in the virginia region, which adds latency for apps hosted far from it.
questions.f: Heroku AppLink currently runs in every Heroku region, so it adds no latency for apps hosted outside the US.
questions.x: AppLink, which publishes Heroku APIs to Salesforce as External Services, is available only in the virginia region today, so distant apps pay a latency cost.

questions.t: An Agentforce Data Library's source is chosen when the library is created and can't be changed afterward.
questions.f: An Agentforce Data Library's source is chosen when the library is created and can be switched later from the library's settings.
questions.x: Each library has a single source, such as Knowledge articles or uploaded files, and Trailhead warns that the choice is permanent; a different source means a new library.

questions.t: Each Agentforce Data Library gets its own retriever, though two libraries can share one search index.
questions.f: Each Agentforce Data Library gets its own search index, though two libraries can share one retriever.
questions.x: Provisioning creates a dedicated retriever per library, while the underlying search index may be shared between libraries. The false statement swaps which piece is shared.

questions.t: An Agentforce Data Library Connect API add-files request can include at most 1,000 files, with unique file names in the batch.
questions.f: An Agentforce Data Library Connect API add-files request can include at most 100 files, with unique file names in the batch.
questions.x: The resource reference caps a single add-files call at 1,000 files, and names must not repeat within that request.

questions.t: In the current Agentforce Specialist exam outline, AI Agents is the heaviest section at 35%, and Multi-Agent Interoperability the lightest at 5%.
questions.f: In the current Agentforce Specialist exam outline, Prompt Engineering is the heaviest section at 35%, and Multi-Agent Interoperability the lightest at 5%.
questions.x: The reorganized outline gives AI Agents 35%, with Prompt Engineering, Data Cloud for Agentforce and Deployment Lifecycle at 20% each. Prompt Builder dominated the older AI Specialist outline, not this one.

questions.t: The Agentforce Specialist prep module lists a 73% passing score for the 60 scored multiple-choice questions.
questions.f: The Agentforce Specialist prep module lists a 65% passing score for the 60 scored multiple-choice questions.
questions.x: The exam has 60 scored questions plus up to five unscored ones, and the prep module sets the pass mark at 73%.

questions.t: When Salesforce renamed AI Specialist to Agentforce Specialist in 2025, existing AI Specialist holders were converted to the new credential without a new exam.
questions.f: When Salesforce renamed AI Specialist to Agentforce Specialist in 2025, existing AI Specialist holders had to pass the new exam to keep the credential.
questions.x: Registration under the new name opened March 3, 2025, and current AI Specialist holders simply received the Agentforce Specialist credential.

questions.t: When the same SKU appears on several contracts, Digital Wallet pools the entitlements on one card and draws usage first from the contract expiring soonest.
questions.f: When the same SKU appears on several contracts, Digital Wallet pools the entitlements on one card and draws usage first from the most recently signed contract.
questions.x: Pooled entitlements are consumed earliest-expiry first, so credits that would lapse soonest are used before newer ones.

questions.t: Data Services credits can be spent only on Data 360, while Flex Credits are interchangeable across Data 360, Agentforce and other features.
questions.f: Flex Credits can be spent only on Agentforce, while Data Services credits are interchangeable across Data 360, Agentforce and other features.
questions.x: Data Services credits are Data 360-only across its usage types; Flex Credits form one pool usable by Data 360, Agentforce and more. Moving between them requires re-contracting.

questions.t: On the November 2026 Flex Credits rate card, an Agentforce standard or custom action costs 20 credits in production and 16 in a sandbox.
questions.f: On the November 2026 Flex Credits rate card, an Agentforce standard or custom action costs 20 credits in production and nothing in a sandbox.
questions.x: Sandbox usage still consumes credits, just at a lower rate: 16 credits per action versus 20 in production.

questions.t: Salesforce archives activities in the background once they are 365 days old, and a standard query() excludes archived rows while queryAll() returns them.
questions.f: Salesforce archives activities in the background once they are 90 days old, and both query() and queryAll() return archived rows.
questions.x: Events and closed tasks are archived after a year. Ordinary queries skip archived activities, so queryAll() or an IsArchived filter is needed to reach them.

questions.t: With multiday events enabled in Activity Settings, a single Salesforce event can't span more than 14 days.
questions.f: With multiday events enabled in Activity Settings, a single Salesforce event can't span more than 31 days.
questions.x: Multiday events must be switched on first, and even then one event is capped at 14 days in length.

questions.t: Shared Activities can take up to 48 hours to enable, and only Salesforce Support can turn it off again.
questions.f: Shared Activities takes effect immediately when enabled, and admins can turn it off again from Activity Settings.
questions.x: Enabling Shared Activities runs a background conversion that can take up to two days, and reversing it requires a Support request, so it's a hard-to-undo choice.

questions.t: Disabling Contacts to Multiple Accounts deletes every indirect account-contact relationship, while primary account links survive.
questions.f: Disabling Contacts to Multiple Accounts hides indirect account-contact relationships, which reappear intact if the feature is turned back on.
questions.x: Turning the setting off permanently removes indirect AccountContactRelation rows; only each contact's direct link to its primary account remains.

questions.t: Indirect contacts don't appear in reports built on the standard Accounts and Contacts report type.
questions.f: Indirect contacts appear alongside direct contacts in reports built on the standard Accounts and Contacts report type.
questions.x: The standard Accounts and Contacts report type follows only the primary account link, so indirect relationships need other reporting, such as a report type on the relationship object.

questions.t: The AccountContactRelation object doesn't support lookup, master-detail or roll-up summary fields, so richer relationship data calls for a custom junction object.
questions.f: The AccountContactRelation object supports lookup, master-detail and roll-up summary fields, so it can replace any custom junction object.
questions.x: The relationship object has a limited schema with no lookups, roll-ups, record types or approvals. When the relationship needs its own children or approvals, build a custom junction object.

questions.t: Aura components at API version 40.0 or later run under Lightning Locker, while a component pinned to 39.0 or earlier runs without it.
questions.f: Aura components at API version 45.0 or later run under Lightning Locker, while a component pinned to 44.0 or earlier runs without it.
questions.x: Locker enforcement for Aura is set per component by its API version, starting at 40.0 (Summer '17). This only matters while Locker, not Lightning Web Security, is active.

questions.t: Lightning Out requires Lightning Locker and isn't supported when Lightning Web Security is enabled.
questions.f: Lightning Out requires Lightning Web Security and isn't supported when Lightning Locker is enabled.
questions.x: A dependency on Lightning Out is the main reason an org stays on Locker, because Lightning Out doesn't run under LWS.

questions.t: Lightning Locker can be disabled only for Aura components, by API version; it can't be turned off for individual Lightning web components.
questions.f: Lightning Locker can be disabled for individual Lightning web components by lowering their API version to 39.0 or earlier.
questions.x: The API-version escape hatch applies to Aura components only. Lightning web components always run under whichever security architecture the org uses.

questions.t: Lightning Web Security changes native JavaScript API behaviour through distortions, rather than by substituting secure wrapper objects as Lightning Locker does.
questions.f: Lightning Web Security changes native JavaScript API behaviour through secure wrapper objects, rather than through distortions as Lightning Locker does.
questions.x: LWS sandboxes each namespace and applies targeted distortions such as content filtering and sanitization. Wrapping globals like SecureWindow is Locker's technique; the false statement swaps them.

questions.t: With Lightning Web Security on, a component can import components and modules from other namespaces, which fails with a cross-namespace error when it's off.
questions.f: With Lightning Web Security on, a component is blocked from importing components and modules from other namespaces, which works only when it's off.
questions.x: Because LWS isolates namespaces in sandboxes instead of walling them off, cross-namespace imports become possible; without it, those imports throw a cross-namespace error.

questions.t: For large collections under Lightning Web Security, Salesforce recommends plain JavaScript objects over Set and Map, because those globals are host-owned and proxied.
questions.f: For large collections under Lightning Web Security, Salesforce recommends Set and Map over plain JavaScript objects, because those globals are sandbox-owned and not proxied.
questions.x: Set, Map and typed arrays come from the host and every access crosses a proxy, which gets noticeably slow at tens of thousands of entries. Plain objects avoid that overhead.

questions.t: DevOps Center creates a temporary feature branch for a work item when the work item moves to In Progress.
questions.f: DevOps Center creates a temporary feature branch for a work item when the work item is first promoted to the Integration stage.
questions.x: The development stage has no stage branch; instead each work item gets its own feature branch, such as feature/WI-000001, as soon as work starts on it.

questions.t: For a branch created by hand to sync with a DevOps Center work item, its name must match the work item ID.
questions.f: For a branch created by hand to sync with a DevOps Center work item, its name must match the target stage branch.
questions.x: DevOps Center links commits to work items through the branch name, so a manually created branch has to carry the work item ID for CLI commits to appear on it.

questions.t: In the Gitflow model for Salesforce, a develop branch feeds the test orgs, release branches are cut for production and hotfixes branch off main.
questions.f: In the Gitflow model for Salesforce, only main lives long, and short-lived feature branches are cut from it and merged straight back.
questions.x: Gitflow adds develop, release and hotfix branches and suits a fixed release cadence. A lone long-lived main with short feature branches describes simple feature branching instead.

questions.t: The official run-code-analyzer GitHub Action should be used at v2, which runs Code Analyzer v5; v1 runs the retired v4.
questions.f: The official run-code-analyzer GitHub Action should be used at v1, which runs Code Analyzer v5; v2 runs the retired v4.
questions.x: Version 2 of the GitHub Action is the one wired to the current Code Analyzer v5 engine. Pinning v1 leaves a pipeline on the retired v4.

questions.t: If an org enforces high-assurance (stepped-up) authentication, the identity verification prompt blocks headless JWT logins from a CI job.
questions.f: If an org enforces high-assurance (stepped-up) authentication, JWT logins from a CI job bypass the identity verification prompt automatically.
questions.x: A headless JWT login can't answer an identity verification challenge, so stepped-up authentication on the org stops the CI login.

questions.t: The beta RunRelevantTests level lets Salesforce choose tests from the deployment payload, and @IsTest(critical=true) forces a test to be included.
questions.f: The beta RunRelevantTests level lets Salesforce choose tests from the deployment payload, and @IsTest(critical=true) excludes a test from the run.
questions.x: RunRelevantTests analyzes the payload and its dependencies to pick tests; marking a test critical, or using testFor, makes sure it always runs.

questions.t: With delegated authentication, Salesforce sends the username, password and source IP to the customer's SOAP web service, which returns true or false.
questions.f: With delegated authentication, Salesforce redirects the user to the customer's identity provider, which returns a signed SAML assertion.
questions.x: Delegated authentication is a credential callout: the customer's endpoint validates the password and answers true or false. Redirecting for a signed assertion is how SAML single sign-on works.

questions.t: Identity Verification History keeps six months of verification attempts, so longer audit evidence has to be exported.
questions.f: Identity Verification History keeps twelve months of verification attempts, so longer audit evidence has to be exported.
questions.x: The VerificationHistory object retains records for six months. Twelve months is too long, which is why teams with longer retention needs export the data.

questions.t: When challenging a user, Salesforce prompts for the most secure registered method and ranks a security key above Salesforce Authenticator.
questions.f: When challenging a user, Salesforce prompts for the most secure registered method and ranks Salesforce Authenticator above a security key.
questions.x: The precedence runs passkey, then physical security key, then Salesforce Authenticator, then TOTP apps. A security key is the more secure, phishing-resistant method, so it comes first.

questions.t: In orgs created before Summer '25, admins must turn on passkeys and security keys, while third-party authenticator apps are available automatically.
questions.f: In orgs created before Summer '25, admins must turn on third-party authenticator apps, while passkeys and security keys are available automatically.
questions.x: Older orgs need an admin to enable passkeys and security keys, but TOTP authenticator apps work out of the box. Newer orgs allow every method by default.

questions.t: In API-led connectivity, System APIs connect directly to systems of record such as ERPs and CRMs and shield consumers from changes in them.
questions.f: In API-led connectivity, Experience APIs connect directly to systems of record such as ERPs and CRMs and shield consumers from changes in them.
questions.x: System APIs form the foundation layer that unlocks data in core systems and insulates callers from their complexity. Experience APIs sit at the top and shape data for a channel instead of touching source systems.

questions.t: MuleSoft architects advise adding an Experience API only when consumers need a different contract or the Process API definition is expected to change.
questions.f: MuleSoft architects advise adding an Experience API only when the system of record behind the System API is expected to be replaced.
questions.x: The layers are not mandatory, and an Experience layer earns its cost only when consumers need their own contract or the Process API is likely to change. Swapping a backend system is what the System layer insulates against, not the reason for an Experience API.

questions.t: Experience APIs in API-led connectivity adapt Process API output for a specific channel and do not depend directly on the source systems.
questions.f: Experience APIs in API-led connectivity adapt System API output for a specific channel and call the source systems directly to cut hops.
questions.x: Experience APIs reshape what Process APIs produce for a particular UI, device or channel, and they are deliberately decoupled from the systems of record. Calling source systems directly would recreate the point-to-point coupling the model avoids.

questions.t: An External Services registration accepts an OpenAPI 2.0.x or 3.0.x schema written in either JSON or YAML.
questions.f: An External Services registration accepts only an OpenAPI 3.0.x schema, and only when it is written in JSON.
questions.x: The ExternalServiceRegistration schema field takes OpenAPI 2.0.x or 3.0.x content in JSON or YAML. Restricting it to 3.0.x JSON understates the supported formats.

questions.t: Operations from a registered External Service become strongly typed Apex classes and methods in the ExternalService namespace.
questions.f: Operations from a registered External Service become loosely typed Apex maps that must be parsed with the JSON class in the Http namespace.
questions.x: Registration generates classes and methods under the ExternalService namespace with schema types mapped to Apex types, so developers skip manual JSON parsing. Hand-parsing with Http and JSON is the alternative that External Services removes.

questions.t: An External Service's read-only systemVersion can't be upgraded in place; you recreate the service from the same spec and repoint references.
questions.f: An External Service's systemVersion can be upgraded in place from Setup, and existing flow references update automatically.
questions.x: systemVersion is read-only, so moving to a newer version means registering the spec again and pointing flows and code at the new service. There is no in-place upgrade that rewires references for you.

questions.t: Salesforce Edge Network is turned on in the Routing section of the My Domain Setup page, which requires the Customize Application permission.
questions.f: Salesforce Edge Network is turned on in the Session Settings Setup page, which requires the Modify All Data permission.
questions.x: Edge routing is a My Domain setting: edit Routing and select Use Salesforce Edge Network, with Customize Application. Session Settings and Modify All Data are not involved.

questions.t: After an org moves to Salesforce Edge Network, only Salesforce Customer Support can switch it back.
questions.f: After an org moves to Salesforce Edge Network, an admin can switch it back by clearing the Routing option in Setup.
questions.x: The move is one-way from the admin's point of view; reversing it takes a Customer Support request. That is why firewalls and pinned certificates should be checked before enabling it.

questions.t: Because Salesforce Edge Network uses data-center-specific certificates, clients that pin should pin the intermediate certificate rather than the leaf.
questions.f: Because Salesforce Edge Network uses one certificate shared by all data centers, clients that pin should pin the leaf certificate rather than the intermediate.
questions.x: Edge Network serves certificates specific to each data center, so a pinned leaf can break when traffic lands elsewhere. Pinning the intermediate certificate is the documented guidance.

questions.t: When an existing production org is migrated into Government Cloud, its org ID and record IDs stay the same.
questions.f: When an existing production org is migrated into Government Cloud, it receives a new org ID and new record IDs.
questions.x: Moving into Government Cloud is an instance migration that keeps the org ID and every record ID. What changes are hosts, IP ranges and WSDLs, which is why hard-coded instance references must be removed.

questions.t: Government Cloud Plus - Defense is priced at 25% applied to net spend, compared with 15% for the standard Government Cloud Plus edition.
questions.f: Government Cloud Plus - Defense is priced at 15% applied to net spend, compared with 25% for the standard Government Cloud Plus edition.
questions.x: The physically isolated Defense edition carries the higher 25% uplift on net spend; the standard Plus edition is 15%. Premium, the air-gapped edition, is priced on request.

questions.t: During an org migration to Government Cloud, Email-to-Case messages are held for at most 24 hours.
questions.f: During an org migration to Government Cloud, Email-to-Case messages are held for at most 72 hours.
questions.x: Salesforce's migration guidance caps the hold on inbound Email-to-Case messages at 24 hours during the move. 72 hours overstates the buffer and could lead a team to plan an over-long cutover window.

questions.t: GovRAMP's Ready status requires an independent third-party assessor to assess 80 NIST controls.
questions.f: GovRAMP's Ready status requires an independent third-party assessor to assess more than 300 NIST controls.
questions.x: Ready covers 80 controls with a 3PAO assessment, monthly monitoring and an annual assessment. More than 300 controls is the bar for Provisionally Authorized and Authorized.

questions.t: StateRAMP began operating as GovRAMP in 2025, but its legal name remained StateRAMP.
questions.f: StateRAMP began operating as GovRAMP in 2025, and its legal name was changed to GovRAMP at the same time.
questions.x: The 2025 rebrand moved the program to govramp.org and a new public name to attract local governments, yet the legal entity kept the StateRAMP name.

questions.t: Under GovRAMP's FedRAMP Fast Track, the program office reviews a provider's existing FedRAMP artifacts, so a FedRAMP authorization feeds verification rather than replacing it.
questions.f: Under GovRAMP's FedRAMP Fast Track, a provider's FedRAMP authorization is accepted automatically, so it grants the matching GovRAMP status without further review.
questions.x: Fast Track cuts duplicate work by letting the PMO review federal readiness, assessment and monitoring documents against GovRAMP's requirements. GovRAMP does not describe it as automatic reciprocity, so a review still happens.

questions.t: Enterprise, Unlimited and Performance orgs each get five free Salesforce Integration user licenses, and Developer Edition gets one.
questions.f: Enterprise, Unlimited and Performance orgs each get ten free Salesforce Integration user licenses, and Developer Edition gets two.
questions.x: The API-only Integration license comes five to an Enterprise, Unlimited or Performance org and one to a Developer Edition org. The doubled counts are wrong.

questions.t: From API 64.0, the UsedLicenses field on UserLicense can't be filtered in a SOQL WHERE clause, so rows must be filtered after retrieval.
questions.f: From API 64.0, the TotalLicenses field on UserLicense can't be filtered in a SOQL WHERE clause, so rows must be filtered after retrieval.
questions.x: The filtering restriction applies to UsedLicenses, the count of assigned seats. Audit queries retrieve the rows and filter in code; TotalLicenses is not the field named.

questions.t: On a UserLicense record, a null MonthlyLoginsEntitlement means the license is billed per user rather than per login.
questions.f: On a UserLicense record, a null MonthlyLoginsEntitlement means the license is billed per login rather than per user.
questions.x: MonthlyLoginsEntitlement is populated only for login-based portal licenses. When it is empty, the license is a per-user license.

questions.t: In Salesforce's LEVERS of Change model, Rewards and Structure are the structural levers, while Values and Enablement are the individual levers.
questions.f: In Salesforce's LEVERS of Change model, Values and Enablement are the structural levers, while Rewards and Structure are the individual levers.
questions.x: LEVERS groups its six levers as social (Leadership, Ecosystem), individual (Values, Enablement) and structural (Rewards, Structure). The false version swaps the individual and structural groups.

questions.t: In Salesforce's Discover, Rollout and Optimize change cycle, the change impact assessment is done in Discover, before rollout begins.
questions.f: In Salesforce's Discover, Rollout and Optimize change cycle, the change impact assessment is done in Optimize, after rollout ends.
questions.x: Discover is where feedback is gathered, sponsors aligned, blockers named and the change impact assessment run. Optimize follows go-live and focuses on adoption metrics and adjustments.

questions.t: Showing in-app guidance prompts on an Experience Cloud site requires an Aura-template site, plus purchased Enablement and PRM.
questions.f: Showing in-app guidance prompts on an Experience Cloud site requires an LWR-template site, plus purchased Enablement and PRM.
questions.x: In-app prompts on Experience Cloud carry extra prerequisites, and one of them is that the site uses an Aura template. An LWR-template site doesn't meet that requirement.

questions.t: Unlike System Architect, the Heroku Architect credential is earned on its own rather than granted automatically as a roll-up of other exams.
questions.f: Like System Architect, the Heroku Architect credential is granted automatically as a roll-up once its prerequisite exams are passed.
questions.x: Application Architect and System Architect are roll-ups of other certifications, but Heroku Architect is a separate product credential that does not feed or come from a roll-up.

questions.t: On Heroku's Fir generation, log export uses OpenTelemetry in place of the syslog drains used on Cedar.
questions.f: On Heroku's Fir generation, log export uses syslog drains in place of the OpenTelemetry pipeline used on Cedar.
questions.x: Fir, the Kubernetes-based generation, swaps syslog drains for OpenTelemetry. The false statement reverses which generation uses which mechanism.

questions.t: Heroku raised its default slug size limit to 1 GB, and up to 2 GB is available on request.
questions.f: Heroku raised its default slug size limit to 500 MB, and up to 1 GB is available on request.
questions.x: The Summer '26 maintenance content covers a 1 GB default slug size that can go to 2 GB on request. The smaller figures in the false statement understate both limits.

questions.t: Trailhead splits requirements elicitation into three stages: Prepare, Conduct and Confirm.
questions.f: Trailhead splits requirements elicitation into three stages: Prepare, Prioritize and Close.
questions.x: Prepare builds a picture of the business need, Conduct meets stakeholders, and Confirm checks that stated requirements match the real problem. Prioritize and Close are not stages in that model.

questions.t: A user story's acceptance criteria should state the intended outcome rather than prescribe a specific solution such as a button.
questions.f: A user story's acceptance criteria should prescribe a specific solution such as a button rather than state the intended outcome.
questions.x: Criteria are pass/fail statements of intent that testers verify. Naming a button is solutioning too early, which locks in a design before options have been weighed.

questions.t: In Trailhead's process mapping guidance, the end-to-end process owner chairs the mapping workshop and settles disagreements.
questions.f: In Trailhead's process mapping guidance, the Salesforce admin chairs the mapping workshop and settles disagreements.
questions.x: Live mapping workshops are led by the end-to-end process owner, who resolves disputes so the group can validate the map as it is drawn. The admin is a participant, not the chair.

questions.t: An @InvocableMethod must return a list the same size and order as its input list, so failed inputs still get a result entry.
questions.f: An @InvocableMethod may return a shorter list than its input, so failed inputs can simply be dropped from the results.
questions.x: The i-th output answers the i-th input, which is what lets the action run in bulk. Dropping failed rows breaks that mapping, so the pattern is a result wrapper that reports success or failure.

questions.t: An @InvocableVariable must be a public or global instance variable; static, final and private variables can't be used.
questions.f: An @InvocableVariable can be a static or private variable, as long as the annotation sets a label for it.
questions.x: Invocable variables must be public or global instance members. Static, local, final, private and protected variables are not allowed, and a label doesn't change that.

questions.t: In a subscriber org, Flow Builder shows only packaged invocable methods and variables that are declared global.
questions.f: In a subscriber org, Flow Builder shows packaged invocable methods and variables declared either public or global.
questions.x: Packaged invocable code is visible to subscriber flows only when it is global. Public members stay hidden outside the package's namespace.

questions.t: After converting a workflow rule, Migrate to Flow's Switch Activations button deactivates the rule and activates the new flow in a single step.
questions.f: After converting a process, Migrate to Flow's Switch Activations button deactivates the process and activates the new flow in a single step.
questions.x: Switch Activations is offered only for migrated workflow rules. For processes, the admin must activate the flow and then deactivate the process in Process Builder manually.

questions.t: When migrating a process, Migrate to Flow lets you send individual criteria to separate flows instead of putting all of them in one flow.
questions.f: When migrating a process, Migrate to Flow always puts all of the process's criteria into one flow and can't split them into separate flows.
questions.x: The tool lets an admin migrate every criterion to one flow or pick specific criteria and migrate them to separate flows, so splitting is supported.

questions.t: A recursive process could evaluate a record up to six times per save, but the flow Migrate to Flow generates from it evaluates the record only once.
questions.f: A recursive process could evaluate a record up to six times per save, and the flow Migrate to Flow generates from it keeps that same six-pass recursion.
questions.x: Migrated flows evaluate the record a single time, so logic that relied on the process's recursion can silently behave differently after conversion.

questions.t: In April 2026, Salesforce merged AppExchange, the Slack Marketplace and the Agentforce-focused AgentExchange into one storefront called AgentExchange.
questions.f: In April 2026, Salesforce merged AppExchange and the Agentforce-focused AgentExchange into one storefront, while the Slack Marketplace stayed separate.
questions.x: The unified AgentExchange absorbed all three marketplaces, including the Slack Marketplace, so Slack apps are listed in the same storefront.

questions.t: Anyone can browse and test-drive AgentExchange listings, but installing one requires an admin or the Download AgentExchange Packages permission.
questions.f: Anyone can browse and test-drive AgentExchange listings, but installing one requires an admin or the Create AgentExchange Packages permission.
questions.x: Installing is gated by admin rights or the Download AgentExchange Packages permission. The Create and Upload permissions are for partners publishing listings, not for installing.

questions.t: The AgentExchange Go-To-Market App for private offers supports only 12-month contracts paid NET30 by ACH debit in USD, and orders don't auto-renew.
questions.f: The AgentExchange Go-To-Market App for private offers supports only 12-month contracts paid NET30 by ACH debit in USD, and orders auto-renew yearly.
questions.x: Private-offer orders from the Go-To-Market App don't renew automatically in Winter '27; cancellations and partner-initiated refunds aren't supported yet either.

questions.t: A Data 360 data graph stores the joined fields of its primary DMO and related DMOs as one read-only JSON record per entity.
questions.f: A Data 360 data graph stores the joined fields of its primary DMO and related DMOs as one editable JSON record per entity that apps can write back to.
questions.x: Data graphs precompute and materialize the joins into a read-only JSON blob, so they serve as a fast lookup source rather than a place to write data.

questions.t: Real-time data graphs in Data 360 update instantly for in-session use but require the separately purchased Real-Time SKU.
questions.f: Standard data graphs in Data 360 update instantly for in-session use but require the separately purchased Real-Time SKU.
questions.x: Instant, in-session updates are the real-time variant, which needs the Real-Time SKU. Standard graphs refresh after a delay of minutes to hours and suit batch and reporting.

questions.t: Non-real-time Data 360 data graphs refresh daily by default, with hourly, 4-hourly, weekly and monthly schedules also available.
questions.f: Non-real-time Data 360 data graphs refresh hourly by default, with 4-hourly, daily, weekly and monthly schedules also available.
questions.x: Daily is the default refresh interval for standard graphs; choosing a less frequent interval saves credits when the data doesn't need to be current.

questions.t: A controlling field can be a standard or custom picklist or a checkbox, but a dependent field must be a custom picklist or multi-select picklist.
questions.f: A dependent field can be a standard or custom picklist or a checkbox, but a controlling field must be a custom picklist or multi-select picklist.
questions.x: The roles are asymmetric: checkboxes and standard picklists can control a dependency, but only custom picklists and multi-select picklists can be dependent.

questions.t: A Visualforce page can include at most 10 dependent picklist pairs across all objects, and it fails at runtime if the controlling field is missing.
questions.f: A Visualforce page can include at most 25 dependent picklist pairs across all objects, and it fails at runtime if the controlling field is missing.
questions.x: apex:inputField renders dependencies automatically, but Visualforce caps a page at 10 dependent picklist pairs, not 25.

questions.t: Field dependencies aren't enforced when only the controlling field is updated, and the Data Import Wizard ignores them entirely.
questions.f: Field dependencies are enforced whenever the controlling field is updated, but the Data Import Wizard ignores them entirely.
questions.x: Updating just the controller skips the dependency check, as do Data Import Wizard loads, so a validation rule is needed when a bad combination must never be stored.

questions.t: A hierarchical relationship field prevents choosing a user who reports to the record's user directly or indirectly, so the chain can't loop.
questions.f: A hierarchical relationship field allows choosing any active user, including one who reports to the record's user, so loops must be prevented by validation rules.
questions.x: Cycle protection is what makes the field hierarchical: like the Manager field, it blocks picking a direct or indirect report, so automation can walk the chain safely.

questions.t: An approval step can route to the manager named on the record owner's user record, or to a custom hierarchical field used as the approver field.
questions.f: An approval step can route only to the submitter's manager via the standard Manager field; custom hierarchical fields can't be used as the approver field.
questions.x: Approvers can be resolved from the submitter's or record owner's Manager, and a custom hierarchical field can serve as the approver field when the approval chain differs from the reporting line.

questions.t: The User object can't be the master side of a master-detail relationship, so user-to-user links rely on lookup-style fields.
questions.f: The User object can be the master side of a master-detail relationship, so user-to-user links can use master-detail fields.
questions.x: The object reference lists User among the standard objects barred from being the master in a master-detail relationship, which is why hierarchical and lookup fields are used.

questions.t: A method defined in a with sharing class still enforces sharing when a without sharing class calls it, because the mode comes from where it is defined.
questions.f: A method defined in a with sharing class drops sharing when a without sharing class calls it, because the mode comes from the calling class.
questions.x: Apex takes the sharing mode from the class that defines the method, not from its caller. Only inherited sharing classes adopt the caller's mode.

questions.t: An Apex subclass declared with no sharing keyword runs in its parent class's sharing mode.
questions.f: An Apex subclass declared with no sharing keyword runs in the sharing mode of whichever class calls it.
questions.x: A subclass without its own keyword picks up its parent's declared mode. Taking the caller's mode at runtime is what inherited sharing does, and inner classes get nothing from their outer class.

questions.t: Apex triggers can't declare a sharing keyword and run without sharing, so logic is best moved into handler classes that declare one.
questions.f: Apex triggers can't declare a sharing keyword and run with sharing, so logic is best moved into handler classes that declare one.
questions.x: Triggers have no sharing declaration and execute without sharing. Putting the logic in a handler class with an explicit keyword lets the developer control record access.

questions.t: Annotating a test utility class with @IsTest excludes it from the org's Apex code size limit, an advantage a plain helper class lacks.
questions.f: Annotating a test utility class with @IsTest excludes it from code coverage calculations, but it still counts toward the Apex code size limit.
questions.x: The @IsTest annotation keeps the factory out of the org's Apex code size limit and restricts it to test context. The false version moves the benefit to coverage and keeps the size cost.

questions.t: An Apex test class can have only one @TestSetup method, and it isn't supported when the class uses @IsTest(SeeAllData=true).
questions.f: An Apex test class can have up to five @TestSetup methods, and they also run when the class uses @IsTest(SeeAllData=true).
questions.x: Test setup is limited to a single method per class and is incompatible with SeeAllData=true. Multiple setup methods are not allowed.

questions.t: If a @TestSetup method hits a fatal error such as a DML exception, the whole test class fails and none of its tests run.
questions.f: If a @TestSetup method hits a fatal error such as a DML exception, only the first test method fails and the remaining tests still run.
questions.x: A setup failure takes down the entire test class, because every method depends on the shared data. No individual test continues after it.

questions.t: Data Mask & Seed is sold as a platform add-on for Enterprise and Unlimited editions, priced at 10% of net spend.
questions.f: Data Mask & Seed is included at no extra cost in Enterprise and Unlimited editions, with no separate add-on fee.
questions.x: It is a paid platform add-on for Enterprise and Unlimited editions, priced at 10% of net spend, not a free inclusion.

questions.t: Data Mask & Seed can seed from a production org, a sandbox or a backup, but seeding from a backup requires Backup & Recover.
questions.f: Data Mask & Seed can seed from a production org, a sandbox or a backup, and seeding from a backup needs no other product.
questions.x: Backups are a valid seeding source only when Backup & Recover is in place, which is why the product integrates with it.

questions.t: A Data Mask & Seed Levels template takes root objects and a number of related-object levels below them to include.
questions.f: A Data Mask & Seed Generate template takes root objects and a number of related-object levels below them to include.
questions.x: Levels templates choose roots plus a depth of related objects. Generate templates create synthetic records instead of copying from a source, and Nodes templates add each object explicitly.

questions.t: In Trailhead's org development model, a release is combined in a shared Developer Pro sandbox and user-acceptance tested in a Partial Copy sandbox.
questions.f: In Trailhead's org development model, a release is combined in a Partial Copy sandbox and user-acceptance tested in a shared Developer Pro sandbox.
questions.x: Individual work in Developer sandboxes is merged in a shared Developer Pro sandbox to build the release, then UAT runs in a Partial Copy sandbox. The false statement swaps the two stages.

questions.t: A deployment run list records the manual steps to do before and after a deployment, while a change list records what each person changed.
questions.f: A change list records the manual steps to do before and after a deployment, while a deployment run list records what each person changed.
questions.x: The run list captures setup that metadata can't carry, so it isn't forgotten; the change list tracks each person's changes in their development org. The false version swaps their roles.

questions.t: Salesforce posts its seasonal upgrade dates on the Trust site up to a year in advance.
questions.f: Salesforce posts its seasonal upgrade dates on the Trust site up to 3 months in advance.
questions.x: Upgrade dates appear on Trust up to a year ahead, letting teams plan backward from the next two or three releases. About 3 months is when a release cycle begins, not how far ahead dates are published.

questions.t: The X.509 certificate uploaded to an app for the Salesforce JWT bearer flow can't exceed 4 KB; a DER-encoded file helps if it does.
questions.f: The X.509 certificate uploaded to an app for the Salesforce JWT bearer flow can't exceed 16 KB; a DER-encoded file helps if it does.
questions.x: Salesforce caps the signing certificate at 4 KB and suggests DER encoding to shrink an oversized file. 16 KB is not the documented limit.

questions.t: Including the jti claim in a JWT bearer assertion makes Salesforce reject any token it has already seen, giving replay protection.
questions.f: Including the iat claim in a JWT bearer assertion makes Salesforce reject any token it has already seen, giving replay protection.
questions.x: The jti claim is a unique token identifier, and Salesforce refuses a jti it has seen before. The iat claim only records when the token was issued.

questions.t: For CLI JWT logins, the DX guide recommends a connected app rather than an external client app when the Dev Hub will create scratch orgs or sandboxes.
questions.f: For CLI JWT logins, the DX guide recommends an external client app rather than a connected app when the Dev Hub will create scratch orgs or sandboxes.
questions.x: The guide generally prefers external client apps, but it carves out Dev Hubs that create scratch orgs or sandboxes, where a connected app is recommended so the new orgs can be authorized with the Dev Hub's key.

questions.t: In Setup, the Add Multiple Users option creates up to 10 users at a time.
questions.f: In Setup, the Add Multiple Users option creates up to 50 users at a time.
questions.x: Add Multiple Users is a quick-entry form capped at 10 users per use. Larger loads need another approach, so 50 overstates the limit.

questions.t: Freezing a user blocks login at once but keeps the license in use; only deactivating the user releases the license.
questions.f: Freezing a user blocks login at once and releases the license, just as deactivating the user does.
questions.x: Freezing is a stopgap while dependencies are untangled, and the frozen user still holds a license seat. Deactivation is the only step that frees it.

questions.t: A Salesforce username must be unique across all Salesforce orgs, while the same email address can be reused across orgs.
questions.f: A Salesforce username only has to be unique within its own org, while an email address must be unique across all orgs.
questions.x: Usernames are global identifiers in email format, so no two orgs can share one. Email addresses carry no such restriction and can repeat across orgs.

questions.t: A Bulk API 1.0 batch can hold at most 10,000 records and 10 MB of data.
questions.f: A Bulk API 1.0 batch can hold at most 50,000 records and 100 MB of data.
questions.x: Each Bulk API 1.0 batch is capped at 10,000 records, 10 MB and 10 million characters. The larger figures don't apply to 1.0 batches.

questions.t: Bulk API 1.0 PK chunking splits a query into ID ranges of 100,000 records by default, with a maximum chunk size of 250,000.
questions.f: Bulk API 1.0 PK chunking splits a query into ID ranges of 250,000 records by default, with a maximum chunk size of 1,000,000.
questions.x: The Sforce-Enable-PKChunking header defaults to 100,000-record chunks and allows up to 250,000. The higher numbers overstate both the default and the ceiling.

questions.t: A Bulk API 1.0 job's contentType defaults to XML, whereas Bulk API 2.0 ingest jobs accept only CSV.
questions.f: A Bulk API 1.0 job's contentType defaults to CSV, whereas Bulk API 2.0 ingest jobs accept only JSON.
questions.x: Bulk API 1.0 defaults to XML and also supports CSV, JSON and ZIP variants for attachments. Bulk API 2.0 is limited to CSV, not JSON.

questions.t: During a recursive save, assignment rules and after-save record-triggered flows are skipped, but before triggers and validation rules run again.
questions.f: During a recursive save, before triggers and validation rules are skipped, but assignment rules and after-save record-triggered flows run again.
questions.x: A recursive pass skips the middle steps of the save order, including assignment rules and after-save flows, while early steps such as before triggers and validation repeat. The false version swaps which steps are skipped.

questions.t: In the extra trigger run caused by a workflow field update, Trigger.old holds the values from before the user's original update.
questions.f: In the extra trigger run caused by a workflow field update, Trigger.old holds the values that the workflow field update just set.
questions.x: Salesforce's example changes a field from 1 to 10, workflow bumps it to 11, and Trigger.old in the repeat run still shows 1. It does not reflect the workflow's intermediate value.

questions.t: Salesforce measured bulk same-record updates as roughly 10 to 20 times faster in before-save flows than in Workflow Rules or Process Builder.
questions.f: Salesforce measured bulk same-record updates as roughly 2 to 3 times faster in before-save flows than in Workflow Rules or Process Builder.
questions.x: Before-save flows change the record in memory and avoid a recursive save, which Salesforce measured at about 10 to 20 times faster in bulk. The smaller multiple understates the gap.

questions.t: Anyone can subscribe to Salesforce Trust Notifications, even without a Salesforce user license.
questions.f: Only users with an active Salesforce user license and admin rights can subscribe to Salesforce Trust Notifications.
questions.x: Trust Notifications are open to any subscriber who confirms by email, with no license required. Admin-only delivery applies to Salesforce's incident emails and webinar invites, not to Trust subscriptions.

questions.t: A sandbox refresh adds the source instance's Trust Notification subscribers automatically, but after an org migration you must update your subscription yourself.
questions.f: An org migration moves your Trust Notification subscription automatically, but after a sandbox refresh you must update the subscription yourself.
questions.x: Refreshes copy subscribers to the destination instance, while org migrations leave the old subscription in place. The false version reverses which event is handled for you.

questions.t: During an incident, Salesforce's Critical Incident Center updates the Trust site roughly every 30 minutes.
questions.f: During an incident, Salesforce's Critical Incident Center updates the Trust site roughly every 2 hours.
questions.x: The around-the-clock Critical Incident Center posts Trust updates about every 30 minutes while an incident is open. A 2-hour cadence is far slower than the stated practice.

questions.t: OCEG's GRC Capability Model organizes integrated GRC into four components: Learn, Align, Perform and Review.
questions.f: OCEG's GRC Capability Model organizes integrated GRC into four components: Plan, Do, Check and Act.
questions.x: The OCEG "Red Book" groups its capabilities under Learn, Align, Perform and Review. Plan-Do-Check-Act is a generic improvement cycle, not the components of OCEG's model.

questions.t: Covering a risk with cyber insurance or outsourcing the activity transfers the risk rather than mitigating it with controls.
questions.f: Covering a risk with cyber insurance or outsourcing the activity mitigates the risk with controls rather than transferring it.
questions.x: Risk treatment options are mitigate with controls, accept within tolerance, or transfer. Insurance and outsourcing shift the impact to another party, which is transfer, not mitigation.

questions.t: In compliance work, a change advisory board is an operational control, while allowlisting is a technical control.
questions.f: In compliance work, a change advisory board is a technical control, while allowlisting is an operational control.
questions.x: Controls are grouped as management (policies, regulations), operational (processes such as a change advisory board) and technical (tooling such as allowlisting). The false version swaps the two categories.

questions.t: In NIST SP 800-60, Volume I describes the categorization method, while Volume II catalogs information types with provisional impact levels.
questions.f: In NIST SP 800-60, Volume II describes the categorization method, while Volume I catalogs information types with provisional impact levels.
questions.x: Volume I is the methodology and Volume II holds the appendices of information types, provisional Low/Moderate/High ratings and their rationale. The false statement swaps the two volumes.

questions.t: Under SP 800-60, a single information type such as public data may be rated not applicable for confidentiality, but a whole system may not.
questions.f: Under SP 800-60, a whole system may be rated not applicable for confidentiality when every information type it handles is public data.
questions.x: Not applicable is allowed for an individual information type, but the guide never lets a system's confidentiality rating fall to not applicable, even if all its data is public.

questions.t: FedRAMP has cloud providers record their SP 800-60 based categorization in the FIPS 199 Categorization Template, Appendix K of the System Security Plan.
questions.f: FedRAMP has cloud providers record their SP 800-60 based categorization in the FIPS 199 Categorization Template, Appendix A of the System Security Plan.
questions.x: FedRAMP points providers to FIPS 199 plus SP 800-60 Volume II Rev. 1 and asks for the result in the Appendix K template of the SSP, not another appendix.

questions.t: Lightning's CSP sets script-src to 'self', so a third-party JavaScript library must be uploaded as a static resource rather than loaded from a CDN.
questions.f: Lightning's CSP sets script-src to any Trusted URL, so a third-party JavaScript library can be loaded from a CDN once its host is trusted.
questions.x: Script sources stay locked to the org, and Trusted URL flags cover connect, font, frame, image, media and style directives but not scripts. Libraries therefore go in static resources.

questions.t: Salesforce advises keeping an org's generated CSP header under 12 KB, since problems have been reported as headers approach 16 KB.
questions.f: Salesforce advises keeping an org's generated CSP header under 64 KB, since problems have been reported as headers approach 128 KB.
questions.x: Every Trusted URL adds to the header, and trouble starts around 16 KB, so the guidance is to stay under 12 KB. The larger figures are far beyond what proxies and browsers tolerate here.

questions.t: In API versions 50.0 to 58.0, a Trusted URL saved with no directive flags set silently defaulted to img-src only.
questions.f: In API versions 50.0 to 58.0, a Trusted URL saved with no directive flags set silently defaulted to connect-src only.
questions.x: Older API versions fell back to the image directive when no flag was chosen. Since API 59.0 at least one directive or permission flag must be true explicitly.

questions.t: Visualforce standard components escape their output by default, and setting escape="false" makes the developer responsible for validating it.
questions.f: Visualforce standard components leave their output unescaped by default, and setting escape="true" makes the platform responsible for validating it.
questions.x: Escaping is on by default for standard Visualforce components. Turning it off with escape="false" is what opens the door to XSS unless the developer validates the output.

questions.t: To write a URL parameter such as retURL into a JavaScript string on a Visualforce page safely, wrap the merge field in JSENCODE.
questions.f: To write a URL parameter such as retURL into a JavaScript string on a Visualforce page safely, wrap the merge field in URLENCODE.
questions.x: Encoding must match the output context, and a JavaScript string needs JavaScript encoding, which JSENCODE provides. URL encoding targets a different context.

questions.t: Lightning Web Security sanitizes HTML and SVG strings that components insert via innerHTML, but it does not sanitize input text.
questions.f: Lightning Web Security sanitizes input text that users type into components, but it does not sanitize HTML strings inserted via innerHTML.
questions.x: LWS filters markup written to the DOM through properties like innerHTML down to allowlisted elements and attributes. It leaves raw input text alone, so output encoding is still needed.

questions.t: The org-wide session timeout picklist in Session Settings ranges from 15 minutes to 24 hours.
questions.f: The org-wide session timeout picklist in Session Settings ranges from 5 minutes to 12 hours.
questions.x: The timeout values run from FifteenMinutes up to TwentyFourHours, with 90 minutes added in API 58.0. Neither 5 minutes nor a 12-hour ceiling matches the picklist.

questions.t: Sessions that use JWT-based access tokens ignore the Session Settings timeout and follow the connected app or external client app policy instead.
questions.f: Sessions that use JWT-based access tokens ignore the connected app or external client app policy and follow the Session Settings timeout instead.
questions.x: For JWT-based access tokens the timeout is owned by the app's policy, not the org-wide page. The org setting only governs ordinary UI sessions.

questions.t: Most community licenses cap external user sessions at 24 hours, while External Identity licenses allow sessions of up to 7 days.
questions.f: External Identity licenses cap external user sessions at 24 hours, while most community licenses allow sessions of up to 7 days.
questions.x: Profile session settings for external users have license-dependent ceilings: 24 hours for most community licenses and up to 7 days for External Identity. The false statement swaps them.

questions.t: Salesforce's commerce guidance estimates TCO as initial costs plus ongoing costs multiplied by the timeframe, and says ongoing costs usually dominate.
questions.f: Salesforce's commerce guidance estimates TCO as initial costs plus ongoing costs multiplied by the timeframe, and says initial costs usually dominate.
questions.x: The formula multiplies ongoing costs by the timeframe, and the guidance notes that this ongoing portion, not the upfront spend, is usually the larger share.

questions.t: To lower TCO, Well-Architected guidance prefers prebuilt platform services first, then AppExchange apps, then low-code customization before code.
questions.f: To lower TCO, Well-Architected guidance prefers custom code first, then low-code customization, then AppExchange apps before prebuilt platform services.
questions.x: Standard features pick up platform innovation with each release, while custom replicas must be maintained by the team, so the order starts with prebuilt services and ends with code.

questions.t: License changes must be mirrored into sandboxes, by refreshing them or using the Match Production License tool, or testing diverges from production.
questions.f: License changes flow into existing sandboxes automatically within a day, so no refresh or Match Production License step is needed.
questions.x: Sandboxes don't pick up new licenses on their own; a refresh or the Match Production License tool keeps them aligned so tests reflect production.

questions.t: Salesforce architects advise finishing LDV load tests at least three to four weeks before go-live, in a sandbox separate from UAT.
