questions.x: The documented cap is 200 managed subscriptions per org. Ten times that figure isn't the limit, and the subscriptions also draw on the normal event delivery allocations.

questions.t: Setting a managed event subscription's state to STOP disconnects the client and deletes the committed replay ID, so the next run starts from defaultReplay.
questions.f: Setting a managed event subscription's state to STOP disconnects the client but keeps the committed replay ID, so the next run resumes where it left off.
questions.x: STOP wipes the stored position, which is why runbooks should treat it as a reset rather than a pause. On restart, delivery begins wherever defaultReplay points.

questions.t: A managed event subscription belongs to exactly one client, so several consumers reading one topic independently should use the classic Subscribe RPC.
questions.f: A managed event subscription can be shared by several clients, each keeping its own committed replay ID on the server for the same topic.
questions.x: Managed subscriptions can't be shared between clients. When multiple consumers need independent positions on a topic, the regular Subscribe RPC with client-stored replay IDs is the fit.

questions.t: ApexGuru labels a method critically expensive when it uses at least 5% of CPU time, and expensive when it uses 2 to 5%.
questions.f: ApexGuru labels a method critically expensive when it uses at least 20% of CPU time, and expensive when it uses 10 to 20%.
questions.x: ApexGuru's expensive-methods report flags methods at 5% or more of CPU time as critically expensive and those at 2 to 5% as expensive. The higher bands in the false version aren't its thresholds.

questions.t: ApexGuru's first reports can take up to 24 hours to appear and are then refreshed weekly, so it isn't a real-time tool.
questions.f: ApexGuru's first reports appear within an hour and are then refreshed hourly, so it works as a near real-time tool.
questions.x: After ApexGuru Insights is enabled, the initial report can take a day and later updates arrive weekly. It's a periodic analysis, not live monitoring.

questions.t: Code Analyzer's ApexGuru engine runs in Advanced Mode when ApexGuru is enabled in the org or its parent org family, and the mode can't be chosen manually.
questions.f: Code Analyzer's ApexGuru engine runs in Advanced Mode only when the developer passes a flag requesting it, whatever the org's ApexGuru setting.
questions.x: The engine picks Advanced Mode, using runtime data, automatically when ApexGuru is on for the org or its parent family, and otherwise falls back to Basic Mode static analysis. There's no manual mode switch.

questions.t: Under Abadi's PACELC model, default Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak are classed PA/EL, favouring availability under partition and latency otherwise.
questions.f: Under Abadi's PACELC model, default Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak are classed PC/EC, favouring consistency under partition and otherwise.
questions.x: Abadi puts these Dynamo-style stores in PA/EL: they stay available during partitions and trade consistency for lower latency in normal running. PC/EC is his class for systems such as VoltDB/H-Store and Megastore.

questions.t: Eric Brewer first presented CAP as a conjecture in his invited PODC talk in July 2000, and Gilbert and Lynch proved it as a theorem in 2002.
questions.f: Eric Brewer first presented CAP as a proved theorem in his invited PODC talk in July 2000, and Gilbert and Lynch disproved one case in 2002.
questions.x: Brewer's 2000 talk offered CAP as a conjecture; Gilbert and Lynch supplied the formal proof in a 2002 ACM SIGACT News note. They proved it rather than disproving any part.

questions.t: In Gilbert and Lynch's CAP proof, consistency means atomic, linearizable operations, which is narrower than the C in ACID transactions.
questions.f: In Gilbert and Lynch's CAP proof, consistency means the same thing as the C in ACID transactions, that each transaction preserves database invariants.
questions.x: Gilbert and Lynch define consistency as a single total order where each operation appears to take effect instantly, and they explicitly say this differs from ACID's consistency. Equating the two is a common confusion.

questions.t: COBIT 2019's Design Guide tailors the core model with eleven design factors, grouped as contextual, strategic and tactical.
questions.f: COBIT 2019's Design Guide tailors the core model with five design factors, grouped as contextual, strategic and tactical.
questions.x: COBIT 2019 uses eleven design factors, such as enterprise size, risk appetite and sourcing model, to rank objectives and set target capability levels. Five is too few.

questions.t: In COBIT 2019, BAI06 is the management objective for managed IT changes, sitting in the Build, Acquire and Implement domain.
questions.f: In COBIT 2019, DSS06 is the management objective for managed IT changes, sitting in the Deliver, Service and Support domain.
questions.x: Change control lives under BAI06 in the Build, Acquire and Implement domain, which is why a Salesforce CoE can map release and change processes to it. The DSS code in the false version is the wrong domain.

questions.t: COBIT 2019 replaced COBIT 5's enablers with governance components and based its performance management model on CMMI.
questions.f: COBIT 2019 kept COBIT 5's enablers unchanged and based its performance management model on ISO/IEC 15504.
questions.x: The 2019 edition swapped enablers for governance components, added design factors and focus areas, and moved its performance management model onto a CMMI basis. The false version wrongly says nothing changed.

questions.t: In the Trust Services Criteria, confidentiality covers any information an entity designates as confidential, while privacy covers only personal information.
questions.f: In the Trust Services Criteria, privacy covers any information an entity designates as confidential, while confidentiality covers only personal information.
questions.x: Confidentiality protects sensitive information of any kind that the entity commits to protect, personal or not. Privacy is narrower and applies to how personal information is collected, used, kept and disposed of.

questions.t: In the 2017 Trust Services Criteria, the CC8 series covers change management, while CC6 covers logical and physical access.
questions.f: In the 2017 Trust Services Criteria, the CC6 series covers change management, while CC8 covers logical and physical access.
questions.x: The technology-specific supplemental series are CC6 logical and physical access, CC7 system operations, CC8 change management and CC9 risk mitigation. The false version swaps CC6 and CC8.

questions.t: The Trust Services Criteria's points of focus are not a checklist: an entity need not address every one and may tailor them to its situation.
questions.f: The Trust Services Criteria's points of focus are a mandatory checklist: an entity must address every one for an auditor to issue an opinion.
questions.x: Points of focus describe important characteristics of each criterion to guide control design and evaluation. The AICPA states they are optional and can be tailored, unlike the criteria themselves.

questions.t: In Security Center, a production parent tenant can connect production or sandbox children, but a sandbox parent can connect only sandbox children.
questions.f: In Security Center, a sandbox parent tenant can connect production or sandbox children, but a production parent can connect only production children.
questions.x: Trailhead says sandbox parents are limited to sandbox children, while production parents can take either kind. That is why a production org is the usual parent for an estate-wide view.

questions.t: Security Center is free in Developer Edition orgs, while other editions need a license obtained through the Salesforce account team.
questions.f: Security Center is free in Enterprise Edition and above, while Developer Edition orgs need a license obtained through the Salesforce account team.
questions.x: Developer Edition includes Security Center at no cost, but production editions must license it. The false version reverses which editions pay.

questions.t: Security Agent in Security Center needs Security Center, Event Monitoring and an Agentforce Platform add-on, because it reads Event Monitoring logs.
questions.f: Security Agent in Security Center needs only Security Center and Security Health Check, because it reads Health Check scores rather than event logs.
questions.x: Security Agent summarizes a user's activity from login, report and API logs, which come from Event Monitoring, and it runs on Agentforce. All three licences are required.

questions.t: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks only fields in a query's SELECT and FROM clauses, so a field used only in WHERE or ORDER BY isn't evaluated.
questions.f: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED checks every field a query references, including fields used only in its WHERE and ORDER BY clauses.
questions.x: The clause enforces object and field permissions on what the query returns, meaning the SELECT and FROM parts. Filter and sort fields slip past it, one reason user mode is now preferred.

questions.t: In SOQL, WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED goes after the WHERE clause, or after FROM if there is none, and before ORDER BY, LIMIT or OFFSET.
questions.f: In SOQL, WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED goes at the very end of the query, after any ORDER BY, LIMIT or OFFSET clauses.
questions.x: The clause has a fixed position: following WHERE (or FROM) and preceding ORDER BY, LIMIT, OFFSET and aggregate clauses. Putting it last breaks the query syntax.

questions.t: Salesforce says hypercare typically lasts one to four weeks after a major launch, shorter for small changes and longer for migrations.
questions.f: Salesforce says hypercare typically lasts three to six months after a major launch, shorter for small changes and longer for migrations.
questions.x: Salesforce's guidance puts hypercare at roughly one to four weeks, adjusted for the size of the change, and suggests ending it on evidence such as stable case volumes. Months-long hypercare isn't the stated norm.

questions.t: Microsoft's implementation guidance recommends rehearsing the handover from hypercare to business-as-usual support during user acceptance testing.
questions.f: Microsoft's implementation guidance recommends rehearsing the handover from hypercare to business-as-usual support only after go-live.
questions.x: Microsoft advises starting the support transition during implementation, practising it in UAT and involving future support staff early. Leaving the rehearsal until after go-live defeats the point.

questions.t: In Salesforce's B2C Commerce project methodology, the formal handover from the build team to the customer's support team is called transition governance.
questions.f: In Salesforce's B2C Commerce project methodology, the formal handover from the build team to the customer's support team is called release governance.
questions.x: The Trailhead unit names this step transition governance: a structured transfer of knowledge, followed by documentation and access checks and a retrospective. Release governance isn't the term it uses.

questions.t: In a RACI matrix, several people can share the Responsible role for an item, but each item should have exactly one Accountable owner.
questions.f: In a RACI matrix, several people can share the Accountable role for an item, but each item should have exactly one Responsible owner.
questions.x: Responsible is the doer and can be shared; Accountable is the single owner who signs off. Two names in the A column invite disputes, which is why every source insists on one A per row.

questions.t: The RASCI variant of a RACI matrix adds Support for people who help with the work without holding formal responsibility.
questions.f: The RASCI variant of a RACI matrix adds Sponsor for the executive who funds the work without holding formal responsibility.
questions.x: The S in RASCI stands for Support, which Cornell suggests instead of piling up extra Rs. A sponsor isn't the added role.

questions.t: PMI says automation and AI agents can be Responsible for bounded tasks in a RACI, but the Accountable role and escalation must stay with a named human.
questions.f: PMI says AI agents can be Accountable for bounded tasks in a RACI, as long as a named human is listed as Responsible for escalation.
questions.x: An agent can do the work, so it can fill an R cell, but PMI keeps accountability and escalation with a person. Making the agent Accountable reverses that guidance.

questions.t: The Flow Data Table screen component can show up to 1,500 records, of which the user can select up to 200.
questions.f: The Flow Data Table screen component can show up to 1,500 records, of which the user can select up to 50.
questions.x: Salesforce Help caps the Data Table at 1,500 displayed records and 200 selected rows. Fifty understates the selection limit.

questions.t: Confirming an inline edit in a Flow Data Table doesn't save it; the changes come back in the Edited Rows output for an Update Records element.
questions.f: Confirming an inline edit in a Flow Data Table saves the record immediately, so no Update Records element is needed afterward.
questions.x: Since Spring '26 the table supports inline editing, but a confirmed edit only updates the Edited Rows collection. The flow must pass that collection to Update Records to commit it.

questions.t: With multiple selection in a Flow Data Table, the First Selected Row output holds the row the user clicked first, not necessarily the first row in the table.
questions.f: With multiple selection in a Flow Data Table, the First Selected Row output always holds the topmost selected row in table order.
questions.x: Trailhead warns that First Selected Row follows the order of the user's clicks. Selected Rows is the output that lists picks in table order.

questions.t: In Flow, the filter conditions of Update Records and Delete Records elements also use a SOQL query, just as each Get Records element does.
questions.f: In Flow, only Get Records elements use a SOQL query; the filter conditions of Update Records and Delete Records don't count as queries.
questions.x: Trailhead notes that filtering in Update Records or Delete Records requires a query, so those elements count against the 100-query limit alongside Get Records. Treating them as query-free leads to surprise limit errors.

questions.t: To check that a Get Records result isn't empty, the Is Empty operator in a Decision catches both a null value and an empty collection.
questions.f: To check that a Get Records result isn't empty, the Is Null operator in a Decision catches both a null value and an empty collection.
questions.x: The Admins guidance recommends Is Empty because it covers null and empty collections alike. Is Null misses a collection that exists but holds no records.

questions.t: In Experience Cloud screen flows, Salesforce advises against storing all fields from Get Records when the records feed screen components, as the data can show in browser developer tools.
questions.f: In Experience Cloud screen flows, Salesforce advises storing all fields from Get Records when the records feed screen components, as unused fields are stripped before reaching the browser.
questions.x: Fields loaded into records passed to screen components travel to the browser, where developer tools can reveal them. Storing only the needed fields limits that exposure; nothing strips them automatically.

questions.t: In Automation Studio, activities in the same step run together, so an activity that reads a data extension must sit in a later step than the query that fills it.
questions.f: In Automation Studio, activities in the same step run in order from top to bottom, so a query and the activity that reads its results can share one step.
questions.x: Steps run sequentially but activities inside one step run together. Putting a query and its consumer in the same step means the consumer finds no results yet.

questions.t: Trailhead states that Automation Studio SQL queries time out after 30 minutes.
questions.f: Trailhead states that Automation Studio SQL queries time out after 120 minutes.
questions.x: The documented query timeout is 30 minutes, which is one reason to limit date ranges and filter on indexed fields. Two hours isn't the stated limit.

questions.t: Click and open data in Marketing Cloud Engagement's system data views is stored in Central Standard Time, with no daylight saving adjustment.
questions.f: Click and open data in Marketing Cloud Engagement's system data views is stored in UTC, adjusted to each account's local time zone at query time.
questions.x: Data views such as _Open and _Click record times in CST year-round, ignoring daylight saving. Queries that compare times must account for that rather than assume UTC.

questions.t: Trailhead advises creating no more than three populations per Marketing Cloud Engagement account in Contact Builder, for performance reasons.
questions.f: Trailhead advises creating no more than ten populations per Marketing Cloud Engagement account in Contact Builder, for performance reasons.
questions.x: Populations are large master subsets of contacts, and Trailhead caps its recommendation at three per account to protect performance. Ten is far above that guidance.

questions.t: In Marketing Cloud Engagement, every subscriber is a contact, but a contact becomes a subscriber only after opting in to a particular channel.
questions.f: In Marketing Cloud Engagement, every contact is a subscriber, but a subscriber becomes a contact only after opting in to a particular channel.
questions.x: A contact is anyone the account messages; a subscriber is a contact who has opted in to a channel. Contacts from Sales or Service Cloud can appear in All Contacts without ever being subscribers.

questions.t: When Contact Builder deletes a contact, it is first suppressed for a configurable default of 2 days, then hard-deleted with no way to undo it.
questions.f: When Contact Builder deletes a contact, it is first suppressed for a configurable default of 30 days, during which the deletion can be undone.
questions.x: Contact Delete starts with a suppression period that defaults to two days, and the final deletion from the account and sendable data extensions is permanent. Thirty days and an undo option aren't how it works.

questions.t: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED doesn't support traversing polymorphic lookups such as What.Name, except for the Owner, CreatedBy and LastModifiedBy relationships.
questions.f: WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED doesn't support traversing polymorphic lookups such as What.Name, except for the Who, Parent and RelatedTo relationships.
questions.x: Polymorphic relationship fields are generally unsupported by the clause; the documented exceptions are Owner, CreatedBy and LastModifiedBy. Who, Parent and RelatedTo aren't on that list.

questions.t: Salesforce says core Agentforce observability, including tracing ingestion and out-of-the-box dashboard queries, is free and unmetered, while building new dashboards still consumes credits.
questions.f: Salesforce says core Agentforce observability, including tracing ingestion and out-of-the-box dashboard queries, consumes credits, while building new dashboards is free and unmetered.
questions.x: Tracing ingestion, metric aggregation and the shipped dashboards cost nothing, but new dashboards, external ingestion and new semantic objects still draw credits. The false version reverses which side is metered.

questions.t: Trailhead recommends reviewing at least 30 days of history before setting an Agentforce health alert threshold where normal variation ends.
questions.f: Trailhead recommends reviewing at least 7 days of history before setting an Agentforce health alert threshold where normal variation ends.
questions.x: The alert guidance asks for a month or more of data so the threshold sits beyond normal variation, and suggests starting with a few owned, high-value alerts. A single week is shorter than advised.

questions.t: In Agentforce observability, the thumbs-up or thumbs-down user satisfaction metric is available only for Employee Agent.
questions.f: In Agentforce observability, the thumbs-up or thumbs-down user satisfaction metric is available only for Service Agent.
questions.x: Trailhead lists user satisfaction via thumbs feedback as an Employee Agent metric. Service Agent isn't where that metric is offered.
